Parliamentary Debates
(HANSARD)
Tuesday, 8 February 2011
(Week 64, Volume 670)
Published under the authority of the House of Representatives—2011
TUESDAY, 8 FEBRUARY 2011
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16495
TUESDAY, 8 FEBRUARY 2011
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
Prayers.
DEBATE ON PRIME MINISTER’S STATEMENT

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I move, That this House express its
confidence in the National-led Governme nt and commend its programme for 2011 as
set out in the Prime Minister’s statement to Parliament . The year 2011 will be a very
important year for New Zealand. For one thing, it will be the year that New Zealand
hosts the Rugby World Cup 2011. Eighty-five thousand tourists from overseas will
enjoy the finest of New Zealand. There will be a thousand events up and down the
country, and, of course, the mighty All Bl acks will be on display on their home turf,
trying to win the Rugby World Cup in 2011.
The year 2011 is also likely to be a year in which the world grows at a faster clip
than it has done in the last 3 years. It will be a year to cement in the structural changes
that are so necessary for our economy. It will be a year in which we must continue to
move from having a debt-fue lled, consumption-based economy to having one in which
there are savings, investments, and exports. The year 2011 will be a year in which we
must continue the rebuilding of the New Zealand economy—an economy that must be
competitive. But maybe, most of all, 2011 has to be a year in which we do not write
cheques that the New Zealand taxpayer cannot a fford to cash. It is a not a year for wild
promises; it is a year for good, strong economics. There is no room for “pixienomics” in
The year 2011 will also be an important year for the families of the 29 men who lost
their lives at the Pike River mine. It is a year in which they deserve to be given answers,
and the royal commission will have good work to  do. It is a year in which we will start
in earnest on the rebuilding of Canterbury after the devastating earthquake, and we will
start the work on the 175,000 claims that have resulted from that earthquake. It is a year
in which we will tackle some very long-term problems and some long-term issues, and
in which will we turn round from the very expensive years of the previous Labour
Government. The year 2011 will be a year in which we continue to work hard for the
hard-fought gains between M āori and P ākehā. It is a year in which there needs to be
hope and promise and aspiration. The year 2011 needs to be New Zealand’s year.
There are some very positive signs. The global economy is starting to look much
stronger, and we are seeing higher commodity prices: the Fonterra auction was up by 7
percent just last week, lamb prices are star ting to rise, and wool prices are starting to
rise. Of course, the Rugby World Cup is likely to have a big impact on the economy,
and we will have the stimulus impact from  the earthquake rebuild ing work. That may
well be the case, but we also n eed to lock in the trends that  we have seen in the last 2
years of the National Government. Despite the fact that we inheri ted books that were a
complete mess and despite the fact that we  had to contend with  the worst recession
since the Great Depression, in th e 2 years that our Government  has been in office after-
tax wages have risen by 16 percent, while co sts rose by 6 percent. That is a 10 percent
net gain in 2 years. I am ashamed to even  talk about Labour’s record, which was a
miserable 4 percent gain over 9 long years.
There are risks, of course, to the global economy. We have seen that in recent weeks,
with the risk that there will be a great period of unsettledness in the Middle East. There
are also risks, of course, in China if ther e is an asset bubble. There are risks around the
global capital markets. We saw that last year with regard to Portugal, Greece, Spain, and
Ireland. There is the risk that our exchange rate will continue to rise against a very weak
16496 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
US economy. There is the risk—although on e would not know it was there, from
listening to the Opposition—tha t comes from a rating agency like Standard and Poor’s,
which has put New Zealand on negative outlook.  So the situation could be patchy, and
there could be periods when it is a case of one step forward and half a step back, but
overall this economy has to change from being one based on consumption and property
to being one based on savings and exports.
One of the first things the Government wi ll continue to work  on is getting its books
back in order. Over the last 5 years of the previous Labour Government, spending
increased by an average of $2.8 billion a year in every si ngle year. My Government has
managed to pull that back to $1.1 billion a ye ar in the last 2 years. In Budget 2011 that
increase is likely to be $800 million. The me ssage is pretty simple: we are going to
spend less, we are going to borrow less, and we are going to take the pressure off the
Reserve Bank and off New Zealand interest rate s. Any political part y that has not even
got out of January before promising $5 bil lion worth of more expenditure, and that
thinks this might help the New Zealand taxp ayer, is completely wrong. We have to get
our books back in order. We cannot afford the decade of deficits that we inherited from
the previous Labour Government.
One of the places where we will be starting is  in relation to the Public Service. New
Zealanders deserve to have be tter value and better service. We have started to work on
that. In the 2 years that we have been in office we have reduced fulltime-equivalent staff
in the State sector by 5 per cent. We have started the pr ocess of merging Government
departments: Archives New Z ealand and the National Librar y have been merged into
the Department of Internal Affairs, a nd the Ministry of Research, Science and
Technology and the Foundation for Resear ch, Science and Technology have been
merged into one new Ministry of Science and Innovation. But we have a long way to
go. There are 80 Crown entities, all with their own boards; 38 Government departments;
70 portfolios; and 60 separate Budget votes. We are, by international comparison,
bloated and inefficient. So there has to be  change. We have put together a group of
officials, asking for advice on how we can stre amline the Public Service. There will be
core principles, and they are simple: we n eed to ensure that, in costing less, we
ultimately deliver more to the taxpayers of  New Zealand. So a big focus of attention
will be around the State sector.
The second thing we need to do is to move towards having greater savings and
investment. We cannot, as a country, continue to  have external liabi lities that are at 85
percent of GDP. We cannot be in the same company as Portugal, Greece, Spain, and
Ireland, and, if we are, we will know what that picture looks like. We are prepared to be
responsible economic managers; the Labour Opposition, quite simply, is not. For that
reason we will be looking at not only the operating budget but also the capital budget.
Late last year we recognised that New Zeal and taxpayers have about $220 billion worth
of assets. As a Government we want to ac quire $33 billion worth of new assets over the
next 5 years. We have a number of options . One is to borrow more. That will not be
acceptable to the rating agencies. The second op tion is to not build that infrastructure.
That will not deliver us the jobs and the economy we want. The third option is to release
some capital from assets that we already ow n. Through the course of this year we will
be finalising our policy on mi xed-ownership models whereby we will be looking to
control 51 percent of Meridi an Energy, Mighty River Po wer, Genesis, and Solid
Energy.
Let us understand the tests in those models. The first test is that the Crown will
always, as a minimum, retain 51 percent contro l. The second thing is that we will be
asking Treasury to provide advice to us on how  we can ensure Kiwi mums and dads are
at the top of the list for buying any of the equity that we release, and that includes the
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16497
$1.6 million KiwiSaver accounts. It is interestin g that we as a Government want those
$1.6 million KiwiSaver accounts and New Zealande rs to invest in our economy and in
our future, and Labour wants them to invest in Australia. That is what Labour wants;
Labour does not want to let them invest in New Zealand. We will ensure that the Crown
financial institutes, the Accident Comp ensation Corporation, and the New Zealand
Superannuation Fund invest in those kinds of assets, along with iwi.
So Budget 2011 will have a focus on savings and investment, and it will take on
board the information that we have received from the Savings Working Group. Again,
the message is very simple: we need to ow n more of our own future, we need to fund
more of our own upsides, and we need to have a stronger economy. Although the
members on the Labour benches cannot add, th e issue is quite simple. When we own
$220 billion of assets, we maybe release $8 bi llion to $10 billion of capital, and we buy
another $33 billion of assets, we will end up owning more assets over 5 years, not
fewer.
The economy has to change and become a more export-led economy. We have to get
away from the position we inherited from Labour, which was quite simple. It was a
world where we bought more from the rest of the world than we sold to it. It was a
world where, in 9 years, Labour created no new jobs in the export sector.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Oh, rubbish!

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It is not rubbish, actually. It was the period when Labour spent
so wildly that interest rate s rose and the exchange rate rose. Maybe overall the way to
test Labour’s commitment to exports is qui te simple: turn back the clock to 2007, and
look at exports under Labour in that year. Labour did about 10 th ings, and do members
know what happened? Exports fe ll in 2007. Why did exports fa ll? It was because in the
end, if we want to have a competitive econom y we have to allow it the freedom to be
competitive. We have to reform the Resource Management Act, we have to have a
flexible labour market, and we have to be pr epared to build the infrastructure and invest
in science and innovation.
This year the Government will be focusing its attention on extending the free-trade
agreements that we have been working so hard on. At the top of the list, of course, is the
Trans-Pacific Partnership, which is an opportunity for New Zealand to have a free-trade
agreement with the United States. We will al so be looking to make further progress on
our free-trade negotiations with Korea and on an exciting opportunity that is presenting
itself in Russia.
The next area in which the Government will be spending and doing some more work
is infrastructure. This year we will begin the roll-out of the $1.5 bi llion Government
investment in ultra-fast broadband—not ju st in urban communities, but in rural
communities right across the country. We will be building more roads, including the
seven roads that we have prioritised as road s of national significance. That will include
the Waterview Connection, which is the largest roading project to be undertaken in New
Zealand. There will be more investment in p ublic transport, in roads, and in rail,
particularly in Auckland and Wellington, and the rebuild of KiwiRail and the KiwiRail
Turnaround Plan will continue.
In the end, though, th e challenge for the Government  is to continue to build
confidence in the business sector, so that it will grow, invest, and prosper. Maybe in the
end that is the single bigge st difference between the Na tional Government and the
Labour Opposition. We trust the private sector to create jobs. We do not think the only
place where we should create jobs is in the core bureaucracy. We back New Zealanders
to back themselves in order to invest and to employ other Kiwis. We will do all of this
for a reason: we will build a strong economy so that we can build better outcomes, with
better value for money and better services.
16498 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
One area where we will be undertaking significant work is that of welfare reform. I
say that one should judge a society by how it looks after the sick and the vulnerable, but
one should also judge a societ y by how many sick and vulne rable people it creates. The
Labour members do not want to talk about th eir record when it comes to the sick and
the vulnerable, because this is what they di d in 9 years: they increased the number of
people on the sickness benefit and the invalids be nefit by 50 percent. That is what they
did. There was no mutual obligation whereby ta xpayers agreed to look after others who
were down on their luck, and there was no attempt to take the 200,000 children who are
currently trapped in welfare-based homes a nd give them a better future. There is a
simple message from the National Governme nt: if one can work, one should work. But
that does not mean that we will necessarily cut costs on day one; we have to tackle the
difficult issues of childcare, of increasing sk ills, and of making su re the required jobs
are there.
The year 2011 will also be a year in which we will focus on vulnerable children.
There will be specific legislative changes to  support children who are in State care.
There will be legislation that  will protect children from abuse. There will be tougher
penalties for those people who fail to protect ch ildren at risk, particularly in relation to
those children who face death, serious injury, or sexual assault.
There will be more progress made on Wh ānau Ora and on housing. Our yardstick
will be how many people we can get into housi ng that they can afford; it will not be a
yardstick of how many State houses we own. From 1 July 2011 reviewable tenancies for
all new State house tenants will be a feature of our programme.
In education we will continue to make gains. This year we will spend $1.4 billion in
early childhood education, which is up from $400 million a decade ago. The interesting
thing is that under the previous Labour Government’s policy, it increased the spending
on early childhood education—we all accept that—but there was no significant change
in the number of children who were being educated, and there was nothing for those in
the poorest communities. Those kids deserve to  have better outcomes. This will be year
2 of national standards. We will continue  to demand that every young New Zealander
leaves school with the ability to read and write properly. The future of those students in
secondary schools will be enhanced by our eight trade academies. We will harvest the
fruits of the 16,500 additional places in tertiary education.
In health, the message is pretty simple: less bureaucracy; more front-line services.
No longer do we have 81 primary health organisations; we have 46. No longer do we
have the bloated numbers in the Ministry of Health or in district health boards. There
will be less bureaucracy. The results that we w ill achieve will continue to go in the way
they have done, with an increase in el ective surgery. Four hundred more people per
week will be seen for elective surgery—20,000 people a year.
The Government will retain its focus on law and order, on the police, and on the
courts, and on making the system more efficient. We will continue to be tough on gangs
and tough on hardened criminals, and to make sure that we have a focus on P.

items.speaker: Let me finish with this
items.text: 2011 will be a big y ear. It will be the time when we work on
reshaping the economy, on delivering better services, and on delivering better outcomes.
At the end of the year we will go to the polls and put ourselves up against the Labour
Opposition, which has learnt absolutely nothing in 9 years. It has not recognised that the
world has changed its shape in one way or th e other. Labour is an Opposition that is in
denial. We are the economic managers who are responsible and careful, and who have a
plan for the future. The Opposition wants futu re generations to pay for more and more
debt. In the end, when one is Phil Goff and one is not prepared to rule out anybody,
what is the message? It is that one is so desperate for power that one does not care what
one has to promise, with whom one has to get into bed, and what  one needs to do. We
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16499
will be the Government of responsible ec onomic management. Labour will be, as John
Roughan described it recently, the “coalition of losers”.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: In my time I have sat through a few
Prime Ministers’ speeches on their statements, but that would be the worst. That would
be the worst. That was a do-nothing speech fr om a do-nothing Government that has sat
on the sidelines while New Zealand has gone  backwards. Do members know that the
Prime Minister’s big claim to  fame was when he began that speech? It was the Rugby
World Cup 2011—all his own work! Helen Clar k and Trevor Mallard got the Rugby
World Cup for New Zealand. We will win that cup—and Labour was responsible for
getting it.
I remember when, a year ago, the Prime Minister came into the House for the same
occasion. He promised us something. He  said that New Zealand would come
aggressively out of recession—aggressively out of recession. I was watching the Prime
Minister on television yesterday morning. Do members know what he said? He said that
he could not rule out that New Zealand wa s slipping back into recession. Mr Key and
his Government have been in office for 2¼ years, and Mr Key and his Government are
responsible for this country going backwards. He came up with all sorts of figures. They
say there are lies, damn lies, and statistics. Let us have a look at them.
The Prime Minister said that the rate of  participation in ea rly childhood education
under Labour had hardly moved forward. Well, in due course I will seek to table the
document I am holding. It shows that the ra te of Pasifika participation in early
childhood education went up nearly 10 percent. During the last  few months I have been
going around the early childhood centres for our M āori, Pasifika, and P ākehā kids, and
people there are saying that Mr Key’s Gove rnment is forcing up costs while dropping
the quality. In the last week mums and dads were paying $25 a week more for their little
ones to have quality early childhood education— and that is Mr Key’s work. Every year
under Labour participation went up.
Mr Key tried to tell us that everyone was better off. The figures on wages came out
last week. There was a 1.7 percent increase in wages in the last calendar year, 2010. The
figures on inflation came out before that, and they show a 4 percent increase in prices
last year. What is it that the Prime Mini ster does not understand about the fact that
prices went up at twice the ra te of wages last year? Then he came out yesterday with a
big increase for people on the minimum wage —the vulnerable, he said. He said he
would stand up for the vulnerable. Do me mbers know what he gave the vulnerable
yesterday? He gave them  25c an hour—25c an hour from the man who took $1,000 a
week from his own tax cuts. He says he sta nds up for the vulnerable, and he gave them
25c an hour.
I wonder about those vulnerable people in  McGehan Close and the vulnerable little
girl whom he exploited by taking her up to Waitangi. Where is she, where is her family,
and why did Mr Key not front up on television on Friday night to explain to the people
of McGehan Close why their power prices we re up, why their petrol prices were up,
why their food prices were up, and why they we re worse off? He would not front up to
answer their challenges. He exploited the little girl for Waitangi Day 3 years ago but he
will not front up, just as he did not front up to  the Pike River families and give them the
news that he was not going to see the recovery of the bodies. That is what the families
told me. They said the Government would spend $400,000 on Television New Zealand
so it could cover the great man’s speech but that when the hard decisions had to be
made, no one from the Government was to be  seen. Those decisions  were passed off to
the coal company, to the receivers of the company, and to the police—
Hon Gerry Brow
nlee: Making it up again.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: —and Mr Brownlee knows it.
16500 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
The economy of New Zealand has stalled. Un employment figures, I say to Mr Key,
are up 8,000. Mr Key and Ms Bennett told us th at they had peaked a year ago, but they
were up 8,000. Seven hundred New Zealande rs—700 Kiwi breadwinners—joined the
unemployment scrap heap each week over the last 3 months. What does Mr Key say?
He said they were old figures. I say to Mr Ke y that they were the latest figures to 31
December 2010. Then he said it was just a survey. Well, New Zealand has relied on that
survey for 25 years as the most accurate por trayal of what is happening in terms of
unemployment.
Let us look at those figures. He talks about  the weak and the vulnerable. I ask Mr
Key why it is satisfactory that one school-leaver in four goes out of school and on to the
unemployment scrap heap—one school-leaver in  four. The Prime Minister talks about
the vulnerable, but what about teenage M āori girls? One in two goes out of school and
on to the unemployment scrap heap. What about the Youth Guarantee? What was the
Youth Guarantee about? Our young people should be either learning or earning, I say to
Mr Key. One in four of them should not be going on to the unemployment scrap heap.
I listened to the stuff about welfare refo rm; Mr Key wants them to work. Mr Key
should look at the front page of the Waikato Times from Saturday. The headline states:
“Where are the jobs?”. I believe in welfare reform, I say to Mr Key. The best type of
welfare reform is to have jobs that pe ople can go to. He is chasing around after the
people whom he and his Minister for Soci al Development and Employment would like
to call bludgers, but what about Petarina Slat er? She is on the front page of that paper.
She has had 150 job interviews, and she has been turned down every time. People in my
electorate understand th at. There were 150 jobs available in a supermarket, with 2,500
people chasing them.
I want to know why Austra lia could create 1,000 jobs a day last year when New
Zealand went backwards. Was it not the boas t of the Prime Minister that we would
catch up with Australia? Was that not th e boast of the Prime Minister? The Prime

items.speaker: Minister will say
items.text: “But they have minera ls.” Mr Key knows that our dairy prices, our
lamb prices, our beef prices, our forestry pr ices, and our wool prices have never been
higher than they are today. That money is rolling into New Zealand, but where is the
plan for employment? We have had enough of the gimmicks: the Job Summit and the
cycleway. In the last quarter 7,000 or 8,000 people joined the unemployment queues,
and Mr Key’s cycleway created 200 jobs—200 jobs.
We want a plan from this Government that would see people back at work. Why
does the Government not listen to Sir Paul Callaghan, New Zealander of the Year? Paul
stood up and asked why, with our “clean, gr een” brand for New Zealand, we would
follow a plan to mine our national parks. Why did National waste 2 years on a plan that
would have destroyed and undermined our im age when it should have been talking
about using brain power—high-skill, high-tech, and high-wage?
I say to Mr Key that I go to the cleantech industries, and they ask what this
Government is doing. It is the fastest-growing area in the world.
PricewaterhouseCoopers says we  could earn at least $8 bil lion a year from cleantech.
And what is this Government doing? In 2 years it has set up a committee. It is a little bit
like savings, is it not? We know we need to  save in order to invest in our future.
National had 9 years in Opposition to work ou t a plan for saving. It has had 2 years in
Government. After 9 years in Opposition and 2 years in Government, it has set up a
committee. It is not good enough, I say to Mr  Key. It is not g ood enough by a long run
to have 158,000 of our fellow New Zealanders out  of work. There is no plan from the
Government to do anything about it.
Then there is the question of prices a nd wages. How can people possibly be better
off, I ask Mr Key, when prices have gone  up by 4 percent and wages have gone up by
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16501
1.7 percent? Mr Key said in his speech th at incomes had gone up. Well, I listened to
Statistics New Zealand representatives, and wh at did they say? They said that median
income fell last year. Median income fell la st year, I tell Mr Key. New Zealanders are
not better off. The Government has ignored the middle-income earners of New Zealand.
At best, middle-income earners stood still. Most of them went backwards.
The Government has forced low-income  people below the poverty line. The only
people who benefited from the National G overnment’s tax swindle were the top 10
percent, who got most of th e money. That is the truth. [ Interruption] That is the truth
and Mr Key knows it. The people who go through the supermarket checkouts know it,
and they will not listen to the National Gove rnment’s spin on this issue. They know
when they are not better off because of the policies of this Government.
Mr Key talked about the block of chees e. Do members remember the block of
cheese? I ask Mr Key how much that costs now. Does the Prime Minister have any
idea?

items.speaker: Rt Hon John Key
items.text: Less.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: “Less.”, he said. It has gone up 20 percent in the last year—20
percent in the last year. What about food prices? They have gone up 5 percent in the last
year. What about power prices? I have constitu ents who have come to me and said they
have had two letters from their power compa ny in the last 4 months: one on 1 October,
when Mr Key’s Government pushed up the price with GST and the emissions trading
scheme, and another one last week to say that the power prices are going up again.
The great plan of the Govern ment to solve our problems  is to slash spending on
health and education, and to  sell off our assets. I wonde r what the private sector
investors will do when they have bought up our power companies. [ Interruption] The
National members say they are going to the mums and dads. What about the mums and
dads who cannot put money together to save because of the rising cost of living? They
will lose ownership of our assets. They will gain nothing.
Do members know what happened to the Contact Energy shares that National
promised for the mums and dads? Those shares  went to the big corporates. They have
ended up with the big corporates. And not only that, I tell Mr Key, they have ended up
in the hands of foreigners. Most of the $1.5 billion in dividends from Contact Energy
does not go back to New Zealanders who on ce owned it; it goes overseas. That money
is going overseas. It makes our country worse off.
Recently I read a newspaper article by an economist. He was asking where Mr Key is
at in thinking it makes sense to sell the asse ts. Where is he at? The economist says we
pay 5.5 percent on the debt and we get a 7.3 percent return on the investment. How does
it make business sense to sell off our assets? What is the Prime Minister’s next trick
when he has sold them? And he can sell them only once, and we will not get them back.
Oh, hang on! We might get them back. I recall being a member of a Labour
Government that had to buy back Air New Zealand and New Zealand Rail. Do members
remember the National members talking about selling Air New Zealand, and the private
sector—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Power
items.text: You sold Air New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Yes, but we learnt. We learnt, but this National Government has
learnt nothing. Labour did not sell a single asset in  the fifth Labour Government. For 9
years we did not sell those assets. We ha d to buy them back. When National sold New
Zealand Rail to Mr Fay and Mr Richwhite, they asset stripped it. They ran it into the
ground. It was sold at bargain-basement prices by a National Government, and we had
to buy it back. I say to this Government: “Go to the electorate in November this year
and talk about selling assets—because you will listen to what New Zealanders are
saying.”
16502 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
Last week Mr Key arrogantly said that he did not care what New Zealanders thought.
Is that not what the member said?

items.speaker: Rt Hon John Key
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Well, maybe we will table the transcript. He said that he did not
care what New Zealanders thought. But New Zealanders care deeply about a
Government selling assets that New Zealanders own. They care about the assets and the
benefits that come back to us. Then th ere was that other issue: farmland. I heard
something that Mr Key said that I agreed with.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: What?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Well, that is not totally surprising. He said that New Zealanders
should not be tenants in their own land. I wonder why German interests bought up, in
the last couple of weeks, $100 million worth of dairy farms—more than that country
had spent in the 5 years previously. We ar e losing those assets. I wonder whether the
National Government will stop the Chines e consortium from buying up the Crafar
farms. I wonder whether it will do that.
I say to Mr Key that yest erday I went to Rotorua and met with a big forestry
company. Does he know what they said to m e? They said that what they were really
worried about was whether the American inte rests that own the cutting rights to the
forests would think it was more  profitable to sell the logs  overseas, without processing
them in New Zealand, rather than keep th e 290 jobs that the company provides for
people in Rotorua. That is what New Z ealand enterprise is worried about. This
Government has mouthed the words and the rh etoric but it has done  nothing about the
sell-off of New Zealand to overseas interests.
This Government has failed. It has failed to create growth, it has failed to bring
unemployment down, it has failed to  keep people’s incomes ahead of the cost of living,
and it has failed to make New Zealand a more  equal and a fairer place. For 9 years a
Labour Government reversed the trend to a more unequal country, and we treated New
Zealanders inclusively. We brought in the Working for Families package, and there
were decent rises in the minimum wage. But Mr Key has turned the clock back to make
this country less fair, less equal, with fe wer opportunities for every New Zealander to
make the most of what he or she can contribute to this country.
After 2¼ years, this is Mr  Key’s responsibility, and th is election will be about
restoring to New Zealanders a fair go, making sure that people pay a fair share and get a
fair share in return, and making sure we do not attack the vulnerable—our children at
early childhood education, whos e parents are paying higher fees; adults who want
second-chance education in ad ult and community education; and the old people from
whom Mr Key has taken the home care that enabled them to live in dignity in their own
homes. There will be a Labour-led Governme nt and we will return fairness to New
Zealand. We will return growth, living standards, and jobs to this country.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: I am here for my father. I am here for my
father and for the many thousands of New Z ealanders just like him. My father was an
ordinary guy from Palmerston North who just wanted to have an ordinary life. He
wanted a decent job, a decent take-home pay, and he wanted a secure home where he
could raise his family. What he got was a lifetime of hardship, and he died of a stroke at
age 48—at just a handful of years older than I am now. I dream of a world in which my
dad is still alive. What would have give n my father a better chance at a long and
satisfying life? What would have made his story more like mine?
Like my dad, I did not do too well at school; I left school at 16 with no qualifications
and few prospects. I worked here and there. I spent time on the dole. After a few years, I
found myself as a solo parent on the domestic  purposes benefit. I had the good luck to
go to university and I got m
y law degree. I used the training incentive allowance to help
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16503
with my study costs. I shared childcare with  family and friends. I sometimes had to use
the special-needs grant—do members remember that—to pay my power bill and to buy
food when things got really tough. I got suppor t when I needed it. My dad did not, so I
am here for my father.
I want every man, woman, and child in th is country to have the chance of a good,
ordinary life. We can do so much more to help New Zealanders just like my dad. We
can build a fairer society, an equal society that does not require the sacrifice of our
people, or the sacrifice of our environment, to an economic dead end.
The Green Party is known as a champion fo r the environment. We love our country,
and we want to protect it. We are passiona te about protecting our rivers, our land, our
forests, and our oceans, but we also want to look after all New Zealanders, and today
that is my focus. How do we mind the gap between the haves and the have-nots? What
can we do about inequality in Aotearoa New Zealand? The first thing we can do is make
sure that everyone gets a fair go at decent work with a living wage. My dad was a
labourer all his life. He worked on farms and in orchards, he shot deer, and he worked in
a bread factory, but in the 1980s the work dried up. There were 300,000 people
unemployed, just like him. As time went on, it became harder and harder for a 40-year-
old, working-class M āori man to find work. Poverty t ook everything from my dad,
including his home.
Here we are, just a couple of decad es later, with 156,000 New Zealanders
unemployed, 100,000 New Zealanders unde remployed, and 180,000 New Zealanders
working at or near the minimum wage. Th e economic reforms of  the 1980s failed my
dad, and those same ideas, those same plans, are now failing our children and
grandchildren. We have hundreds of thousa nds of New Zealanders struggling to
survive, just like my father did.
Wage growth has kept up w ith the rising cost of liv ing—John Key talked about
that—but that is good news only for those who still have their jobs. J ohn Key’s talk
simply hides what is actually happening to families today: his Government is not
protecting families from the rising cost of living.
Unemployment has increased by 50 percent si nce John Key took office—in just a
few short years. Families affected by unemployment are falling behind at the fastest
rate, unable to find jobs while having to meet the rising cost of fuel and food. The
Government’s answer to job losses in the pr ivate sector has been to cut jobs in the
public sector. That is the extent of John Key’s Government’s jobs plan. The Prime
Minister took great pride in pointing out today that his Government has reduced the
number of full-time staff positions in core G overnment administrations by 5 percent. In
reality, many of the workers whom John Key bo asts about sacking will be driven to the
wall. That will mean less spending and it will mean more job losses, and John Key
boasts about those job losses.

items.speaker: Hon Tariana Turia
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My apologies to the
member for cutting in on her speech, but there is somebody up behind us who is
constantly shouting things a nd making it very difficult for us to hear. We do want to
listen to this speech.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I appreciate the honourable member’s point. In fact, I particularly
ask members on the Government benches to pl ease show a little more courtesy to the
House. There are so many conversations going on, including one right now on my right.
The member is clearly taking no notice of what the Speaker is saying, whatsoever. I ask
the Government whip to make sure members stop the endless, quite loud conversations.
To the person interjecting regularly down the back, please show the House some
courtesy. When members are listening and inte rjecting, that is one th ing, but when they
16504 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
are just carrying on loud private discussions , it is discourteous. I apologise to the
honourable member.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Thank you Mr Speaker. T ēnā koe e te whaea. John Key is
boasting about job cuts. Our minimum wage in  this country is so low that Kiwis who
work full-time still need top-ups from the G overnment just to cover the basics—food
and rent. The current take-home pay for a 40-hour-a-week job on the minimum wage is
$409 a week, and in April it will go up by about $28. Meanwhile, the average rent in
Auckland is $416. One simply cannot suppor t a family on 400-odd bucks a week—one
cannot. The minimum wage must go up to $ 15 an hour as soon as possible. The
minimum wage must go up immediately to help the poorest and most vulnerable
families in our community. We know that  lifting the minimum wage is good for the
economy. There is an increased demand for goods and services, because people on low
incomes spend most of their money. We know that lifting the minimum wage would
also save the Government money. It would save a billion dollars in the Government’s
social assistance budget. But instead of saving this money, we are subsidising
employers who pay low wages. Their workers will put in 40 hours a week, but they will
still need help to pay the rent and put food on the table. Businesses who employ the
most low-wage workers are big corporates: supermarkets such as New World, and fast
food outlets such as Burger King. Last year Foodstuffs supermarket companies made
$16 million in profit while their minimum wage workers continued to struggle.
My dad was a kind man, he was a decent ma n, and he was a peaceful man whether
he was in work or out, just like the thousands of New Zeal anders who now find
themselves out of work. John Key’s Govern ment suggests those pe ople are bludgers,
but New Zealanders use support when they need it and they move on when they can.
That is what I did, that is what my dad trie d to do, and that is what thousands of New
Zealanders are doing today. A bout three-quarters of those people on the dole are on it
for less than a year.
John Key has outlined major reforms to welf are that will severe ly hurt families and
children. I want to describe what that means in a real life. If John Key’s reforms were in
place when I had become a solo mum, I w ould have been forced to work in an
unskilled, low-paid job instead of being able to care for my daughter. Because I had no
school qualifications, John Key would have cons idered me unsuited to university, and I
would probably never have been  able to go to university, let alone go to law school.
Even if I had made it as far as the university door, with no training incentive allowance I
simply could not have made ends meet while I studied. That is the ladder of opportunity
that Paula Bennett kicked out from behind he r. That is the ladde r of opportunity that
John Key would have taken from me and my  dad’s first moko. Our vulnerable families
are not the enemy, I say to Mr Key. They ar e families just like mine, and they are
families just like yours.
Since the Green Party arrived in Parliament we have said that benefits must go up,
and we are firmly opposed to the benefit cuts  that are signalled by the Prime Minister
today. Instead of suggesting that we need to punish the victim s of the recession and
punish the victims of poverty, let us talk about how we can help them.
John Key talks about the importance of early childhood education, but his cuts in that
sector have already seen parents pulling th eir kids out of early  childhood education
because they cannot afford the increased fees. There is no better investment in our
fa
milies and our children than in early ch ildhood education. For every single dollar that
we spend—every dollar—in early childhood ed ucation, we save up to $17 in health
costs, justice costs, and other social costs. That is a better return than a hundred roads of
national significance.
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16505
John Key talks of the 220,000 children who are dependent on benefits as if that is
their own fault and as if they  are to blame. We can help  by extending to those families
the Working for Families support to help th em pay rent and power bills and pay for
food and warm clothes. Instead we are star ing down the barrel of changes to welfare
that will widen the gap between those who have the most and those who need the most.
We will pay for John Key’s mistake in hospital bills, in new prisons, and in future
welfare payments. We will pay for John Key’s mistake in the lives we will lose to
poverty.
Growing up, one of the challenges that my  parents faced was finding us a decent
place to live. When my parent s went out looking for a house to rent, they would always
send my mother. My mother is Pākehā. If my father went with her, we would not get the
house, because he was M āori. One time when we were very small, my mother had
managed to find us a good house. But over the next few days, the landlord came to visit
and he met my dad, and within  the week we had an evic tion notice. We moved from
that house into our car. We lived in our ca r for a period until we could find another
home. We moved out into a house in the count ry. My family lived in a lot of country
houses because my Dad could work on the surrounding farms and those houses were
very cheap.
Housing remains a critical problem in this country. We have more than 10,000
families on the waiting list for a State home. We have exceptionally high rents. We have
poor-quality rental properties. We have severe overcrowding. We have Third World
rates of rheumatic fever that come from that  overcrowding and cost  our health system
some $10 million a year. Poor housing costs lives—the lives of men and women in their
prime. The Green Party has long said that a comprehensive State house building
programme to increase the stock of State houses by 6,000 over 3 years is the right thing
to do. This building programme not only w ould provide homes for our families but
would create some 28,000 jobs. This buildi ng programme would help New Zealanders
who need a home, help New Zealanders w ho need a job, and help our struggling
construction industry.
I tell members that my dad would have l oved a job like that—a job where he was
building homes for the people and the communities he cared most about. But last year
John Key cut the State house building budge t by $100 million. What we have heard
from the Prime Minister today suggests that he does not care enough about the 20,000
New Zealand families with chronic housing pr oblems to bother to solve the problem.
John Key aims to shuffle existing housing stock around and to push people out of their
homes through the reviewable tenancies process. That will do nothing for the problem.
There are not enough homes for the families who need them.
This Government’s lack of compassion and absence of solutions for our families is
gutting. We can be a better c ountry than this. There are other choices that we can make.
We can help our families.
One of those areas where we can help is with power bills. It is no t just rent or food
that is the problem but power bills, too. One way to do that is with progressive pricing,
which would lock in a low electricity price for every household up to a certain threshold
of around 4,000 kilowatt hours a year. In many  homes, that would be enough to keep
people warm and dry at an affordable price. In New Zealand we are unique in that we
still own the majority of our electricity generation assets, the big renewable projects that
our grandparents built. We ha ve the ability to look at pr ogressive pricing schemes,
which would help our most vulnerable fam ilies stay healthy and warm. Ensuring fair
power prices for families is just one of the reasons we must maintain full public
ownership of our power com
panies. Selling our power companies, as National is
16506 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
promising to do, will make it harder to achie ve cheaper and sustainable power for those
who need it the most.
MMP is also part of the solution. I know that my being in Parliament would have
blown my dad’s mind—he did not live to see it. No one in this place ever talked about
the reality of his life. No one in this place ever saw him as a person to whom they were
responsible. No one in this place bothere d to reflect that their decisions would
determine the course of his life. That was until MMP allowed people like him to be here
and to speak on his behalf. So in this year’s referendum I am voting to keep MMP and
to improve it.
The gap between rich and poor grew very ra pidly here in Aotearoa between the mid-
1980s and 2000. Real incomes for lower and middle income families fell while the
income of wealthy households soared. Work  dried up for my dad in the mid-1980s; he
died in 1995. When my dad had a stroke, he could not even get decent help from the
hospital. He was disbelieved, he was discounte d, and he was even dropped on the floor.
This was not intentional mistreatment; it was just the same casual disregard that dogged
my dad for his whole life. At th e hospital in those last hours of his life, he really needed
to be treated with some dignity, just as he  deserved to be trea ted with dignity and
respect throughout his whole working life as he  sought to take care of his family. My
dad was sacrificed to dead-end economic ideas. He did not live to see the shift to smart
green economics. I wish he had, because smart green economics does not demand the
sacrifice of our environment, smart green economics does not demand the sacrifice of
our people, and it would not have demanded his.
Our Government plays a key role in shaping a fair society. This Parliament can help
to guarantee the essentials and make sure that every New Zealand person—man,
woman, and child—gets a fair go and a bit of respect. So I am here for my father,
Richard Ropata Eruera Turei, and I am here  for the many thousands of New Zealanders
just like my dad. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon RODNEY HIDE
items.text: I wish everyone in the House a happy New
Year. First of all, I expre ss ACT’s support for the John Key - led Government and the
Māori Party’s role in Government. I say, further, that like the great many New
Zealanders in this great country of ours we think that we are very lucky to have John
Key as Prime Minister at this time.
Why is that? It is because John Key knows a simple thing. He knows that a country,
like a family and like a business, cannot spend a dollar until it has ea rned a dollar. That
is precisely the situation that New Zealand confronts. It is also the case that, unlike
many politicians, John Key has some real-world  experience in the area of business and
making a dollar. I say that we are lucky at this  time to have the Prime Minister that we
have. Before the previous election the ACT Party promised the people of New Zealand
that we would support National, and we made  that promise again on election night. The
ACT Party has been true to its word.
But there is a lot more that we have to  do, as a country and as a Government. We
have to work much harder to get jobs for our young people in this country, and to
provide them with opportunities. We have to do much more to lift wages in this country,
so that we can enjoy the standard of living that we aspire to. It is especially important to
point this out, with an election coming up.
It is also ACT’s role to te ll it like it is. I know that Labou r members want to live in
fairyland, but let me make this point. The count ry is broke; there is no other way to say
it. The Government is borrowing $300 million a week. Let me explain what that means.
It means $200 a week for every household in New Zealand. For every family in New
Zealand, the Government alone is borrowing $2 00 a week. Debt is set to triple in the
next 5 years.
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16507
What is Mr Goff’s solution? It is to spend more. Mr Goff needs to give—and he
owes—an explanation to the people of New Zealand, and indeed to the Labour Party,
about where the money is coming from. If we want to see what can happen in New
Zealand if we do not reverse that borrowi ng, we can just look at the economic and
social chaos in Ireland, in Italy, in Greece, and in Spain.
It is also ACT’s role to be part of the solution in terms of addressing this nation’s
problems, and that means working with the National-led Government. I am proud to say
that under MMP we have a Prime Minister who has had the confidence, in election year,
to set the election date already, at 26 November. That shows the trust and stability that
John Key has in the support parties. He know s that we can continue to deliver good
centre-right policies.
It is also the ACT Party’s job to be bo ld, to be courageous , to nudge National along
towards doing the right thing, and to stick to its principles. We support the mixed-
ownership model that National has a nnounced, but it is not enough. We cannot
indefinitely sell assets and hope to cure  our problem of borrowing $300 million a week.
Like a household, like a business, and like a family, we have to get spending under
control. That is why the ACT Party will be  bringing to Parliament measures to get
spending under control this year and to take  the squeeze off families and off businesses.
The ACT Party believes that the Government  has to live within a budget, just as
everyone else in New Zealand has to.
We need to do so much better for business in this country. Business is being
squeezed. Business is where the jobs come from, where the wealth comes from, and
where the wages come from, but businesses ar e being squeezed by re d tape, high taxes,
and Government debt. What is the ACT Part y doing? ACT is bringing to the House the
Regulatory Reform Bill, which will update 13 separate Acts in order to reduce
compliance costs, and the Regulatory Reform  (Repeals) Bill, which will eliminate 31
Acts and will include an executive order to eliminate 206 redundant regulations.
All that is good, but it is not enough. We n eed to do much, much more. That is why
the ACT Party has been work ing with National and the M āori Party on a Regulatory
Responsibility Bill to set a higher standard for ourselves, in terms of bringing ever more
legislation to this Parliament.
I think it is important that we do much, much better on the economic front. I think it
is important that the Government gets its spending under control. But for the future we
all have to do much better for education. Recently I was at a function where the Prime
Minister announced a sta tistic that was truly ho rrific. It was so horri fic that I had to get
it checked, and I found that it was true. It  showed that last week 60,000 New Zealand
children started school, and, on present statistics, 12,000 of those students will leave
school unable to read and to write at a level sufficient for the workplace. That is 20
percent of new entrants—20 percent.
What horrified me was that for M āori, horrifically and sadly, that figure was one in
two. On present statistics, 50 percent of Māori students turning up to school aged 5 will
have years and years at school, but will leav e without the ability to read and write
sufficiently to enter the workforce. If one want s to know the cause of crime, I think that
is a big issue. If one wants to know the cause  of poverty and of disparity, that is a big
one. I say that I am proud—and the ACT Party is proud—to be working with the
National Government, with the Māori Party, and with teachers and professionals up and
down New Zealand to get a bett er result for those kids an d our country. I believe that
the parties that want to deny the facts shoul d hang their heads in sham e, because they
are letting down our kids.
16508 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
It will be a great year for the country. We look forward to continui ng to contribute to
the solution, and to not being part of the pr oblem that the previous Labour Government
left us.

items.speaker: Hon TARIANA TURIA
items.text: T ēnei te mihi atu ki te
whāene P īmia We’i kua ngaro ki te p ō, e takoto ana ki Waih īrere Marae, te w ā’ine o
Ngāpō We’i. Nā reira, e te māreikura, e te kuia, ’aere atu rā.
[I acknowledge the death of aunty Pīmia Wehi, beloved wife of Ngāpō Wehi, who lies
in state at Waihīrere Marae. Farewell, noble matriarch and grandmother.]
First of all, I take the oppor tunity to mihi to my collea gue Metiria Turei for sharing
with us the story of her dad, who was a mokopuna and uri o te K āhui Maunga n ō
Hiruhārama, no te awa o W’anganui. Ka nui te mihi rawa atu ki a koe, Mētīria.
[a grandchild from Jerusalem and the W’ anganui River, and a descendant of the
Cluster of Mountains. I acknowledge you greatly, Mētīria.]
The Māori Party implores this Parliament to wa ke up to the age-old crisis associated
with the lack of social investment. It brings  no joy to my heart to see headlines such as
those in the Taranaki Daily News just 3 days ago: “Maori worst-off in jobless figures”.
The Māori unemployment rate is now more th an double the unemployment rate for all
ethnicities, and it is particularly marked  for our young. I stand here feeling almost
ashamed, given that I have  responsibility for young M āori and young Pacific
unemployment.
But as every politician in this House knows, the appalling statistics of M āori
unemployment are not a new s ong of the last 2 years only. W hen we cast our minds
back over the past decades we see that the figures have been consistently depressing, the
worst being those of the 1980s. There was high youth, M āori, and Pacific
unemployment during the years of so- called plenty in the 2000s. As for M āori nurses
working in the non-governmental organisation sector, there was no pa y parity for them
in the years of plenty. Those issues repres ent Governments that ha ve routinely failed
Māori and failed this country.
The M āori Party spoke of that history when we were a party of one member and
when we were a party on the benches of O pposition, and we speak of it now as a party
in a coalition arrangement with the Government. We speak of that history to remind the
House that we must all own the structural factors that have led to system breakdown.
Why is it that in a time of plenty the previous Labour G overnment did so little to
address the collateral damage of M āori and Pacific unemployment? Why is it that in a
National Government so ready to talk about building the conditions for more enduring
and better-paid jobs there is seemingly su ch an unwillingness to be bold enough to
invest in rangata’i Māori, to equip them to be the leaders of tomorrow?
Of course, I could take us back much furt her to assess the impacts of the price of
citizenship, the loss of land, the myth that employment would come from the waves of
urban migration, the pain of betrayal from political parties, which carried our boat with
careless disregard, and generations of aspirations unfulfilled and expectations
unrealised. But we have always known that it could be—it should be—so different.
In the very first Māori Party speech in this Parliament on 27 July 2004 I spoke about
why a Māori Party was so important: “Ko tēnei te wa o te Ao Māori. It is time to look to
ourselves. That is how we are different from other political parties. We are a political
movement, creating change from the peopl e up, and our policies reflect that. Our
politicians will not be telli ng you what is good for you. Our po liticians will be listening
to you for that.” Those words are as relevant today as they were then. We are a proudly
self-determining people who were devisi ng our own solutions  and creating our
strategies long before the State considered welfare reform to be the answer.
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16509
It is time for a bold Government to orient ate itself to the biggest challenge of our
time—social investment in our future. Wh at we put off today will threaten our
tomorrow. Every party knows that there is  a large number of young people who have
been failed by the system. Anyone can point th e finger at families, at Government, and
at politicians for where we have all gone wrong, but who will be brave enough to turn
that finger back on themselves to face up to their responsibilities, and to make decisions
on what is right, fair, and just, rather than out of political expediency?
What we really need are solutions that will be enduring. We all know that so many of
our w’ ānau, both tangata w’enua and Pacific nations, are fi ghting for their survival.
They are working two or three jobs just to  tread water, and their income levels are
insufficient for them to stay  afloat. That is why the Mā ori Party has consistently raised
with both Labour and National the point that if they really wanted to make a difference,
they would raise the minimum wage. We called for the minimum wage to be lifted to at
least two-thirds of the average wage, which, conservatively calculated, would be at least
$15 an hour. If we are really dedicated to our pursuit of economic transformation, low
wages cannot be tolerated.
And what do we get? A miserable 25c. The argument is always the same: that
minimum wage growth above $13 will constrai n employment growth. We need to be
able to demonstrate that we will protect workers on low incomes, that we will value
fairness, that we will reduce the gross income -inequalities, and that we will incentivise
workers to maintain participation in the labour market.
But we need to do more than raise incomes and create jobs. We must take seriously
all the evidence that tells us that education will be the dr iver of opportunity and that
culture counts. We know what works, but we  must provide authentic cultural learning
environments for our children. We must acknow ledge that this is a systemic issue and
that we have the power to change it.
We need to focus on science and innovatio n to create long-term jobs for our
rangata’i, who have a right to be included and seen for their potential and for what they
can do, rather than for what they cannot. We need to learn from the example of schools
like Clover Park Middle School and Te Wh ānau o Tupuranga in Auckland, which take
up the responsibility to right the wrongs. They unde rstand the importance of
contributing to the development of a strong, secu re cultural identity in their students as
integral to successful participation and achievement.
I want to address some of the misinformation that has come into the public arena
about the coalition arrangement that our me mbers agreed to take up. Our constituents
thought long and hard about whether it was better to spend our days in anger,
bemoaning what could have been, or whether we should do all that we could to make a
difference for our w’ānau, hapū, and iwi by taking on the challenge of government.
Let me assure the House that we have not been a docile partne r by any means. We
have fought the line, and we have put the case with all the vigour that our people
expected of us to set a better foundation fo r our tamariki and mokopuna. All I want to
say is that the Labour Party is in no position to exploit our situati on for political gain.
There would not be a party in  the House that has not experienced conflict within its
midst.
Finally, I return to the challenge given to us by matua Whatarangi Winiata, who told
us that the most important task we had in Parliament was to work for the survival of our
people. We will do whatever it takes to focu s o n that goal. We will form alliances, we
will reach agreements, and we will demand the very highest standards of ourselves as a
team, because this is the greatest opportunity that we have to make a difference. We
know that if our people survive and flourish, our country will only be the better for it,
16510 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
and that is why we have travel led so constantly and so far afield in order to bring the
people’s voices into this Chamber.
We have sat in the company of M āori providers, we have seen at firsthand the
success of Māori businesses, and we ha ve learnt about the i nnovative approaches being
taken by w’ānau Māori. We have brought those stories to  the table, and we have trusted
our people, investing in their sense of se lf-belief and building on their impressive
resilience in the context of their w’ ānau, hapū, and iwi. All that we ask of any
Government is that it, too, invest in our success by placing its trust in the power of the
people to do for themselves. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon JIM ANDERTON
items.text: Mr Key told the House today that
a society should be judged by how it treats  its most vulnerable citizens. By any
measurement the young seriously disabl ed children in c onductive education
programmes across New Zealand must be count ed as amongst the most vulnerable of
New Zealand, and, despite promises to the contrary by Mr Key himself, the funding for
those conductive education programmes has been cut by 30 percent this year and will be
entirely ended by the year  2014. If members wanted a measurement of the most
vulnerable kids in New Zealand, those kids would be it, and the National Government
has completely ended their funding in spite of pleas from all over the country about how
successful and important those programmes are.
The front-page headline in the Christchurch Press from the weekend asks “Does this
look like the road to recovery?”. The obvious answer is that it does not. In my electorate
office area of Selwyn village every single business on the opposite side of the road has
left its premises. Nothing has changed or been done since 4 September, and the only
answer we get from our urgent inquiries is that the council is talking to the owner, who I
understand lives in Taiwan. Those talks have been going on for 5 months and not one
single action has been taken except to cordon off the whole area, and every single
business has gone. All the businesses on the other side of the street—except mine,
which happens to be funded by Parliamentary Service—are at risk as we speak.
If we fast-forward the headline “Does this look like the road to recovery?” to New
Zealand’s economic recovery, how do J ohn Key’s words abou t an aspirational
Government and heroic television appearan ces pledging progress and prosperity match
up with the same kind of rhetoric we saw night after night on television at the time of
the earthquake in Christchurch ? Again the obvious answer is  about the same: lots of
hype and no action.
Here are the problems that the Prime Minister should have talked about this
afternoon. After more than 2 years in Government, economic growth has stopped. Any
so-called recovery has stalled. Unemployme nt is going up, not down. The co-leader of
the Māori Party has a very short memory as to the reduction in unemployment for Māori
around New Zealand in the 9 years of the La bour-led Government: it went from 28
percent to 4 percent. I would have thought th at was something to be celebrated, not to
be castigated for. Jobs are being lost, not created. The cost of liv ing is increasing, but
incomes are not keeping pace, particularly for low-middle income New Zealanders.
W
hat is the Prime Minister’s strategy to tackle these problems? He does not have
one. He has had all summer—in Hawaii, even—ye t he comes to this House with a plan
to just muddle through. It is a shopping list that will not create jobs, will not lift
incomes, and will not help. His economic policy consists of asset sales. That is not an
economic policy; it is a surrender of the sovereignty of New Zealand. Not one new job
will be created by selling off the people’s ownership of power companies. But every
one of us will be paying the new overseas  owners higher prices for power. We know
this because we have seen it all before. John Key was not in New Zealand for most of
the 1980s and 1990s; he was helping speculate  against the New Zealand dollar on the
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16511
international market. But I was here, and I hear d all of the arguments for asset sales last
time around. The arguments for asset sales were fatally flawed then, and they are just as
fatally flawed now. I walked out on the then Government caucus because asset sales
were a bad idea, and the idea has not got a ny better. That is why we had to buy the
assets back.
We had to buy back the rail system because  National privatised it for less than the
price of the wooden sleepers. The rail system was an integral part of the transport
system, and it had been wrecked by overseas owners who disinvested and saw it ruined.
We had to buy back Air New Zealand because it was privatised into the capable hands
of private owners, who sent it bankrupt. We were in danger of not getting our planes
back from wherever they were, because th ey were leased and we could not pay the
rentals on them. That is how bad privatisation got for our most strategic industry.
We had to start a new bank because the foreign owners of our entire banking industry
sucked New Zealand’s banking industry dr y. They closed 1,300 branches, and they
increased fees and their own profits. These pr ofits were shipped overs eas at the rate of
$1,300 million a year. How do we get a better le vel of indebtedness and a level of
ownership of our own country if we are expor ting all our money to overseas owners? If
anyone can square that circle, I would like to know what the answer is. I have not seen
one single rational explanation. Why woul d selling our power companies be any
different? Why would the new foreign owners suddenly discover the virtue of charity
over shareholder profit? Why w ould the assets not fall into foreign ownership just like
the last lot, which were going to be kept for Kiwi mums a nd dads? If I ev er hear “Kiwi
mums and dads” again, I thi nk I will scream into the te levision set. Kiwi mums and
dads? Get a life! The first thing that happens  is that the overseas buyers turn up with a
bit better offer for the Kiwi mums and dads, who sell the shares, which are then owned
by overseas companies quick smart. If anyon e thinks that owning 49 percent of a
company does not give one some right to a say in how the company is run, they must be
dreaming.
The same tired old lines from the past ar e being trotted out, and the same promises
that will be made this time w ill fail exactly the same as they did last time. I am here to
bear witness that the same mistakes are being proposed as were made last time a
Government paid for tax cuts by selling off public assets. I was told—and we all were—
that if we sold $19 billion worth of assets , debt would be ended:  it would be a new
nirvana. New Zealand ended up owing more mone y after we sold the assets than we did
before we sold them. How does that work? Now we talk about the indebtedness of New
Zealand. Let us talk about the indebtedness of the whole of New Zealand, not just the
public debt. If anyone is to be thanked for the public debt being in a position where we
can borrow money in a recession, it is former Minister of Finance Michael Cullen, not
Bill English or the National Government.
The only thing that has rest rained the rapaciousness of the power companies in the
last 10 years is the hold that the Government has on board appointments. The fact that
the Government will potentially give that control away and have no control over power
prices should be a scary fact  for all New Zealanders. When the power companies are
sold and the boards are free to do what they li ke, even worse is what they have to do by
law, which is actually to cede to the minority interests of shareholders before any other
interests. If that does no t ring alarm bells in somebody’ s head, I do not what would.
Those companies will have to protect those shareholders’ interests in terms of earning
as much money as they possibly can fr om m onopoly interests, which actually,
ironically, are served if they make less power  available, because they can charge more
for it. How bright does one have to be to figure that one out? I do not know—it does not
seem to have occurred to anyone on the other side of the House.
16512 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
I said in last year’s Budge t debate that a few things would happen in New Zealand.
Let us look at what I said and what has happened. I said that the average New Zealander
would not be better off, because if people are not on high incomes, this Government
will not help them. That is exactly what  has happened. People who are on average or
below-average incomes, which is the majority of New Zealanders, are worse off now
than they were a year ago. I said that unemployment would be higher, and it is.
Unemployment is higher today than it was when National took office. It is higher than it
was last December. We were going to stop al l New Zealanders going  to Australia, yet
more people are going to Australia than ever  before. We cannot even get people to fix
the buildings in Christchurch, because they can earn more in Australia. Where is John
Key now? I tell John to come back. All is forg iven if he can  actually prove that he can
fix that one. The Government has stopped even pretending it has any idea where the
new jobs will come from.
What happened to John Key’s bike trail? That was going to fix everything with 4,000
jobs. Nothing the Prime Minister said today will increase exports; nothing he said today
will boost investment in research and development or help productivity. Last year I said
that the gap between rich and poor would incr ease. One does not have to be a rocket
scientist to work out that if the Prime Mini ster gets $1,000 a week in tax cuts and the
poor people in New Zealand get nothing from  tax cuts, the income and wealth gap
between rich and poor actually increases in New Zealand. Surely it is bad enough.
The Leader of the Opposition has alrea dy mentioned what happened in McGehan
Close, where John Key went in 2008 to pr etend he was compassionate about child
poverty. The poor kid is now in Child, Youth and Family care. John was going to fix all
that, too. What was announced today that w ould make her better off? The answer is
nothing. A respected professor of epidemiology in New Zealand said last year: “In New
Zealand social injustice is killing and maim ing our children on a grand scale.” We top
the scales in the OECD for rates of w hooping cough, rheumatic fever, pneumonia, and
other diseases in children. Twenty-eight per cent of our children st ill live in poverty.
What do they have to hope for? There is more unemployment, more GST, more price
rises, higher rents, and a Government that does not care a fig about what happens to 90
percent of New Zealanders, as long as the 10 percent at the top are looked after.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: The Prime Minister properly
spoke earlier this afternoon of his aspirations for New Zealand, and he couched them in
very positive tones. But the reality is that  this country today—like many others around
the world—is in the doldrums. This c ountry is feeling buffeted by all of the
consequences of the hugest international economic recession since the 1930s. Right
around the world, jobs have b een shed. Right around the world, debt has increased.
People have struggled to overcome adversity. In Australia we have seen huge natural
disasters. We have seen the Christchurch ea rthquake and the Pike Ri ver tragedy in this
country. All of those impact on the ability of  this country to pull itself up and move
forward for the future. When we start to hear people offer easy solutions—more of the
same: borrow and hope, and tax more—we c ondemn New Zealanders today who are
feeling uneasy to more uncertainty, to more unease, and to a greater  lack of confidence
in the future. That is the distinction to be drawn from the two opening speeches today.
When we look at what is happening in other countries, as they face the same range of
problems we face, we are starting to see some  extreme reactions occur. Sadly, the usual
trend is for people to become set against one another, to try to find a scapegoat within
and blame that as being the cause of all our problems. To some extent, we are seeing
that in this country today with aspects of debate on the foreshore and seabed. It is a
tragedy in that New Zealand we are starti ng to see division created amongst the people
of this country for political ends. If we go and talk to people over their barbecues at
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16513
summertime and speak to our neighbours, frie nds, and associates we learn what people
actually want and that their aspirations are unfailingly positive for the country, for
themselves, and for their children. They line up with the sort of thing the Prime Minister
is talking about, but they want to see an oppor tunity for them to have some say at the
national table about the things that are of c oncern to them. They want a reassertion of a
sense of nationhood and national unity, because the continuation of either the ignoring
of their situation or the setting of one against the other simply feeds national
disharmony and prevents a stable, cohesive, and enduring recovery from occurring.
It is against that backgro und that I think it is importan t that New Zealand takes the
opportunities provided this year to start to focu s again on the sort of country we wish to
become. In recent days the issue of our nati onal day has come back on to the national
agenda. People want to be involved, they want to be included, and they want to have the
opportunity to celebrate what being a New Zealander means to them. We have seen too
much of the division, too much of the sideshows, and too much of the capture by certain
interests of particular part s of our nationhood. What in fact  the people of New Zealand
are saying is that we are all, by force of history and nature, in these islands. We are all
by those same forces part of the solution, not part of the problem. We all have an
opportunity and a right to contribute. What New Zealand really lacks is that sense of
purpose and national unity.
We look across the Tasman. In the depth of the despair caused by the Queensland
floods and the fires in Western Australia, th at country came together on 26 January to
celebrate being Australian and to celebrate what being an Australian means to the
various peoples who make up Australia. Why can we in New Zealand not have a similar
enduring national opportunity wh ere all of us—whatever our particular heritage and
lineage—talk about why we are proud to be Kiwis, where we bring our particular
features to the national tabl e, and where the country be nefits from the collective
goodness that endures from that? What we have  instead, if one believes the polls, is
either a sense of vast indifference to the f act that a national day is occurring, or a sense
of betrayal and alienation and a feeling that a series of meetings and occasions are being
captured by a particular vest ed interest. It is not good enough. A country set against
itself is one that will not endure and will not survive. New Zealand is proud externally
to portray a certain image. But why as New Zealanders can we not start the process of
working with each other, celebrating th e cultures and backgrounds that make this
country the unique place it is, putting those on display a nd sharing them, and learning
from each other, rather than what we have seen to an extensive and unacceptable degree
over the last weekend?
New Zealand does face some very difficult challenges. There are going to be some
hard debates this year about  aspects of economic and soci al policy, and some choices
will need to be made that inevitably create the argument about winners and losers as we
come out of a recession and position this economy for th e future. Those debates and
choices can occur positively onl y if they do so against the backdrop of a real sense of
identity and purpose about what it is to be a New Zealander today. Why can we not
approach this subject with the same boldness that in so many other areas we have
lauded individual New Zealanders for demonstrating? Why in talking about our
nationhood can we not show the spirit and i ndomitability that Hillary showed in
conquering Everest? Why can we not show th e sense of innovation of Peter Jackson or
Paul Callaghan in terms of looking at the sense of our national purpose and our national
identity? Why can we not bring these strands together to say to all New Zealanders that
these rem
arkable individuals, for instance, w hom we laud as being our great achievers,
did not do that necessarily by their own dint, that there was something in their national
16514 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
psyche that as New Zealanders made it possible for them to be so innovative and
successful? Why can we not nurture that feeling in terms of taking this country forward?
Alongside the opportunities th at events like the Rugby World Cup 2011 and other
similar spectacles provide, the opportunity to  take forward New Zealanders’ abilities
and to carve and forge a new sense of na tionhood based around the unique potential of
everyone in this country is one we cannot a fford to lose sight of. As the world comes
out of economic crisis and as th e world starts to reposition itself for the first half of the
21st century, that sense of identity will be fa r more powerful and far more important to
demonstrate than ever before.
I say that as this Parliament resumes its business for 2011, alongside the particular
matters that will be on the Government’s agenda and will be debated, the issue of
nationhood, the issue of our identity as a pe ople, and the issue of  ensuring that we
proceed united and cohesive and do not succumb to the sorts of divisions we are starting
to see occur in similar jurisdictions elsewhere that are facing the same pressures will be
important and powerful issues for all of us to  focus on. As this year unfolds, I want to
see New Zealanders not only feel better economically but also, perhaps far more
important, feel better in themselves about who they are, what they can contribute to
their country, and what their country means to them.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I am pleased
to support the motion moved by the Prime Minist er today in support of his statement to
the House. The Prime Minister outlined the programme for the Government that will
lead us into the November el ection. The Prime Minister made it very clear that this is a
Government that is not prepared to mi slead New Zealanders about the difficult
economic circumstances that we live in. It is  not prepared to mislead New Zealanders
about how tough it is at the mo ment to make progress and it is not prepared to go to
