New Zealanders with outrageous promises of expenditure, without any plan for where
that money may come from.
In reply to the Prime Minister’s speech, Mr Goff essentially outlined—if I may
paraphrase his 20 minutes—a pile of what one could say were the worst aspects of his 9
years as a Minister in the previous Government  with all of the misfortunate events that
occurred during that time. Mr Goff outlined the rise in so many bad social statistics
during that time, then said that Mr Key had had 2¼ years to fix them, but he had not and
had failed. Mr Goff said that was why Ne w Zealanders would go running back to the
Labour Party. Well, that shows the headspace that the Opposition is in. It shows that
those members are not connected to what Ne w Zealanders are thinking and feeling on a
daily basis.
It is no wonder, then, that at the end of Mr Goff’s speech he failed to move a vote of
no confidence in the Government. He knows that when it come s to the simple thing of
the wages that New Zealanders collect t oday, those on the average wage are taking
home $64 more a week than they were in 2008. He knows that the rise in wages for
New Zealanders over the last 2 years has mo re than twice outstripped what Labour
achieved in 9 years of Government. In those 9 years, wages rose by 4 percent for those
on the average wage. After 2 years of a Na tional Government, the increase in the
average wage is a bit over 10 percent. Mr Goff knows that, and that is why he was not
prepared to move a vote of no confidence against the Government.
Mr Goff went on and talked about some of the pressures that New Zealanders face in
their lives and his abhorrence of the concept of asset sales. Everyone knows that this
country has a very heavy borrowing programme. This country is deeply, deeply in debt.
Our debt is 85 percent of GDP. As measured against other countries, we are a Portugal,
we are an Ireland, and we are a Greece. Ou r country is in significant economic
difficulty. Mr Goff and his party goes out there and freely promise $5 billion of extra
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16515
spending a year, without telling New Zeala nders where that money will come from.
New Zealanders are not silly. They know it w ill come from that $64 a week extra that
this National Government has ensured they  get each week in their pay packets.
[Interruption] That is not a bad title. Mr Goff talked about the asset sales issue as if his
own hands were completely clean in that ma tter. He was a Minister in a Government
that sold hundreds of millions of dollars worth of New Zealand’s assets, and got nothing
for them. Mr Key and this Government have outlined to New Zealanders the prospect of
asking why we should not sell off a little bit of the assets that we have, if that enables us
to acquire bigger assets.
The interesting thing is that the Oppositio n lauds the fact that it bought back New
Zealand rail. That is like buying a lame horse  and telling everyone that it will win the
Melbourne Cup. It is not credible for the Labo ur Party to run a policy that says not to
look at that particular aspect. David Cunli ffe knows that; he said it in a speech just
recently. Mr Goff himself has repeatedly said  that a public-private mix in the asset
portfolio would not be a bad thing. We have  quotes from him, but I will not go into
them today.
The most extraordinary thing is his suggestion that if there was a minor shareholding
sold in the State generating assets, power prices would go through the roof. I ask New
Zealanders to consider why power prices rose by 72 percent under 9 years of Labour,
when over the same period of time we saw only 28 percent inflation. That is the sort of
extortion that comes from State-owned enterprises at the present time. Before Christmas
Mr Goff went out with a polic y that said that Labour would not take dividends from
State-owned enterprises. He said it would not take an y dividends fro m electricity
companies and that that would keep prices  down. Then after Christmas he came back
and said: “Oh no, we need that $700 million a ye ar to pay for part of our programme.” I
tell him that he cannot have it both ways. Mr Goff cannot go out with a record like
Labour has on power prices and make the sort of claims he is making.
The last 2¼ years of a National Government have seen a considerable slowing in the
pace of power price rises. This Government  conducted the most comprehensive reform
of the electricity industry th at this country has seen in 20 years with the Electricity
Industry Act passed last year. That legislati on will lead to stable prices. The record
speaks for itself. Between November 2008 a nd November 2010 the price in real terms
was a 1.1 percent increase. That excludes GS T and excludes the costs of carbon that are
applied to those things, but, none the less, it is an extremely impressive record for the
Government to date.
If we couple the regulatory environment with that record, then New Zealanders
should not fear that they will not get the oppo rtunity to invest in those companies. I
want to answer Mr Anderton in respect of his suggestion that somehow those companies
will end up in foreign ownership. For a start, the Government has made it clear that if
New Zealanders return National to these benches beyond 26 November, the
Government will continue to hold 51 per cent of those companies. Today Contact
Energy is 24 percent owned by New Zeala nders and 16 percent owned by local fund
managers and local funds, including A CC, the New Zealand Superannuation Fund, and
KiwiSaver providers. That is a significant amount of Contact Energy where there is no
protection for the majority of the shareholdi ng. The same could be said of Auckland
Airport. New Zealanders currently hold 35 percent of it, the fourth-biggest company in
New Zealand, with a further 9 percent held  by institutions. Air New Zealand is 70-odd
percent owned by the Government and 26 perc ent owned by New Zealanders. That is
the model that we should be following. That is the m odel that we will follow, and we
will give New Zealanders that opportunity.
16516 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
The irony in all this, of cour se, is that the Labour Part y says that New Zealanders
must save more. They pushed forward th e KiwiSaver programme, which has proved
very good, but where are the KiwiSaver funds in vested? By and large, they are invested
offshore. So it is an utterly—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Safe.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: “Safe”, says Mr Mallard. The financial genius on the
other side of the House says “safe”. I tell him to have a look at what has happened to the
financial markets internationally over the last couple of years and see just how safe they
are. Mr Mallard forgets that, as I said at the start of my speech, New Zealand is heavily
indebted.
I suggest to the Labour Party that it might like to think about this: no one owns the
family silver if the debt is bigger than its va lue. It is wrong for the Labour Party to even
try to convince New Zealanders that they can have their ca ke and eat it too. We are a
Government that is led by an extraordinary Prime Minister, who is straight-up with New
Zealanders and will give them a good opportunity to prosper beyond the 26 November
election.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: That was not a great speech made by Mr
Brownlee, who is also the Leader of the Ho use, but at least it  was better than John
Key’s speech. John Key’s speech had very, ve ry little substance on the economic plan
for this country, because in reality John Key’s Government does not have an economic
plan for this country. It has only one policy: tax cuts weighted to the rich.
We heard today how the battle lines will be drawn for the election. The theme we
have heard from Mr Key—and repeated, no doubt by arrangement, by the ACT
contribution from Rodney Hide, by United Futu re’s contribution from Peter Dunne, and
again by Gerry Brownlee—was the accusation that a Labour-led Government would be
fiscally irresponsible and that Phil Goff w ould borrow and spend. That is the rhetoric
they used, but New Zealanders will not be fooled by it. They know  that in Phil Goff
they have a man who has been in 15 Budgets  as a Minister in Labour-led Governments
and that he, of all people, cannot be accused of being fiscally irresponsible. Mr Goff is
not a spendthrift in either his public life as a 15-year - Cabinet Minister or his private
life. That rhetoric will not run. Phil Goff—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: It’s the opposite.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: That is right; some people might say the opposite. He is not
a spendthrift. He would never put this coun try’s finances at ri sk, and neither would
Labour. Let no one be fooled by National’s rhetoric to the contrary.
It is because of the prudence of the previous Labour Governments that New
Zealand’s Government debt was reduced between 2000 and 2008, or else we would be
in the position of Greece, we would be in the position of Portugal, and we would be in
the position of Great Britain and Italy, wher e there is high Government debt. But New
Zealand does not have high Government de bt because the last Labour Government
reduced Government debt. Who opposed thos e Budgets? National! Every one of those
Budgets, where the Labour Governments ran Budget surpluses, was criticised by the
National Opposition. They were criticised by Bill English, who said that Labour was
being greedy and for it not to run Budget surplu ses but to give more tax cuts. If Labour
had done that, we would have further fuelle d inflation, debt, and the asset bubbles that
New Zealand and the rest of the Western World was experiencing at the time.
It was National members who called for i rresponsible Budget ta x cuts that would
have reduced those surpluses. It was Nati onal, when it was in power under Muldoon,
that left New Zealand with staggering levels of Government debt. It is National that this
time has put through unaffordable tax cuts, we ighted to the top 10 percent of earners,
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16517
which means that the Government is borrowi ng billions of dollars every year. As a
consequence, Government debt is rising under National.
Members do not just have to believe me on that, because I have here an article from
the New Zealand Herald of 18 December 2008. That is  about a month after the 2008
election. We have Bill English, who is quoted here in an article from the New Zealand

items.speaker: Herald by Audrey Young
items.text: “Bill English had to swallow the proverbial dead rat this
morning and effectively acknowledge that Mi chael Cullen had done something right in
his stewardship of the Government’s finances in the past nine years. Having condemned
his predecessor for many years for paying off de bt too quickly, English said: ‘I want to
stress that New Zealand starts from a reasonable position in dealing with the uncertainty
of our economic outlook. … In New Zealand we have room to respond. This is the rainy
day that Government has been saving up for. ’” But that was not his Government; it was
the prior Labour Government. We were the ones who ran surpluses and reduced debts.
He told that to reporters and it was reported in the New Zealand Herald on 18
December 2008. He could also have said that  his incoming Government inherited either
the lowest or second-lowest rate of unemployment in the world.
It is once again a National Government whose poor economic performance—with 42
percent of income tax cuts goi ng to the top 10 pe rcent of earners—has contributed to a
large deficit and a stagnating economy. As  I have said prev iously, the current
Government has only one major plank to its po licy: tax cuts for those who already earn
the most. That is what the Government believ es in, but plainly its plan has failed. The
economy has stalled and deficits have grow n. There is little good news in terms of
exports. The current accounts deficit is projected by Treasury to widen to over 6 percent
of GDP again.
Having undermined the country’s finances, the National Government is now trying
to convince us that the last card in its hand that it wants to play is right, which is the one
that Gerry Brownlee spent some time on. He said that New Zealand should now sell the
family silver or borrow against it. The Government is proposing that we flog off schools
into public-private partnerships. Schools ha ve always been run on the Government
balance sheet because Governments do it chea per than if they are leased from the
private sector. Now the Government is co ming out and saying that we should flog off
half of the State-owned electricity enterp rises, and we had the audacity of Gerry
Brownlee in pretending that that would not result in an increase in electricity prices.
Who believes that the profit motivation to maximise price will overcome? We know
that those markets are not properly compe titive. We have had reports from the
Commerce Commission to that very effect within just the last couple of years. People
should make no mistake: Labour will be high lighting the fact that if the National
Government gets its way, retu rns to the Treasury benches,  and flogs off those State-
owned enterprises, electricity prices will go up.
We are 2½ years into this Government—2½ years. The economy is stagnating, and it
is time to ask whether the Government is performing. How should we judge that? Well,
we should judge that upon the promises it ma de when it was elected. First off was to
narrow the wage gap with Au stralia. Is it doing that? Of course it is not. The
Government is exposed on that promise. It has become a meaningless promise that the
Government cannot be judged on by any milest one. Next, the Government promised an
aggressive recovery from recession. Are we getting that?

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: No!
Hon DAVI

items.speaker: D PARKER
items.text: No. Then it said that it was going to have a step change in
the New Zealand economy, but that phrase has disappeared from Government members’
lexicon. They do not even talk about that now. They have even taken it off their
publications. If we look back a few months, we see that National sought a step change
16518 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
in the economy, but if we look at its current plans, we see that that phrase is nowhere to
be seen. National has given up on its rhetoric about a step change.
Last year some of the commentators at the Labour Party conference said they thought
that the next election might be about economic  policy, and they are absolutely right.
They will see a difference between National and Labour, because Labour believes in
truly resetting the economy on an export focus. You know, the National Government’s
Tax Working Group actually got close to ring-fe ncing losses. It is pretty evident from
its papers that some people in National thought that that was necessary because we
over-invest in the speculative economy, but National could not  do it. It could not bring
itself to ring-fence losses. It left the tax preference in favour of that $200 billion of
private residential rental investment, wh ich returns nothing to the taxpayer; those
investors offset their losses against other lo sses. Even worse than that, the Government
misdirected precious investment funds that should be going into  the export economy
into residential property.
Already this year Labour has announced mo re economic policy than National. Last
year we announced changes to monetary policy to help things for exporters, and we will
see that through if we get elected. This  year we have already had two major
announcements. The first was in respect of th e ring-fencing of losse s. There has been a
lot of emphasis on how that will pay for a tax-free zone for every New Zealander, and
that is good, but for me the second most impo rtant part of that is  that it resets the
investment signal in New Zealand so that some  of that $200 billion that is presently in
residential rental investment will be redirected to investment in the export economy. We
can make a difference to growing this economy by growing exports and by giving the
right signals through the tax system. It will not be by continuing to prefer the interests
of a small financial elite, w ho own more than their share of property and use that tax
advantage to offset losses against their other income. Most importantly, that tax
advantage drags money away from the export sector, where it is best invested for new
jobs and higher incomes.
The other announcement that Phil Goff ma de was that we need a research and
development tax credit. We all know that. Ev eryone else in the OECD has one except
for New Zealand. We even had one in New Zealand for a brief time under the previous
Labour Government, but then the National Government axed it. Now, of course,
research and development investment increasingly happens in Australia, where there are
deeper capital markets and research and develo pment tax credits. So, belatedly, what is
our Government’s response? It is anothe r committee on savings. After 2½ years, we
need a proactive Government. We need a Gove rnment that will help New Zealanders to
save more, to invest in the export sector, and to become wealthier.
There is no doubt that there is very little  substance in the National Government’s
economic philosophy; it is tax cuts, tax cuts, and tax cuts. That is all it has. It has
nothing to grow the economy. The cupboard is  now so bare that the Government is
going to flog off State-owned enterprises and increase electricity prices.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: Let me begin on behalf
of the Wellington MPs by welcoming everyone back to Wellington, where we have had
a great summer. I say to the previous speak er, David Parker—Labour’s rising star—that
I was disappointed in that contribution becau se I do not think he listened to what the
Prime Minister said. The Prime Minister outlined policies today about building a
stronger economy, building savings and inve stment, building exports, building skills
and knowledge, and building infrastructure fo r growth, reducing the cost of business,
and getting better results from the Public Service—an exciting vision. We are here to
build a better New Zealand, and to act on be half of the people of New Zealand in a
positive way; as usual, Labour members are stuc k in the past with higher taxes, more
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16519
regulation, and less freedom. New Zealanders have heard it before, and they do not like
it.
A few days ago Mr Goff announced a reshu ffle of his caucus, and it reminded me of
what was once said of Harold Macmillan’s Cabinet reshuffle in 1962: “greater love hath
no man than this, that he lay down his frie nds for his life.” To be fair, Phil Goff has
shown us in renewing his front  bench that he has at least some intestinal fortitude,
propelling Ruth Dyson from her lofty position at  No. 4 down to the infernal depths of
No. 5. As I understand it, her poison tree is already working overtime. It is great to see
Mr Jones back in the Chamber. Last year Annette King said he would have to work very
hard to rebuild his reputation, and I think all Labour colleagues who were demoted or
passed over for the shadow Cabinet will ag ree with Phil Goff that no one has worked
harder than Mr Jones over the last 6 months. It is great to see him back.
We heard that Mr Jones was apparently one of the new generation of M āori leaders.
The next day we learned that this new generation of Labour M āori leaders would also
include Winston Peters, whom Labour hoped to have on its team after the election. Let
us face it, that is not rejuvenation, it is not even rebranding; it is an exercise in nostalgia.
Mr Goff’s attempts to seize momentum this year have been not so much Back to the
Future as “Full Steam Ahead to the Past”.
Interestingly, Labour now has a grand total of three arts spokespeople—

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: Three! Taking New Zealand by storm!

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: —as a result of its re shuffle, and I am so
delighted Mrs Chadwick is still there, leadin g this disparate team. If I knew that their
party was struggling to keep up that much, I would have offered to slow down, but there
is just so much damage that needs to be fi xed up as a result of th e previous Labour arts
Minister.
But I have a bit of time in which to offer some advice to Mrs Chadwick, to Ms
Ardern, and to Mr Robertson, and it is this: there is important policy work, which this
Government is addressing. For many year s the Arts Council had a pretty ropey
bureaucratic structure, and that  is now being refined throug h legislation that we will
debate this year. [ Interruption] I am very disappointed to hear that Mrs Chadwick and
the other Labour members are opposing that measure, because the artistic community
wants those changes.
Last year, the Government managed to get some extra funding for the Historic Places
Trust, which had been neglected for 9 years by Helen Clark. We are now reviewing that
legislation to make sure the structure is appropriate for the Crown entity that the
Historic Places Trust has now become.
A very important area we work ed on last year was saving The Hobbit, and I pay a
particular tribute to the wo rk of the Prime Minister and the Minister for Economic
Development. Their work ensured that The Hobbit would stay in New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: At what cost?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: It will bring in h undreds of millions of
dollars, I say to Mrs Chadwick, and it will create thousands of jobs. Where was Annette
King—the self-proclaimed MP for Weta Workshop—when Labour’s union friends were
trying to destroy The Hobbit? Where was she when Sir Peter Jackson was being abused
by her own colleagues? That is another issue I am very much looking forward to
debating on the hustings with Mrs King in the m arginal seat of Rongotai this year.
I now turn to Treaty negotiations, and I am sorry Mr Parekura Horomia is not with
us, because I want to express to him my very best wishes. He was out on the road with
me on 17 December last year, first in M ōhaka when the Crown signed a deed of
settlement with Ng āti P āhauwera, and later that day at Muriwai Marae just south of
16520 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
Gisborne, when the Crown initialled an agreement with Ng āi Tamanuhiri. They were
great occasions, and I really valued his being with me.
Then on 22 December the Crown signed a deed of settlement with Ng āti Porou here
at Parliament. Again, Mr Horomia was presen t, and he spoke, and I thank him for his
support on those and other occasions. I very  much look forward to keeping him fully
informed of Treaty settlement work, because at least he, in Labour, understands how
important it is.
Let me say something about Treaty settle ments, because, try as they may, Labour
members cannot escape the cold statis tics. Labour managed only about 1½
settlements—1½ settlements—per year in its la st term of office. When visiting iwi, I
have been told on more than one occasion th at the last Minister who spoke to them
before me was Sir Douglas Graham, and I think that that is a shocking record.
This Government takes the matter seriousl y. Since the previous election we have
achieved over 90 milestones, an average of one every 9 days. That includes 21
agreements in principle, and 13 deeds of se ttlement. In just 2 years we have achieved
more than Labour did over 9 years.
This will be a very busy time for settleme nt legislation in th is House. I know Mr
Jones, who always makes a tremendous contribution in those debates, will be looking
forward to those bills being debated. The Human Rights Commission noted the
significant increase in Treaty se ttlements and the benefits they bring to New Zealand.
Last year was the most productive year in settlements history, ex ceeding the previous
most productive year, which was 2009.
That is not the work of an i ndividual, it is the work of a team, and in that context I
particularly mention my colleagues in the M āori Party. Their contribution to Treaty
settlements has been substantial. I thank them for the good work they have done, and I
very much look forward to working with them again this year.
The battle lines are drawn. The themes a ppear to be emerging. Does New Zealand
want a forward-looking Government addressing issues that matter to New Zealanders—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Selling assets!

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: —issues such as growt h, I tell Mr Twyford,
the importance of front-line services, and developing our infrastructure? Or are New
Zealanders more interested in Mr Twyfor d’s prescription of bureaucracy, of regulation,
of waste, and of “Nanny knows all”?
Do they want a Government that goes out and supports the creative industries such as
film, I ask Mrs Chadwick, or do they want a Government that is beholden to the unions?
Do they want a Government that enthusiasti cally gets on with the hugely important job
of achieving just and durable settlements with iwi, or do they want a Government that
could achieve only 1½ settlements a year—1½ settlements a year? Do they want an
aspirational Government led by principled, pr agmatic, and youthful leaders, or do they
want a Government of retreads from 30 years ago who have embraced every position on
the political spectrum, from far right to far left?
Most of all, do they want a Government that is upfront with the people, does not play
funny games with election dates, spells out a clear and articulate vision such as that
outlined by our great Prime Minister this afternoon, and refuses to deal with people such
as Winston Peters? Or would they prefer a coalition of the absurd: Labour, the Greens,
New Zealand First, and Chris Carter? Enough said.

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: Kia ora an ō tātou. Firstly, Mr Assistant Speaker
Barker, I greet you and your colleagues for the beginning of this year, and our
colleagues throughout Parliament for what will be—as the previous speaker, Chris
Finlayson, just said—a battle. I will start by identifying a fe w of the themes that will
ripple through our discussions as parliamentarians—our debates this year in the M āori
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16521
area. Then I will talk about the tawdry speech and the very dismal performance given by
the Prime Minister, as reflected in his failed attempt to appear as hot as Liz Hurley.
Firstly, let the record show that that very pompous speech given by someone who
currently enjoys his lifelong dream of being the Attorney-General, for a mercifully short
period of time, overlooked one single fact. This side of the House and Dr Cullen
brought into this House and passed through this  House the largest si ngle restoration of
land and the largest single restoration of capital into M āori hands, through the
Kaingaroa Plains claims—multiple iwi. He may be able to say, boasting to his legal
friends and endeavouring to curry favour as our friends from the M āori Party slowly
implode, that he has lots of little hap ūs and iwis. I mean not to deprecate any of them,
because they all know this year that the vote s they directed in that direction over there
have dashed their hopes and expectations.
So let the record show that it is all very well to identify the large number of iwi, but
one should deal with the facts, because thos e iwi all know that this  year’s debate is
about a split society. Our leader said it. Now, I am not talking about Rodney Hide’s
rubbish, etc., about Pākehā and Māori. I am talking about the fact that the only people in
New Zealand who will enjoy the opportunity to enrich themselves are merchant bankers
and their attendant parasites—otherwise known as corporate la wyers—and a narrow
cast of New Zealanders who enjoyed a disp roportionate benefit of the tax giveaway
under John Key’s tax policy. They are the only ones who will be in a fit state to come
forward and gobble the share that will be made available in a garage-sale style. They are
the ones who will be rewarded for continuing to support those very foul policies.
It could be said that the St ate-owned enterprises need to  be sold for purely fiscal
reasons. Well, Bernard Hickey and an economis t working with Dr Gareth Morgan said
this morning those are not the reasons. There are no compelling reasons as to why the
descendants of Fay Richwhite need to enj oy privileged access to  this bout of State-
owned enterprises sales. OK, so if it is not purely for fiscal policy, maybe it is—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: What about iwi?

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: Do not worry; I will get to iwi very soon. It may be about
social transformation—that is, turning New Zealand into a share-owning democracy.
Well, if that is what the Prime Minister is promoting, then let us have that debate, but he
should not mask it under $300 million of borro wing a week when in actual fact the
Government’s finances in comparison with t hose of a host of other nation States are in
quite a strong state, purely because our previous deputy leader, Michael Cullen, took the
hard route.
The sale of State-owned enterprises masks the fact that there is no economic strategy
and that this is a reward fo r the shadowy forces that have  always supported that Prime
Minister. They want to come back a nd get hold of monopoly rent-gouging assets,
which, for a short period of time, may be with mums and dads, but the instructiveness of
the Contact Energy episode shows that the assets will soon disappear into foreign
ownership. So not only will that worsen th e vulnerabilities, etc., around our energy
estate and worsen the amount of capital that  disappears overseas but it will worsen the
split. A narrow cast of people will enjoy a disproportionately growing percentage of the
nation’s wealth—and somehow that will make us all richer. All that will do is widen the
chasm
. So this is an election debate that we look forward to. We will love having it. The
reality is that New Zealanders will hear from this side of the House that there is just a
very, very tiny percentage of people who will enjoy it.
I want to talk as well about the most recent United Nation’s report, a report that
received a submission called Tamariki Māori: A Māori view of children’s rights . It is a
report that lambastes the current Government  and reminds day-to-day New Zealanders
that the well-being statistics of our most vul nerable people—and that is who they are, I
16522 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
say to Mr Key—children, are being shafted. No w, there was not a single word from Dr
Pita Sharples, who paraded, kapa haka-ed, haka-ed, yelled, and took all sorts of
characters with him to the other side of th e world to boast his cr edentials about a UN
declaration on indigenous rights.
This is the UN report that really counts. Th is is the one that shows that the very
people who sent him here to Parliament are not enjoying a single element of well-being
growth. They are actually enduring worsening employment statistics, worsening health
statistics, worsening housing situations, wors ening criminal statistics—and what do we
hear? We hear that it is all Hone Harawira’s fault. There is  not a single reason why that
person should celebrate his a ssociation with the UN when this report shows that under
the Māori Party’s stewardship things have got significantly worse.
I have to continue with this theme of split. It was evidenced while we were in
Waitangi that the co-leader of the M āori Party used an opport unity to go touting and
scouting for alternative candidates to run against their colleague, the sitting member. He
was suspended, but before the suspension notice hit the media, the Parliamentary
Service was told to find a new office for th is guy. That is evidence of the duplicity. But
we know that there will be those double standa rds because the architect sits next to Dr
Sharples—the person who, when she was in  association with us, found every single
reason as to why she was the victim. She is continuing on, and thinks somehow Mā ori
voters will view that party as a stronger proposition, and M āori voters will view that
party as a more credible bunch of representati ves for their interest. No, the split society
is splitting them, and when a house is split,  that house eventually falls. It may not
completely fall at this election, but fall it will.
At that point, what the M āori will say is something that we do on the marae in our
oratory. The political representatives misled  their people, practised duplicity on their
own, and showed an inordinate level of grove lling to the Prime Minister—acting as if
they were like the lion in The Wizard of Oz who found the courage, after the Prime
Minister said he wanted to govern again with the Māori Party—and not an hour went by
before Dr Sharples begun his character assassination of Hone Ha rawira in order to
prepare as bride for the Prime Mini ster the next time around. So the M āori voters will
say, as we say on the marae, that they w ill go to Hawaiki nui, Hawaiki roa, Hawaiki
pāmamao. What mainstream voters will say to the Prime Minister, who is worsening the
splits and hocking off the assets, oblivious to the wrongdoing of his Ministers in terms
of their policies to the average wh ānau, and increasing the misery, they will say to him,
as the M āori go to political Hawaiki nui, he will go to Hawaii nui, Hawaii roa, Hawaii
pāmamao and to his apartment and he can en joy a pampered life over there, because
New Zealanders want to see the rear end of this Prime Minister. Kia ora tātou.
Hon KATE WILKINSON (Minis
ter of Conservation) : It is a pleasure to be able
to speak today and reinforce our Prime Minist er’s message to all New Zealanders. It is
2011, and New Zealanders now ha ve a choice. The contrast is stark; the choices are
obvious. New Zealanders can c hoose this year. They can ch oose to vote for National,
with a focus on spending less, borrowing le ss, and growing the economy, or they can
choose to vote for Labour, which wants to focus on spending more, borrowing more,
taxing more, and shrinking the economy.
This Government has worked hard over the past couple of years to introduce policies
that will be conducive to long-term economi c growth in order to build a stronger
economy. We have been focused on a creating an environment that provides New
Zealanders with opportunities to succeed in  life, because we want to see families
prospering. We want them to be proud of this country and what it ha s to offer, and we
want them to raise their children safe in  the knowledge that th ey will have every
opportunity to achieve great th ings. Already this year we have seen a stark difference
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16523
laid out between this Government and th e Opposition. On the one hand we have an
aspirational Government with a proven track  record in managing the economy in tough
times. On the other we have a tax-and-spend Opposition that wants New Zealanders to
be depend on the State for everything, including their jobs.
New Zealanders have a clear choice this year, and just recently we have again seen a
prime example of a policy that clearly dis tinguishes National from Labour. The 90-day
trial period was one of the first policies th at the Government introduced following the
2008 election. It came into effect on 1 Marc h 2009. At that time we spoke at length
about how trial periods would provide opportu nities for New Zealand workers and how
they would give businesses the confidence to take on wo rkers that they might not
otherwise have taken on. This policy was ai med, and had always been aimed, at getting
more New Zealanders into work. It is used all over the world, and we know from
international experience that it actual ly does work. Under the previous Labour
Government small businesses were scared of hiring people. They did not want to run the
risk of taking someone on only to find out the person was unsuitable and then to end up
in court. They needed to be given the c onfidence that this Nati onal Government gave
them by introducing a 90-day trial period, so that they could ta ke on workers whom
they might not otherwise have taken on. W ithout that trial peri od there was a huge
hindrance to growth for small businesses. Business owners were reluctant to expand
their operations because of fear and a lack of  confidence, and jobs that could have been
created were abandoned.
National set out to fix that. Labour’s own Small Business Advisory Group had found
that the introduction of trial periods was the si ngle most important change that could be
made in employment legislation. That advisory group was right. The 90-day trial period
has been a success. Everywhere I go businesse s tell me success stories about how they
took someone on whom they would not have taken on otherwise. The Department of

items.speaker: Labour report Trial Employment Periods
items.text: An Evaluation of the First Year of Operation
backed that up. It stated that 40 percent of employers said the last person they hired on a
trial period would not have been taken on if this measure had not been available.
Recently the New Zealand Institute of Econo mic Research analysed data from the
first 6 months since the introduction of th e trial period. Its c onclusions are worth
reading. The economist who wrote the report spoke on the radio about what the data
showed. The impact was in terms of job numbers, and that impact was 13,000 jobs—
13,000 jobs. The data indicated th at the 90-day trial had the positive impact of creating
13,000 jobs in small businesses. That is 13,000 people who would not have had jobs
otherwise. That is 13,000 families who are not standing in the dole queue. That is
13,000 people who were given a chance to prove themselves. The Opposition’s
response, and the Council of Trade Union’s re sponse, was to say that was feeble. To
call 13,000 jobs feeble, I think, is ridiculous. I think we need to ask Helen Kelly why
she is so opposed to small businesses wanti ng to hire new staff. What does she have
against people getting jobs with these comp anies? We know that 96 to 97 percent of
businesses in New Zealand are small to medi um sized enterprises, yet Labour does not
want them to succeed. It would take away one of the very instruments that has just
resulted in an extra 13,000 jobs.
Why does Labour not like small businesses? Why does Labour not want small
businesses to succeed? Why does Labour not want  them to hire more people and create
more jobs—why? I think Labour needs to answ er that, because the analysis says there
are 13,000 more jobs because of one of Nationa l’s policies. That is only one of our
policies. If Labour had its way, none of t hose 13,000 people would be in work. I ask
Labour members to pick up the phone and be  up front with every one of those 13,000
fa
milies, and to tell them that Labour woul d sacrifice their livelihoods on the altar of
16524 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
ideology. I ask Labour members to tell them that Labour does not believe they deserve
to have jobs. They should ring them up and tell them why Labour does not believe they
deserve to have their jobs. Labour member s should tell those people that Labour will
make it harder for them to get a job in the future.
While I am at it, I say that Labour s hould call another 6,000 New Zealanders. It
should ring them up and tell them to join the dole queue, so that  Labour can introduce a
$15 an hour minimum wage—it should tell them  that. It should tell  that to the 6,000
people who will lose their jobs if Labour has its way and in creases the hourly minimum
wage to $15 an hour, which we know is simply not sustainable. We wish it was
sustainable, but unfortunately it is simply not sustainable. We are not prepared to
jeopardise 6,000 New Zealanders—6,000 jobs—for  ideology. We will not allow that to
happen.
Suddenly the Labour members had another id ea. They said “Let’s bribe the public.
We’ll give them another holiday. We will M ondayise it.” This is Labour’s solution in
respect of the issue of productivity. This is  its great new idea. Do members know what
it means? Because this year Anzac Day falls on Easter Monday, Labour wants to
Mondayise it. Does the House know how many times Anzac Day has fallen on Easter
Monday?

items.speaker: Amy Adams
items.text: Is it once?

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: Never! Never before has Anzac Day fallen on Easter
Monday. Does the House know when this will  next occur? When will Easter Monday
next occur on Anzac Day? It is in 2095! This is Labour’s great idea!
Our trial period works well. This Government backs New Zealanders. We set out to
give small businesses the confidence to take  on new staff, and they have responded.
Employers want to take people on, and they  want to take a chance on someone whom
they might not otherwise have taken on. We all know that there will always be rogue
employers that will make the rest look bad. I have no time for bad employers. The
Labour Opposition will know that we have doubled the penalties relating to bad
employers, because we do not condone bad behaviour by bad employers. But the
majority of employers are fair-minded, ha rd-working Kiwis who want to see their
company, or their business, and the people w hom they employ succeed. I back them to
achieve that. Trial periods will be extended to all employers from 1 April this year,
because we want to create more jobs. If this policy created 13,000 jobs in small
businesses, members can imagine what it could do for all businesses.
This policy has made a difference in New Zealand, just as it has overseas. It is one of
many policies that this Government has intr oduced to assist New Zealanders with the
choices and opportunities availabl e to them. What we do is  to allow flexibility and
choice. We are also allowing New Zealanders to actually cash in 1 week of holiday, if
they want to—only if they want to. If they do not want to do so, they do not have to.
They might be told that, no, they cannot do so, as—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I regret to advise the member
that her time has expired.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: John Key’s vision is dull. It has no
substance. There is no other way to put it: he  is out of touch with real New Zealanders
who are struggling to cope with skyrocketi ng power, petrol, and grocery bills. He does
not have any new ideas. The ideas he has had are questionable in terms of whether they
can be delivered on, and whether he is committed to delivering on them. After more
than 2 years in Government the pressure is now on John Key and National to deliver a
stronger economy, and once all the spin and pr omises are stripped away, they will be
judged on their results. John Key’s speech to Parliament today spelt out National’s plan
for the year, and I heard no plan to grow jobs in the economy or help families under
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16525
financial pressure. National’s big idea is to se ll our most valuable public assets to the
highest bidder, which means that more and mo re of our wealth will go offshore. Only
Labour will stop asset sales.
Labour has a plan for a strong export economy, a fairer tax system, and strong public
services. We will introduce a tax-free zone to help middle and lower income families
with the rising cost of living, and we know that it is jobs that matter.
What do New Zealanders want? They want certainty of incomes and direction, not
more of the same. They want to know where we are headed as a nation, and they want
to know that we have a plan involving jobs for them now and securing jobs of the future
for their kids—good jobs with a future. I re cently asked people in my electorate in
Dunedin South to tell me their three biggest issues, and they told me that those issues
were the rising cost of living, the cost of electricity, and ri sing inequalities. It does not
sound like a step change; it sounds more like a step backwards. What will National do?
It will provide 25c an hour extra for the vuln erable, it will make more cuts to services,
and it will sell our energy companies so that electricity prices will go up even further.
John Key talked today about the fact that New Zealand needs world-class
infrastructure to ensure that our workers and businesses can compete as efficiently and
productively as possible. He said that broadband is the revolutiona ry technology of our
country and that the Government wants Ne w Zealanders up and down the country to
have access to ultra-fast services at an affordable price. Well, I agree with him. But will
we get it? It does not look like it. The ultr a-fast broadband policy was No. 2 in John
Key’s top 10 pledges before  the 2008 election. He gave his personal guarantee to
deliver ultra-fast broadband fibre to 75 percent of New Z ealand homes, for $1.5 billion.
People thought that sounded good, but wondered whether they would get it and just how
committed the Government is to ultra-fast broadband. A recent Dominion Post article
quoted from a Cabinet paper that was released under the Official Information Act, under
great duress. The paper said that the ultra-fast broadband roll-out would proceed in three
or four phases, but then it said: “The ro ll-out could halt before the third phase—the
widespread deployment of fibre across subur bs—if factors such as a lack of demand
made the project too financially risky.” Too ri sky? Does that mean that the poorer parts
of New Zealand might not get ultra-fast broa dband? Does it mean th at the more remote
parts of New Zealand will not get rural fibre? Does it mean that the Government is not
really committed to its election pledge? What  is the Government’s plan, then? What is
its vision? Is it to deliver on the biggest commitment that it made before the election?
Well, I am not even sure the Government  will do that. Yesterday Steven Joyce
announced that the Government was negot iating a $300 million contract for rural
broadband with a consortium of Telecom an d Vodafone, which are the two biggest
players in the telecommunications scene. They are the incumbents. National’s decision
is to negotiate rural broadband contracts with the incumbent providers, which have
repeatedly failed rural customers. This is not being anti-Telecom or anti-Vodafone; they
are important companies in our telecomm unications industry. But the industry is
evolving fast. It is rapidly merging w ith the broadcasting industry with new
technologies. The Internet is the future.
There has been an outcry about yesterday’ s decision. Federated Farmers, National’s
mate, has questioned whether there will be a step change, and has suggested the policy
is not ambitious enough or competitive enough. Conor English, Bill’s brother, who
works for Federated Farmers, said: “If you’ve got two incumbents and they’re just
going to get bigger, then naturally that does raise competition concerns.” So there are
big concerns from Federated Farmers about this issue.
A couple of weeks ago Selwyn Pellett from the Productive Economy Council wrote
about the long-term consequences of asset sales. Labour has learnt that lesson. He wrote
16526 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
about the sale of Telecom, wh ich saw a dividend stream flow out of this country that
could have seen broadband infrastructure in place a decade ago. Labour tried to do
something about that. He said that Telecom’s monopolistic pricing effectively became a
foreign tax on all New Zealanders and a handbrake on economic development. Now we
are proposing to hand over our newest and mo st important piece of infrastructure to
Telecom and Vodafone not only in rural areas  but, likely, in urban areas too. Let them
have a role, but do not give them a monopol y. There are innovative solutions available
to deliver broadband faster to the 800,000 ru ral New Zealanders who are crying out for
it. They are people like the man who contacted  me last year from Winchester, near
Timaru. He had moved there from Auckland. He now needs to move back north for
personal and health reasons, but he cannot sell his home. Why? Because he cannot get
broadband. The response from Telecom and the Minister for Communications and
Information Technology was that he would have to wait 5 or 6 years. Winchester is not
remote. FX Networks already runs fibre st raight down State Highway 1, right near his
house. That company was part of a bid for rural broadband that committed to delivering
a fourth-generation wireless network in 2 y ears with better speeds and at a lower cost.
That man cancelled his life insurance. He was told by the local National MP to go on a
benefit. How innovative was that? There ha s been too much s ecrecy, not enough
transparency, and too many questions about th is particularly important infrastructure.
There is no evidence of a wider plan ab out what the Government will do with
broadband.
Labour wants New Zealanders to have ultr a-fast broadband, but broadband is just
part of what is needed to deliver a digita l transformation strategy for this country. We
need a digital vision and a concrete digital agenda. Under this Government and this
Minister we do not have either. Instead, there is the absence of a cohesive regulatory
environment to enable New Zealand to ta ke advantage of broadband investment, the
destruction of New Zealand - developed content,  the lack of a clearly articulated vision
for New Zealand as a 21 st century digital economy, and the failure of our education
system to equip young Kiwis with the digital skills needed to transform this economy.
The way the Government spends its mone y is important. How can we provide New
Zealanders and our children with the knowledge that we ca n have sustainable jobs and
industries? The Government, as the biggest  purchaser of goods and services, has the
capacity and the responsibility to develop domestic industry from the way we spend our
money. This Government is committed to big de als that cut out local suppliers at lowest
cost. We have seen it in this Government’s approach to spending $500 million of
taxpayers’ money on building trains for Auck land. The objective is a lowest-cost bid,
which is unlikely to see that money spent in side New Zealand, to sustain and build our
rail engineering industry. That is despite the Prime Minister’s claim that National will
build the financial durability of KiwiRail. It  is a joke. National’s reluctant commitment
to KiwiRail is the sign of a Government that  would prefer to see more heavy freight on
our roads than on rail.
I want to talk about how the Government spends its money on information and
communications technology. Members might be su rprised to learn that the information
and communications technology industry in this country contribute s $20 billion a year
to our economy. It is worth $5 billion in expor ts a year and is second only to the dairy
sector. It employs around 40,000 people and invests on average around 9 percent of
revenue in research and development. It attracts $2 billion worth of Government
procurement, which is 7 percent of all Government procurement. It is on the precipice
of vast opportunities with ultra-fast br oadband and rural broadband. These are the
industries of the future, and finding skilled wo rkers is that industry’s biggest challenge.
But what does the Government say? It says: “It’s not our problem. We’re not investing
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16527
in training. That’s the industry’s responsib ility.” So what is this Government’s
responsibility? What is its pl an? People need to know that they can trust their elected
representatives to have their best interests at heart, and to have a plan. That is not using
the tired-old strategies from the past, but  some new ideas, some innovative solutions
that build confidence in our local industries, and create jobs for the future for our kids.
We are not a corporation, I say to Mr Key. We are a country.

items.speaker: Hon Dr WAYNE MAPP
items.text: New Zealand has a clear challenge
ahead, and that is to build exports and growt h. That is the critical  issue facing this
nation, beyond all else. Opposition members sp end all their time talking about social
issues. They did that during 9 years in Government. What happened during that period?
New Zealand exports since 2005 have gone backwards. That is what happens when we
take the eye off the ball. The previous Government did that, and that is why we are in
our present situation. That is why this Government has a relentless focus on the
economy. We are dealing with a global financial crisis. We are dealing with debt—$300
million per week. I know that Opposition members ju st airily dismiss it as if it is of no
particular consequence and no particular constraint on thei r $5 billion of promises in
just 1 month. They are truly in la-la land on th at issue. That is why National is building
the conditions for growth. That is why we are building on science and innovation.
I heard Mr Goff talk today about Sir Paul  Callaghan. He obviously does not read
what Sir Paul writes. This is what he wrote in the Dominion Post today; today, I note:
“… our thinking is too often mi red in fashionable cliché rather than serious analysis.
Ten years ago we went for ‘biotech’ … Now politicians tout ‘clean-tech.’ ” What did
we hear Mr Goff talking about today? I think it was about cleantech. Fashionable cliché,
rather than serious analysis, is exactly where Mr Goff is mired.

items.speaker: Sir Paul went on to say
items.text: “Our future lie s in the niches of a world economy … We
will creep up on our competitors in the odd sp ots, in respiratory humidifiers”—such as
Fisher and Paykel Healthcare— “in crystal-controlled osci llators for GPS on a chip”—
such as with Rakon—“in magnetic resonance sensors for the oil industry.”—such as
Magritek.”
Building science and innovation has been my central focus as a Minister. I have been
systematic in this regard over the last 2 years. In 2009 there was a focus on fundamental
science, building up the Crown Research Institute Capability Fund, building up the
Marsden Fund, building up the Health Research Council and establishing the Prime
Minister’s science prizes, and also arranging the appointment of Sir Peter Gluckman as
the Prime Minister’s Chief Science Adviser.
Early in 2010 we then moved to the reform of the Crown research institutes. We
established a taskforce, gave  them clear objectives and bulk funding for core science
and a clear recommendation from the OECD. That  has been rolled out. Also last year in
the Budget there was building business support for science and innovation. This year on
1 February the Ministry of Science and Innovation was estab lished. Members will hear
a great deal more about that over the next  few months. However, I note that when
Labour published the new appointments, Mr Shearer, who apparently supports the
Ministry of Science and Innovation, still described himself as a spokesman for research,
science, and technology. All I can say to Da vid is “Catch up.” Th at is indicative of
Labour, really. It has to catch up all the time. That is just one small microcosm.
The programme, in each of thos e 2 years, essentially rolls out over 4 years. I shall
focus on some of the key initiatives. The technology development grants will grow from
$22 million this year to $62 million 3 years fr om now. The  commercialisation transfer
budget will grow from $4 million this year to $8 million, 3 years from now. The
Rutherford Discovery Fellowships, primarily for advanced post-doctorates, will grow
from $1 million this year to $9 million, 3 year s from now. That will fund in that year
16528 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
alone 50 new Rutherford Discovery Fellowships. That is 50 scientists who will be able
to stay in New Zealand, building their care ers as they advance on from post-doctorates.
That is a significant change. Also the scie nce infrastructure f und will grow from $7
million this year to $15 million in 3 years.
This week we announced $30 million for th e national supercomputer project, an
infrastructure project spread across the University of Canterbury, the University of
Auckland, the National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research, and GNS Science,
and using other infrastructure as well. I will give members an insight on the companies
that get those technology development grants , because that is where the rubber hits the
road. These are the sorts of companies: Fi sher and Paykel Healthcare, $500 million of
sales last year; Gallagher Group, $160 million of sales last year and the one New
Zealand company mentioned in a publica tion in German by Hermann Simon called
Hidden Champions of the 21 st Century, about companies that dominate in their field;
Rakon, with sales of $144 million; Tait Electr onics and security, $200 million of sales;
and the list goes on, including Skope Industries, Weta Digital, and 27 other companies.
Each of these companies has its niche, the kind of approach identified by Sir Bill
Gallagher. Each of these companies are leaders in their fields. Our challenge is to grow
these companies, and a whole range of othe r companies around them , much faster than
we have done in the past. That, in a sense, points to New Zealand’s future. We are
already strong in primary indus tries. That has been the foundation of the New Zealand
economy for 150 years. There have been good  prices for those primary products in
recent years, but it is not enough.
We are strong in tourism. That generates j obs across all the skil l levels, but with a
particular concentration of employment in  lower-skilled opportunitie s. It is a huge
sector of our economy. These sectors will grow , and, particularly in the tourism sector,
they are job rich. But in truth we also n eed to add a third sector, loosely called high
technology. Some of that might be in biotechnology; some might be in information
technology or digital media. Much of it, ho wever, will be in niche manufacturing.
Today those companies generate $5 billion of  exports. Some, as I have said, are quite
large, like Fisher and Paykel Healthcare; many are in the $30 million to $100 million
range of exports. They are all listed in the Technology Investment Network publication,
known as the TIN 100. I know this is well known to various members around this
House, including, I note, Mr Shearer.
The companies in this publication are the ones we need to grow. We need to see the
Fisher and Paykel Healthcares grow to be billion-dollar companies. We need a hundred
companies to grow from $50 million of e xports or thereabouts up to $100 million. That
way we would get to $10 billion of exports. That would be just the start of the
challenge. Many of the companies are yet to exist or are in their infancy. That is why we
also have the technology vouchers, a pilot programme with $5 million this year, but it
has been oversubscribed. We will grow it acco rding to demand. That really sets out the
challenge for this nation to grow a new sect or of our economy. That is the way we will
close the gap with Australia over time. That will be a very substantial challenge in its
own right.
The new Ministry of Science and Innovation also has an innovation board. We have
included on that board some of New Zealand’ s leading science entrepreneurs, including
Dr William Rolleston, who also runs a company within the TIN 100 group, South
Pacific Sera, a biotechnology company in the Canterbury area. My colleague Amy
Adams will know that company particularly well. Also included on the board is Mr
Grant Ryan of YikeBike, also another Canterbury company. Why have I mentioned that
company? The YikeBike was one of the 50 top inventions.
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16529

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: In the next month my son and his partner will join
the exodus to live and work overseas. Like ma ny of his generation he is going for better
opportunities, but that is  not the only reason. He and hi s partner are tertiary qualified,
and both have good and relatively well-paid jobs. So it is not money that is driving them
away; it is a lack of conf idence in the future of our country under John Key’s
Government, and a growing belief that they would have a better future elsewhere.
John Key promised the New Zealand electo rate in 2008 that his Government would
stop our children leaving the country. He talked  it up, he melodramatised it, and he said
he would stop our best and brightest leav ing our shores. But only 2 days ago the
Weekend Herald reported that there was a net loss of almost 22,000 Kiwis to Australia
last year. All the signs are there that this e xodus will only get worse. So that is a broken
promise among the silly slogans, the empty promises, of John Key and this National
Government. John Key promised there would be a step change. We still do not know
what that means. He promised there would be  a brighter future. He promised that New
Zealand incomes would catch up with Australia’s. He promised to tackle what he called
the growing underclass in our country, and wh at a sad indictment there was about that
this week, with the story about Aroha and her mother.
The Prime Minister’s statement to Parliame nt today signals a Government that has
run out of ideas, if indeed it ever had any. He is finding out the awful truth: promises
are easy to make, but it takes a lot more than words to deliver on them. There is no
brighter future, for example, for the 2,500 families on the North Shore and Rodney who
have had to apply for non-benefit special-needs grants in the last year. I think that is
symbolic of just how widely and deeply fe lt this Government’s inaction has spread. We
are talking about the North Shore and R odney, the home of five National MPs,
including the Prime Minister. There is no brighter future for families who are struggling
with the rising cost of living, which has actually been caused by National. GST and
rents have gone up, rates are going up, general practitioners’ f ees are going up, early
childhood education costs are rising, petr ol has gone up, ACC costs are going up, and
power prices are going up. How are families supposed to cope with these increases,
when their wages have hardly moved, and in many cases have actually gone backwards?
There is no brighter future for the 178,000 people who have no jobs. There is no
brighter future for the 100-odd workers who we re laid off in the wood industry over the
holiday period, when John Key was in Hawaii sunning himself. There is little hope for
the thousands of workers who have lost their jobs in the manufacturing sector during the
period of this Government. Every worker who loses a job represents a social tragedy.
There is the humiliation and loss of self-est eem from getting the sack in the first place.
There are the consequences for a family’s income, and the indignity and degrading
experience of having to seek assistance from  Work and Income. There are the hundreds
of job applications that are never answered or even ac knowledged. There are the little
bits of work from time to time—casual,  temporary, minimum wage jobs—as people
scratch around to make something in order to put food on the table.
I think we all agree that a job is the best poverty eradication measure available,
provided that it is a decent, well-paid j ob where training, skills recognition, and the
contribution of workers are acknowledged as an important part of our economy. But,
unfortunately, this Government lacks the imagination to re ally develop job creation and
stimulus. It has decided that New Zealand wo rkers are lazy, untrust worthy, and need to
be punished through harsher la bour laws. National really be lieves that the removal of
rights for all workers in their first 90 days of employment will encourage employers to
take workers on. It cites research that is, qu ite frankly, baloney, and it absolves itself of
any responsibility for skills training, for industry development, and for doing something
16530 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
about the large and growing number of our young people who are not in a job or even in
training.
I note, after the contribution from the Minister of Labour, Kate Wilkinson, that in the
UK David Cameron, the Prime Minister, is now proposing a 2-year trial period. The UK
has had a 1-year trial period for years, a nd David Cameron is using exactly the same
language that we are hearing from that Minister about it. Obviously a 1-year period did
not work, so there will be something else.
National is developing a narr ative that says employers are saviours, and workers,
particularly low-paid workers, should be grateful for any job, and if they are not, the
Government will punish them. Not all employers agree with this, and I want to make
that clear. I know that sin ce we have had the 90-day employment law many employers
have entered into agreements with unions, be cause they say they do not need to have
those sorts of tools. They ha ve relationships with unions, and they have the ability to
think beyond harsh measures like that.
But this Government is now telling workers in the State sector—and has been for at
least the last 2 years—that they are worth nothing either, that they  can expect nothing
from this Government, and, again, that they sh ould be grateful to keep their jobs. No
one has a problem with regard to impr oving efficiency and productivity, but the
National-ACT Government believes that a job in the public sector is not a real job. I ask
the Government to tell that to the nurses and see how it gets on.
I heard the Greens and the M āori Party calling today fo r there to be a higher
minimum wage. I have to say it seems as though the phone is off the hook when it
comes to the M āori Party talking to National about such important measures. But I say
good on the Greens and the Mā ori Party, because Labour agrees with them. If Labour
had not been in power for the previous 9 y ears, I believe that the minimum wage would
still be sitting at around $10 an hour and $7 an hour for under 20-year-olds. I am
grateful for small mercies: at  least the minimum wage for our lowest paid has not gone
backwards. But how will a 1.9 percent increase in  pay cover 4 percent inflation? That is
all that workers on the minimum wage will re ceive. That 25c an hour will not add up to
the cost of a litre of milk at the end of th e day, let alone a block of  cheese at the end of
the week. We are talking about an increase of $8 a week. A person who works full-time
on the minimum wage will now receive $437.24 a week after tax, while John Key gave
himself and his wealthy mates $1,000 extra per week in tax cuts. [ Interruption] I tell
National members not to lecture members on this side of the House about the minimum
wage.
It is no wonder that more and more peopl e in New Zealand are talking about the
growing inequalities in New Zealand, and no wonder that young people like my son and
his partner are feeling disillusioned. John Key promised that life would be better for all
Kiwis under National, but his bonus for those who slave for the minimum wage is $8 a
week. It is $8, and then we have to add in a ll of the extra costs that those workers have
to fork out on. The increases in the cost of power that workers read about in the notices
that they received in the mail in the last w eek will absorb that $8 a week, for a start.
That promise has been broken, as well. J ohn Key said all New Z ealanders would be
better off under National. They are not; things are getting worse, not better.
John Key also promised that we would catch up with Australia. Its minimum wage is
now NZ$19.75 an hour—more than 50 percent greater than our minimum wage—and
that is just the minimum wage. Actually, mo st industries in Aust ralia have a higher
minimum wage set in its modern awards system based around the industries. So again
we can see why more and more people are moving over there.
W
hat is really galling for low-paid work ers is that when South Canterbury Finance
needed to be bailed out, money was no problem. Money was no object when John Key
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16531
gave tax cuts to the wealthiest people in the country and gave himself $1,000 a week.
Money was no object when the Americans came calling with their threats about The
Hobbit, nor was the removal of rights for thousa nds of workers in the video and film
production industry. That was not just for the actors but for the tradespeople, the
cleaners, and the catering workers. It wa s a disgusting sell-out of New Zealand
sovereignty and a sombre message for New Zealand workers.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Wayne Mapp
items.text: It was not. Labour was prepared to sell out the whole
industry.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: It was a disgusting sell-out, I say to Dr Mapp. But for this
Government money is always a problem when it comes to the lower-paid and the
struggling middle-income families in New Zealand. Money is always a problem for
them, but not for the better-off. The message to the large number of New Zealanders in
this situation is that their contribution doe s not matter. So our children will leave,
because John Key’s claim that he is ambitious for New Zealand has been shown to be
just a lot of hot air.

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: The gloves are starting to be taken off as
we face up to the choice at the end of N ovember. I have to say that the choice has
become rather clearer a lot sooner than I would have expected.
From the Government’s side, the Prime Minister has laid out what we represent
today for New Zealanders. Essentially the cen trepiece from an economic perspective is,
to use his own words, that we must m ove this economy away from debt-fuelled
consumption. There are other ways of putting it but that is as good as any way one
could find. What does that mean in practical terms? It means a number of different
things. First of all, it means continuing with  what I would describe as a very moderate
programme of fiscal consolid ation. We know what happened  with 9 years of Labour:
core Crown expenditure went from $32 billi on to $60 billion as truckloads of money
were deposited outside Government agencies’ doors. We know that the average annual
increase in core Government spending was $2.8 billion and we have tried to hold it to a
tad under $1 billion. It is not an extrem e position but fiscal consolidation is an
absolutely central part of moving away from debt-fuelled consumption.
Secondly, we are trying to streamline the public services and although we will hear
an enormous amount of rhetoric from other pol itical parties on this issue, it is actually
entirely possible to do that while deliveri ng better services to New Zealanders with
fewer resources—not radically fewer res ources, but we are essentially seeking
efficiency gains. In the last 9 years of the Labour Government, the public sector was not
asked seriously to face up to the need to produ ce more with either the same or slightly
fewer resources. Seeking efficiency gains is the second objective. It is the way that we
will try to move this economy away from debt-fuelled consumption.
Thirdly, we are absolutely 100 percent seri ous about not letting this very delicate
international economic situation spook us. We are proceeding with further investment in
the infrastructure of this country. We must i nvest in our own future in order to generate
the growth that New Zealanders will need to  pay for all the social services, education,
and other things that we all want and value. Part of that process will involve, in terms of
capital expenditure, looking a little more cr eatively at mixed-ownership models. Again,
we will hear from Labour for the next 10 months that we are selling off the family
jewels and silver, blah-blah-blah, but that party is not listening to the conditions that the
Prime Minister and Mr English have so very clearly laid out. We will retain 51 percent
Government ownership of those assets, and we will deliver good services. When Labour
talks about electricity prices , we are reminded that the average annual increase in
electricity prices over the 9 years of the previous Government was 9 percent per annum.
Yet Labour talks about the threat of electricity price rises.
16532 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
The next element carefully laid out in the Prime Minister’s speech on our programme
for this year—a programme in which he sa id that 2011 must be the year for New
Zealand—is that we will vigor ously promote export growth. We have some advantages
now of a very good pattern of trade opportunities. We have excellent commodity prices.
Let us back ourselves. Let us back ourselves to shift more and more resources into the
export side. As the Prime Minister pointed out,  when we look at the last 5 years of the
Labour Government, we see that not one new net job was added to either the efficient
import-competing or export sect ors. It was all in the cons umption side of the economy,
fuelled by debt.
The next element in our choice for New Zealanders is that we will continue—again,
in a very moderate and sensible way—to simplify, which is the word I use, the
regulatory frameworks. Members heard the Pr ime Minister outline the key elements
around more sophisticated work on the Resource Management Act and more flexible
labour markets. This work will actually end up creating jobs for companies that need the
flexibility to take the risk of employing people as they m ove forward in the uncertain
environment that New Zealand, along with all countries in the world, faces.
Finally, I instance that we are about incentivising middle New Zealand. We are about
creating a basis where middle New Zealanders  can see a way forward for themselves
and their families. Since September 2008 th e average after-tax income of all New
Zealanders on the average wage has increa sed by $64 per week, which is a 16 percent
increase.

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: Rubbish!

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: The member should just look at the statistics. That is a 16
percent increase in the average after-tax sala ry. After taking away 6 percent in price
increases, it means that a Kiwi on the average wage is earning after tax 10 percent more
today than they were in September 2008. That is on the Government side.
I talked earlier about a rather clear choice that I think is emerging for the public to
make in late November. So what does it look like on the Labour si de? I was reading an
offbeat article in the New Zealand Herald by Mr Brian Rudman. I was reading it
carefully. I cannot say that I always agree with Mr Rudman, but I thought he made a
very interesting point. His thesis was sort of like this: the summer holidays are over, it is
back to work for everyone including the politicians, and what is the first thing that the
new white hope of the Labour Party, Grant R obertson, thinks would be a great idea to
kick off the year with? It is to have a new holiday, paid for by somebody else.
The same debate is going on about the minimum wage. We have made a very modest
adjustment that preserves the after-infla tion current minimum wage. Labour wants to
add $2 or something to it.
We have to try to reduce this debate to the actual reality of New Zealand. By normal
international standards, we do not have ma ny genuine small and medium enterprises;
we have micro enterprises. According to one study I recall, in 2005, 86 percent of New
Zealand enterprises consiste d of 5 people or fewer. Grant Robertson is asking
companies like that to pay for another da y’s holiday and a massive increase in the
minimum wage, if they happen to be empl oying minimum wage workers, which would
immediately generate demands for relativity  from the other workers they employ. How
could anyone believe that our companies ar e in a position, under the circumstances
facing New Zealand along with all devel oped countries—this very uncertain
international environment—to just sign a cheque with no consequences for the viability
of either their company or continuing the employment of those people? I am just
absolutely astonished by that.
When we put those two examples in the current debate alongside Labour’s emerging
programme, what does it really add up to when stripp ed of all rhetoric? I think it is very
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16533
clear what it adds up to. It is a policy of  spending more Government money and taxing
more. We have to ask ourselves what is go ing on here. If I look, for example, at the
interim report of the Savings Working Group, I find a couple of quotations that nail the
underlying position that I think we as a country  are facing. We can have different views
on what adjectives to use about New Zealand. We can have different views about the
specific policies that the interim report of the Savings Working Group, chaired by Kerry
McDonald, puts forward. That is legitimate. But I do not understand how anyone could
seriously have a different view about the unde rlying driver of what the group is talking
about. I will give members a couple of quotations: “The bottom line is that New
Zealanders collectively have been spending too much and saving too little … Its credit
is about maxed out. It’s time to get real … we’ve had the fun, the big spend-up … it’s
time to pay and lay a more secure foundation for future sustainable wealth.”
What is going on with Labour? Is that rea lly a tax-and-spend policy? As the Prime
Minister pointed out in his concluding comments, it suggests Labour has learnt
absolutely nothing from its last 9 years in Government. What is going on here? Is that
seriously an alternative Government policy structure that it is asking New Zealanders to
endorse at the end of November this year? One could provide different explanations, but
I am rather inclined to think that the re al motive here is to avoid an electoral
catastrophe. It is about shoring up the core vote to position itself for a possible win in

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: That was a very
interesting speech from the previous speak er, Tim Groser. There were some very
interesting points in there about shoring up the votes. He takes the flip side of the pain
and poverty that is being felt by a lot of fam ilies in this country and decries more tax or
whatever else. When one has ideologies th at mean that 82 percent of the tax cuts
recently given went to 3 percent of the people in this country, one has to ask what that is
about. What is that about, when we are ta lking about balancing the books and whatever
else? That is about looking after a certain clique, and making sure that it travels through.
It was very interesting that he talked about power prices. There has been a haphazard
return to the 9 years of Labour—the problem  supposedly is the 9 years of Labour. Let
us talk about the power prices that he talked about in relation to the figure of 9 percent.
Is it not funny that Genesis Energy recently increased its prices to consumers in
Gisborne by 10 percent? That came on top of the 2.5 percent rise in GST. Genesis
Energy is about to raise the price again, by 2.7 percent. Doing the maths quickly, in a
very short time the price will be nearly doubl e the increases that the previous speaker
