purported had happened under the last Labour Government. That is not counting all the
other times it has happened. At the moment it is a bit like cuckoo-land and like the king
with no clothes. National members are saying that everything is great, that all these jobs
are going to manifest out of space and out of the fog, that we will all be happy chappies,
and that we should just trust the Government.
There was so much talk about the national cycleway. I say that the only bike that will
be parked up around here in November is the one that the previous speaker, Mr Groser,
will get on and leave that building. Then he will  be back here sitti ng on this side of the
Chamber.
What are the costs and what are the realitie s for people? With these sorts of rises in
power prices the old people will not turn on their heaters over winter. They will snuggle
up in the blankets to get warm. We heard a lapdog speech from that member opposite,
in the sense of sucking up to the Prime Mi nister along with that lot over there, knowing
full well that they have achieved the 90-day employm ent legislati on that is stymying
people’s rights. It has cost a lot of our people their jobs.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: Oh, rubbish!
16534 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: Tau Henare knows that. In my electorate the
average wage is $15,000. It does not even come close to the $24,000 figure. National
members want to huff and puff about the unemployment rate. When the previous
National Government moved off the Treasury  benches it left behind a 28 percent
unemployment rate. In some places around th is country, like Wairoa and parts of
Hastings, unemployment is 50 percent.  Members should ask Craig Foss and Mr
Tremain about that rate. It is high, and Craig Foss knows that. Members should then ask
Mr Foss—because I know it pains him, and I respect him for that—about the closure of
the small businesses in Hastings and Napier at the moment. They total nearly 32.
If the Prime Minister’s stat ement is supposed to be a platform of policy that gives
surety to small and medium sized business, then something is going chronically wrong
in Napier and Hastings, I te ll Mr Foss. Even the good old latte drinkers are suffering
from a 3 percent rise. Coffee has gone up 15 percent. Poor people do not even have the
chance to have a go at that.
One of the most fascinating debates out th ere is about the great Public Service.
National members create all this doom and gl oom. They slip out of the framework of
proper budgeting and decent fiscals and in stead make people poorer, make people
suffer, and make them miss out. If we go to the chemist in Camberley at the moment or
the chemist in Kaiti and have a look at all the bloody medication that people—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: I am sorry, Mr Assistant Speaker.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Your speech will be terminated if you
are going to use that language.

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: The Assistant Speaker should have a look at the
bottles of medication that are pi led up there that people cannot afford to collect. It is a
disgrace. Members should go to Wairoa and go to the chemist. That is what they will
see. That is how we can measure things.

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: Why aren’t you sitting over here?

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: That is how we can meas ure things. That is why I
am sitting in this seat and that member is still sitting on the backbenches on the other
side. He will learn these thi ngs as he goes along, as I did in Government for 9 years.
That is why I am sitting here and the member is sitting there.
At the end of the day, that is the sort of  pain the Government has been inflicting on
our people. It is a shocker. The fact that the M āori Party signed up to the 90-day
legislation, which punishes the freezing workers and all of t hose other people, is quite
dippy. The previous National Government left us with 28 percent unemployment.
Labour brought it down to 4 percent. National members should put that in their pipe and
smoke it. Labour brought it down to 4 percent and generated skills. When this
Government came in, it cut in half the money for skills and training.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: Rubbish!

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: Oh yes, it did. Rents have increased by 9.5 percent.
Rates have increased by 9.3 percent. Doct ors’ fees are up by 6.5 percent. Early
childhood education costs have risen. The price of petrol has risen. I filled up the car the
other day and it cost $141. Boo hoo hoo! How is the average family going to manage
that? That is success? This economic adjustment is causing most people to be scared
about their jobs.
The previous speaker, in a mean-spirited way, said we should not Mondayise public
holidays. Let us not care about the peopl e. Why was every embassy in this city,
representing other countries,  closed yesterday? They ga ve their staff a holiday. Do
members know why? It is because we have a mean-spirited Government that believes
that the people do not deserv e an extra break. It would not hurt the majority of
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16535
companies. We have the highest price bei ng paid at the moment  for stock in this
country. We have the highest return on logs for 16 years in this country. The milk
butterfat price is up higher than it has ever  been. It is nearly double. That is good, but
what is happening with the wealth? Who is sharing it?
A lot of parents have been through agony and pain. The ones I talked to over the last
2 weeks cannot afford their kids’ school uniforms. What is that about? That is real stuff.
That is also about people wondering about what they should eat. They buy more spuds
than anything else. It is an indictment on this Government.
The tertiary institutions are announcing an increase of 4 percent. The universities
have capped the entries. Guess who suffers? Guess who misses out? It is the Māoris and
Pacific Islanders. It is all right for th e balding eagles who sit around, whose policies
pervade this country, and who believe th ey are helping people. Early childhood
education costs are going up. A lot of the kids are not getting the early childhood
education support. The Minister of Labour said a very interesting thing about the labour
market. She said the 90-day bill was the princi pal platform that would help. So we have
all the skill sets being cut.  Labour is clear on developi ng skills, on training, and on
ensuring that our economy is much like th e Australian economy and that our people
stop jumping over the ditch to live there.
Why are they leaving? One of the things we often heard in this Chamber when the
current Prime Minister was in Opposition was that everybody was leaving to go to
Australia. He has forgotten that tune. More pe ople have moved to Australia in the last 2
years than moved in any of the last 18 years. What does that tell us?

items.speaker: Hon Dr Wayne Mapp
items.text: Rubbish!

items.speaker: Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA
items.text: The member who interjects wants to spend
hundreds of millions of dollars on putting skyrockets on ships and planes. That is what
he wants to do. He wants to waste taxpayers ’ money on bombarding other people. He is
in cuckoo-land. He wants to go to war. At the moment the Government is warring on
the people in this country. It is making them  poorer. He does not want the Government
to give money to support the social services; he wants to put skyrockets on warships and
on tanks, and to play “boys’ ar my” with them. That is a disgrace; it re ally is. The
member should reconsider that stuff.
I know that Mr Foss is dying to get up an d explain why small and medium sized
businesses in Hawke’s Bay and Napier ar e closing down. He can explain why the
unemployment rate in Wairoa is between 40 and 50 percent, and why in those areas the
people do not know how they are going to pay the bills over the next week.
National members think they can use their old trick of gutting the Public Service.
Good old Public Service, we do not need it! But if the Government inflicts more bills on
people and puts more people into the poverty trap, then it will need the services of those
professionals and everybody else to help those people along the way.

items.speaker: National has a policy for saving money
items.text: put  skyrockets on the blinking frigates and
close down the Public Service. What a mess!

items.speaker: CRAIG FOSS
items.text: It is an absolute pleasure to follow the Hon
Parekura Horomia because no matter what I say, it will make more sense than what we
have heard over the last 10 mi nutes. I suppose there was so me kind of revelation there
that Labour is looking at priva tising the frigates or skyrockets or something, or that it is
trying to Mondayise Guy Fawkes Night or something. W hat is it up to? Members over
there are focusing on the issues that matter!
I say happy New Year to you, Mr Assistant Speaker, and to collea gues in the House.
It is 2011, and I am sure members opposite will  join me in backing the ABs this year. I
am sure they will. Like them, I am backing the “All Blues”. I am backing National and I
am backing the other ABs, the All Blacks, for Rugby World Cup 2011.
16536 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011

items.speaker: Hon Parekura Horomia
items.text: Oh, cut it out!

items.speaker: CRAIG FOSS
items.text: The Hon Parekura Horomia has joined me in backing the other ABs,
the “All Blues”, this year for election year 2011.
I must put some things straight. I have heard screeching from members on the other
side about borrowing for tax cuts or some thing ridiculous. There was a tax switch,
which kicked in last 1 October with some balance on 1 April this year. Yes, revenue
was lost from making the PAYE rates more fa ir and equitable. The losses of revenue
there were picked up by increasing GST, by changes to loss attributing qualifying
companies, which the members opposite sudd enly seem to have discovered, and by
various other changes to depreciation, etc.  The fiscal cost—both sides of the balance
sheet—of the tax changes introduced by this  Government and implemented last 1
October and this coming 1 April are actually fiscally neutral. So to hear screeching from
various members on the other side that ther e is borrowing for tax cuts or something
somewhat absurd is exactly that: just absurd.
I have heard some other points from member s opposite that I need to correct, for the
benefit of listeners out there. The early childhood education spend by this Government
is the highest on r ecord. It is $1.4 b illion—the highest on r ecord—and the Minister
announced another $100 million just the other day. But members opposite somehow
construe that increasing spending from $400 million to $1.4 billion over about the last 7
to 10 years is a “cut” in early childhood education. To be fair, the previous Government
put a lot of that spending in place. I do not know how members opposite get there with
that claim. It shows that further work on numeracy and literacy standards is demanded,
if they cannot even work that out.
I want to correct another point made by th e Hon Phil Goff in his speech. He talked
about early childhood education and I think he said there had been a 10 percent increase
in participation by Pacific Island children in  the last few years of the previous Labour
Government. He is totally wrong. There was a 10 percent increase in the number of
enrolment forms filled out for various instituti ons. In fact, the parents of a child could
have filled out many, many forms. The actua l participation rate by children in the
Pacific Island sector in particular, because  the member brought this up in his speech,
was basically stagnant. That is appalling given the increase in fiscal spend on early
childhood education. I note, for the recor d, how quiet members opposite became once
the brutal, hard facts hit the floor.
In 2011 National will continue to focus on the issues that matter. Members on the
other side will continue to disguise themselves with their tinkering and reshuffling of
the fresh new faces of Labour. But even Mr Goff is somewhat of a slow learner. I
understand that in his speech he did not move  an amendment to the motion, to show a
lack of confidence, which is traditional fo r the Leader of the Opposition to do. So after
26 long years in Parliament he did not even get that bit right . He is still learning, and
maybe after another 26 years he will get going.
In 2011 this Government will continue to  rebuild the New Zealand economy, after
the demolition job by the previous administration in its 9 long, wasted, fiscally rampant
years. However much members opposite try to  reinvent history, the numbers speak for
themselves. It was a decade of deficits, when thousands upon thousands of New
Zealanders abandoned this country and moved offshore. The previous speaker
mentioned migration numbers but he was absolutely wrong.
We will continue to reallocate resources from head offices, headquarters, and
bureaucrats and move them to the front line. We have found $4 billion of savings so far.
That is $4 billion that does not have to be borrowed or raised by taxes. That is $4 billion
of better allocation of taxpayers’ hard-earne d money, exactly as householders have to
do every single day. We will continue to keep in terest rates lower. Members will recall
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16537
mortgage rates at 10 percen t under the previous administ ration. They are nowhere near
that under this current administration, because of our prudent fiscal management.
The “borrow and spend” and “borrow and co nsume” game is over. It is no more. It
does not happen. We will continue to constrai n the growth of the Government sector,
which constantly crowds out the real sector that creates real jobs and real income for
real families. We will keep an eye on ne w spending. Members will recall that the Hon
Michael Cullen had about $2.8 billion of ex tra spending each and every single year
under that administration. We have brought  that $2.8 billion down to $1.1 billion and
now we are targeting $800 million to $900 million. That is still huge money but it is on
top of us discovering and reallocating $4 b illion within the economy. We will continue
to get more value from each and every single tax dollar and we will treat it as preciously
as every single household has to. We are transparent about this.
I congratulate the Hon Bill English on the investment statement on the accounts of
the Government of New Zealand. For the firs t time we have some hard numbers where
we can make some hard or difficult choices on the allocation of scar ce capital, which is
basically borrowed money. I ag ree with the quote made by Hon David Cunliffe just
before this House rose at Christmas. He said that New Zealand needs “to unleash State-
owned enterprises to create and grow new subsidiaries with private partners and
shareholders”. That was said some 50-odd days ago. What has changed? I agree; we
should unleash the awesome potential that is in our balance sheet. When we allocate
capital in the wrong place, that means the non-development of a hospital or less for our
health sector. I do not know whether Mr Goff agrees with this, and it appears he does
not, although maybe that is part  of the leadership stuff goi ng on over there, but I cannot
believe that Labour members oppose such th ings. Why do they oppose the ability of
New Zealanders to invest in their own future—in their own assets? Why do they oppose
the ability of New Zealanders to have a m odel to invest in for 20, 30, or 40 years for
their own future? Why do they oppose the changes proposed to allow KiwiSaver
accounts to allocate investments within these borders?
The previous Government set up KiwiSave r, and I say: “Good on them.”. Members
opposite should claim that, but they will not a llow KiwiSaver to be all that it could be.
Why would they do that? I do not understand. They introduced it, to be fair. They
should watch this space because we will be concentrating on savings, investment, and
better management of every single taxpayer dolla r this year. But I guess it is part of the
confusion about why they are opposing it. Mr Go ff now says that the asset sales of the
1980s and 1990s by a former Labour Government  were all a mistake. Yet the previous
Labour administration had 9 years to buy those assets back. It did not, although it had 9
years to buy back those assets that it says now should not have been sold. Their past 9
years in Government were the best economic times and they blew it. I will not go into
too much detail about the facetiousness of , and lack of integrity in, Mr Goff’s
observation.
The world has changed over recent years. It  is no longer an option to spend, borrow,
and consume. The global financial crisis or recession has put a brutal focus on
countries’ balance sheets, both private and public, in terms of their total debt. Whether
or not they like it, the creditors are watching very, very carefully. If this Government is
able to do what the Prime Minister outlined in his speech—to star t to bring the spend
down, to bring back more efficiency to the taxpayers’ balance sheet—then we will be in
a much, much better place and we will begi n to build a much better and stronger
economy. Thank you.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: How quickly those members opposite
forget about the people who put them into Government. How quickly they forget about
the hard-working New Zealanders who pay their taxes, who ar e doing it tough, and
16538 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
whom the Government now talks about as if  they are simply numbers. They forget
about the personal lives that lie behind thos e numbers. When Bill English comes down
to the House and talks about the increase in unemployment he talks about the numbers
but he forgets the people who are behind thos e numbers. He forgets the people, their
families, their mortgages or rents, their supermarket shopping bills, and their power
bills. He forgets the people who are doing it tough.
This Government has already forgotten a bout those people. It has forgotten about
them because Government members are interested  in only one thing: they are interested
in rewarding people who are like themselv es—that is, people with money. They are
interested in the people who backed them. That is where this Government has been
focusing its efforts. It has focused its ta x cuts on the people on the highest incomes
while the people on the lowest income s and other ordinary, hard-working New
Zealanders—middle New Zealand—get clobbered  with an increase in GST that more
than cancelled out the tax cuts they r eceived under the National Government. Those
people get clobbered. The people in the middle a nd the people at the bottom of the heap
get clobbered by this Government—by the “Paris Hilton” economics espoused by
people like Wayne Mapp. They get absolutely  clobbered by the National Government,
while the people on the highest incomes get rewarded.
That is the first message that this G overnment is sending through the Prime
Minister’s statement this year. It does not  care about the people at  the bottom. It does
not care about the people in the middle. It cares only for the people at the top. Bill
English inherited an economy in very good sh ape, and he set about running it into the
ground. New Zealand had record low debt when Bill English became the Minister of
Finance. What did he say? He said this is the rainy day we have been saving for. The
previous Labour Government saved. It paid  down debt. What has this Government
done? It has given out tax cuts to the people who needed support the least, and now it is
borrowing—what is it—$300 million a week to pay for the tax cuts for those at the top
of the heap. This Government inherited a record low unemployment rate, which was
either the first or second-lowest unemployme nt rate in the developed world. That is
what National had when it became the Govern ment, but what has it done? Well, it has
turned that round. It has turned that r ound well and truly. This National Government
wanted to catch up with Australia. Well, it has caught up with Australia in respect of the
unemployment rate; we now have a much higher unemployment rate than do the
Australians.
So what is the Government’s solution to the problems of the New Zealand economy,
and to the fact that we are borrowing $300 m illion a week? It is to sell some stuff:
“Let’s sell some stuff! We’ll sell the SOEs.” The Government will sell the energy State-
owned enterprises, it will priv atise accident compensation, a nd it will privatise prisons.
It says “Let’s sell things.”, because that is what people do. When they cannot afford to
pay the mortgage they sell the house. But they can sell the house only once, and then
where do they live once they have sold the house? That is not a solution to our
economic woes and our financial difficulties. We should not sell stuff, because it can be
sold only once. What will the Government do? What will Bill English do once he has
sold those assets that first time? Actually, Bill English will not need to worry about it
because he will be long gone by the time that eventuality rolls around.
This Government is clobbering the people at the bottom, and it is clobbering the
people in the middle. John Key said in his speech that a society could be judged by how
it treats the most vulnerable. Well, let us judge this Government on that. Let us judge
this Government on that sentiment expresse d in John Key’s speech. Children are pretty
vulnerable; what has the Gove rnment done for children? It has cut funding out of early
childhood education, and as a result kids will either not participate in early childhood
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16539
education or have a lower qua lity of early childhood educa tion, or their parents will
have to pay more for that education. Those are the only three outcomes from the
Government’s funding cuts to early childhood education—pay more, get less, or simply
have a lower quality. Those are the things that will come out of the cuts to early
childhood education.
The Government has cut home-help time for elderly people. They are vulnerable, so
what has the Government done for them? It has cut their home-help hours. It has cut
support to some of the most vulnerable peop le. Victims of sexual abuse have had their
cover under ACC eroded away und er this National Government. It has cut the training
incentive allowance for people who are tryi ng to pull themselves up by their bootstraps
and get themselves back into the workforce.  This is a Government with no plan, but
what it is very good at doing is spin, and nothing illustrates its spin more than what it
has been doing in accident compensation. It is very clear that from the day this
Government came into office it had an agenda  to privatise our accident compensation
scheme, and it has set about trying to destroy the credibility of that  scheme in order to
justify more cuts and privatisation.
When people come from overseas they look at our ACC and our Pharmac, and they
say that they wish they had schemes like  that. Those schemes take lawyers and big
pharmaceutical drug money out of the health system, which means that health dollars
actually get spent on health care. But this G overnment wants to erode that and to do
away with that. How is it doing that? First of  all, it is attacking ACC’s credibility.
Government members have talked up a cris is. They have manufactured a crisis. ACC
does not have a financial crisis. In fact, it is on track to have a $2 billion surplus this
year, so there is no crisis despite what the Government is trying to do. But what is it
doing? It hiked up accident compensation levies so that people would get annoyed with
ACC. The Government did not need to hike up the levies, but it has done that anyway.
Then the Government cut ACC entitlements. It  cut entitlements so that 90 percent of
sexual abuse victims have been denied cover for counselling—90 percent of sexual
abuse victims have been denied cover through ACC for counselling. Government
members have nothing to say about that, because they know that if we judge them on
the sentiment that John Ke y expressed—about judging a so ciety by how it treats the
most vulnerable—there are not many more people more vulnerable in society than
someone who has been the victim of sexual abuse. Yet 90 percen t of them under this
Government cannot access counselling; 90 percent of them have been turned down for
counselling because of this Government’s cuts in ACC.
So why is the Government doing all this? It is doing all this because it wants to
privatise ACC, and because it wants to open up accident compensation to competition.
Why does it want to do that? Well, we ca n look at Merrill Lync h. Is Merrill Lynch
connected to the Government in any way? I cannot think of any. I think that  Merrill
Lynch may have some passing connection to the Government. Merrill Lynch let the cat
out of the bag when it said that the priv atisation of ACC under a National Government
would result in $200 million a year of wi ndfall profits for the private insurance
industry—$200 million a year of money woul d be transferred from hard-working
taxpaying levy-paying New Zealanders to the coffers of private insurance companies.
That is why the Government wants to privatis e ACC. That is why it  wants to do it. It
wants to increase the profits of private insurance companies. It wants to do that by
opening up ACC to privatisation, which will result not in money going into health care
or into injury prevention and rehabilitati on, but in m oney going into the bottom line—
the profits—of private insurance companies. What will the private insurance companies
do? Of course they will erode cover and erode entitlements.
16540 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
Any New Zealanders who have made claims to an insurance company, whether it is
for a burglary or a car accident, will know th at those insurance companies will screw
them down for every possible dollar they can,  but that is what every New Zealander
now faces under a privatised accident comp ensation scheme when they have an
accident. So when people are at their most  vulnerable they will be on the phone to a
private insurance company that will try to  screw them out of every possible dollar it
can. I think that that is not good enough, and Labour members think that that is not good
enough, which is the reason why we will oppose, tooth and nail, the National
Government’s plan to privatise ACC.
We have a good accident compensation scheme, despite what the Government is
trying to do in order to ruin its  credibility. Why do we know that?
PricewaterhouseCoopers was given a brief to  go anywhere in the world and find the
Government a scheme that was better a nd cheaper. Do members know how many they
could find? Not one! PricewaterhouseCoopers could not find a single scheme anywhere
else in the world that was cheaper, more efficient, or provided better cover than ACC—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Wayne Mapp
items.text: I can tell them one—the scheme we had in 1999.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Rubbish! That is not right; I w ill tell members about the scheme
in 1999, which was partially privatised. Wh at happened to one of the insurance
companies that was offering cover under th at scheme—HIH? It went broke, and the
Australian Government had to bail it out for $500 million worth of Australian taxpayer
dollars. It bailed out one of the schemes that was delivering cover under National’s
privatised accident compensation scheme. That  is what we can expect: the Government
will privatise the profit and socialise the losse s. That is what the Government will want
to do to ACC, but it will have a fight on its hands because Labour is opposed to the
privatisation of ACC and we will not have a bar of it.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Just before I start I think the
public of New Zealand need an explanation of the tactics that Labour and Green Party
members have been using today. It is a ve ry common tactic, which those parties use
when they are in this House: they try to build on the fear factor. They try to take
advantage of people in a time of weakness, and they try to have a submissive country of
people who will just listen and be told wh at should be done by the Government or
political party that those members attempt to  be. They use personal stories about people
who are in trouble, and about th eir family members, and all that. They are really saying
that a person has been in a situation but that it is the system’s fault. It is the system’s
fault that that person has been in that situation, it is the system’s fault that that person
has not had help, and it is th e system’s fault that that is  the situation we have as a
country, when there is actually a bigger and deeper reason for a lot of those situations.
People have choices in life, and in lif e people do make some choices. But Labour
members stand there and use fear tactics on pe ople. They go out ther e and say that this
is the big bad system that is against people,  but that Labour members are there trying to
save people from the system. But the reality is that Labour wants people to be under that
system so that it can control them and control that system.
Labour and Green members today have not wanted people to think for themselves;
they have wanted them to be told what will be done, because people can trust them.
That is their motto—people can trust those par ties to deliver what is needed in their
lives. These guys are so good; they can deliver all of that to people. That is just not
reality. It is not life, it is not how it works, and it is not how the Government works.
The Government is there to provide servi ces when it can. The Government is not
there to make your life a better place, nece ssarily. One has some choices in how one
does that; one has some choices in the educ ation one gets, the j ob one takes, and the
career one makes. It is not all about the Government and the people in this room
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16541
deciding that. People need to look at th at. They understand that, and that is the
fundamental problem that Labour has at the moment—they do not trust New
Zealanders. They do not trust the instinct of New Zealanders to recognise that New
Zealanders can build their own future, and they want a Government that gives them the
tools to build their own future. They do not want the Government to give them that
future, but to give them the right to build that future fo r themselves. There is a big
difference there, and it is a difference the public understands and the public wants. They
do not want us in this room to tell them, or to  make their lives. But they want us in this
room to let them live their lives and build those futures.
That is what National has done in the last 3 years, and that is what we will continue
to do. We will continue to give people the t ools to build a better future for themselves.
That is the guts of why people will vote for National at this election, because they know
that and, instinctively, that is what they wa nt. That is human nature, and that is what
National stands for.
Labour said they left this economy in good sh ape. Let us have a look at this. This
country was in recession before the rest of the world. Labour put this country in
recession before the rest of the world. Before we had the world meltdown in financial
markets, Labour had put New Zealand into recession.

items.speaker: Hon Steve Chadwick
items.text: The Government inherited the books in a wonderful state.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Oh, the wonderful start! We were in recession when we came
into power because Labour had put us there. They had put us there, and in the best of
times. Those were the best of times—those times were the golden years that people
were talking about in the House earlier  today. Labour managed to squander those
golden years and put this country into reces sion. Then we had a world recession on top
of that. If we had had Labour in power wh en we had that situation, it would have
worsened. We would not be dea ling with the unemployment rates we have to deal with,
we would be dealing with the unemployment rates the US and England have to deal
with. That would be the legacy of Labour if they had their power.
But the reality is that National came i n. We actually delivere d a situation and a
system that will enable New Zealanders to go through this recession and to deal with it
in the best manner they can so that there is the least impact on our lives and on our
country’s finances, while at the same time setting up the structures and the vision for a
stronger country. That is what John Key was talking about over the last year or so when
he talked about infrastructure, when he ta lked about those changes in the tax system,
and when he talked about using outside capital and investing in Government enterprises.
It is about building a new system, a system that will enable New Zealanders to take
advantage of their opportunities—for example,  when we look at the tax switch where
we have taken away from consumption and given people a return for their income. It is
about sending a signal to New Zealanders that they do not have to spend to have the
lifestyle they want; they can invest and get the lifestyle they want. If they earn money
from having a good job and a good education, that  can lead to prosperity in the future
for themselves and their country, rather th an going for the consumption, debt-driven
approach that Labour has been portraying.
That fundamental difference has been portr ayed when talking a bout investment in
Government assets. It is about giving New Zealanders the abili ty to invest in things for
their retirement, and it is about giving them the opport unity to put money into
constructive, growing enterprises that deliver real goods, real services, and real jobs for
New Zealanders. It is about building a st ronger country so we do not have the
Government of the day going in there, nick ing those assets, and taking the cash out of
them when they desire to pay for petty election promises. That has happened in previous
administrations. It is about building a new culture, a new attitude to investment, and a
16542 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
new attitude to how we approach the way we deal with our economic and personal lives.
That is something that was very strong in  what the Prime Mini ster has been going
through, and that is a message that is coming together.
New Zealanders are seeing that message, th ey understand what it  means, and they
understand that they have been given that  opportunity by the G overnment. They have
been given a chance to take advantage of th eir circumstances. They will do so because
we are backing them, and New Zealanders are fundamentally going to take advantage of
those opportunities.
When we look at the economy at the moment we see that we are getting good prices
overseas for our commodities. That will continue ; that is part of where we live in this
world. We have those Asian economies doing so well, and we truly need to take
advantage of that. But we cannot take adva ntage of that if we do not have the
infrastructure in our country to enable those industries to actually provide those
products at the best possible quality and at the lowest possible cost. We also need to
provide the infrastructure so that othe r industries can develop and grow around our
fundamental core industries.
National has been doing that, and I would like to pay tribute to the Hon Wayne Mapp
in the science and innovation field. He has done a tremendous  job in that area, and it
will be a shame to see him leave Parliament. His contribution to that area is very
important, because it delivers those indus tries that will actually build on our
fundamental core industries, and give New Zealanders a lot of opportunity and direction
going forward.
We live in very difficult times, but these di fficult times have been navigated by this
Government as best as was possible. We have not only navigated those very difficult
times but we have set up a vision for New Zeal anders that they can share and be part of.
It is not a vision based on fear, or on subm issive tactics of saying that somebody has
something and other people should have it, even though they have not earned it. Our
vision is not that the world is some kind of fearful place, or that everything just drops
down from the sky—we are not saying that. We  are saying that people have the chance
to go out there and make the most of their opportunities in this country and in this
world. It is our job to provide the infrastructure and the ability for New Zealanders to do
that. That is what we are doing.
We are not providing people with  the solution in their hands so they can eat it then
and there; we are giving people the seeds so  they can go out there and make their own
solutions and their own visions and directions  in life. That is a big difference; New
Zealanders want that, and Ne w Zealanders will vote for that at the end of the year,
because they understand that that is a funda mentally more important thing for them to
have than for them to be given. They want to earn it, not be given it.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: I endorse the
comments from my Hamilton colleague David Bennett. He outlined the reasons why
those tax-and-spend and tax-and-consume days are over. He understands that New
Zealanders now understand that we can no long er have a Government that sprays cash
around every 3 years, and then spends its last year explaining why things have not
improved. We are not going to enter this election in a competition with Labour
members about how we can lolly scramble out  there more than th ey can. I tell those
members to listen: we surrender. Labour me mbers can throw cash around this country
better than we can. All of them in Father Christmas uniforms look much more
convincing than we do. Goff running around, lo oking like Father Christmas with his 30
or 29—or are there 17 MPs left , I do not know—elves left on that side of the House,
spraying around lollies and cash, looks much  more convincing than John Key doing it,
because people expect from John Key, Bill English, and this Government a lot more
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16543
thriftiness, a much more conservative appr oach, and a much more frugal and sensible
approach than they expect from Phil Goff. So we surrender—we surrender. We are not
going to spray cash, we are not going to throw out presents, and we are not going to
tempt the public with sweets; we give in. We are quite simply saying that the days of
tax-and-spend, consumption, and increasing borrowing are over. I think the member
from Hamilton put that quite succinctly.
I would like to explain something else to Labour colleagues and those who are
listening. I have been extremely concerne d as to why Labour members are asking
questions about housing, and perhaps their questions are why the Prime Minister
decided to address housing in his speech today. They are asking why rents are going up.
I remember that when they were in Govern ment they were asking why the prices of
houses were going up, so I will back up to quite basic, straightforward economics.
Nothing has changed. The more houses there are on the market, the lower the price of
the houses.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Say it again?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: The more houses there are on the market, the lower the
prices of the houses. That is because when there are plenty of houses to choose from
and there are just a few buyers, house vendor s and people building houses have to drop
their prices. So that is the fi rst concept for Labour. The second concept is that the fewer
houses there are and the more buyers, then  house prices will go up more. The fewer
houses there are on the market, the more buyers there are, then house prices go up. Why
is that? That is because there are very fe w houses and lots of buyers, and, therefore,
people are competing for the houses, so the hous e prices go up. I want to explain that to
the Labour members.
Labour members might ask why, when they were in Government for 9 years, house
prices went through the roof. Moving back to what I previously sa id, that is because
over the term of the previous Labour Gove rnment we were not building enough houses.
Builders found it hard to build houses. Why? First, it was because consents—building
consents and resource consents,—took so long to go through the system because of the
bureaucracy. Second, it was because land wa s not released. The previous Labour
Government had the view that there was no land in New Zealand around any town or
city that would be useful fo r housing. Even if land was covere d in gorse or tea-tree or
had no other use whatsoever, Labour was ve ry scared to open up new land to housing.
The third reason was that interest rates dur ing the period of the previous Labour
Government, particularly during those middl e years, were around 8, 9, and 10 percent,
so people were not prepared to borrow m oney to buy or build a house. House prices
went up because fewer houses were being built and more and more people wanted them.
Why were fewer houses being built? It wa s because the consenting process was
difficult, no land was made available to bu ild the houses on, and in terest rates were
high.
Now Labour members ask why rents are goin g up, particularly in Auckland. It is
quite simple. I will go back to those initial principles. More people want to rent houses
than there are houses available to rent. So what happens is that 10 houses are available
to rent but 100 people want them, so the rents go up. Why are there fewer houses to
rent? It is because fewer houses have been  built. So we need to build more houses;
whether one is buying or renting, the fact is that in New Zealand we need to build more
houses. The first way we will be able to do that  is simply to maintain interest rates at a
level where people want to borrow to either build or buy. Maintaining interest rates at 6
or 7 percent, which we have now, would be a good thing for New Zealand. John Key
and Bill English have laid out their economic pl ans to make sure that we keep interest
rates low and at a reasonable level—at the moment about 6, 6.5, 7 percent—in order for
16544 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
people to be prepared to build and to  buy. The second thing we can do—as we are
talking about Auckland—is start talking a bout what areas of la nd we can open up for
new housing. Do not be afraid of this. There are areas around Auckland where we could
have some new housing. In Auckland we coul d also demolish some housing that is old,
cold, and mouldy and make housing denser—in other words, not have so many quarter
acre sections, and perhaps put two houses on those quarter acre sections. The third thing
we can do is look at the Resource Management Act and the Building Act and look at the
way we allow the consenting process to drag on for 2 or 3 or 4 years.
National has made its views pretty clear to people. We want to make sure that house
prices remain stable and no longer spiral out of control into the future. We want to make
sure that rental prices are kept under cont rol, and the only way we will do that is to
build more houses. In fact, co lleagues might be in terested to know th at over the last
decade, including the period of the recession, builders have not been building enough
houses across New Zealand to keep up with either immigration or population growth.
Even before the recession, each year we needed about 22,000 to 23,000 houses, but
builders across the country were building only 15,000 or 16,000 houses. So we have a
housing shortage. Keeping interest rates under control, managing the economy, making
sure that we are streamlining consenting processes, freeing up new land for housing
developments, and allowing densification in towns and cities is the only way we will get
more houses.
Why does Labour insist on maintaining the red tape of resource consenting, the red
tape of the Building Act, insist there is no land in New Zealand for residential housing,
and maintain policies that spray cash around in  an election year and can only ever have
the result of sending interest rates sky high to  8 or 9 or 10 percent, where they were
roughly when Labour left office. I do not know why Labour is coming out with these
solutions. All I say is that we surrender. We will not run around with bags of cash trying
to bribe the public this electi on. Labour is better at that th en we are. We are not going
down that road. Labour can compete alone. This  election will not be a contact sport if
Labour is going to spray cash, because National will not engage in that at all.
It is fair to say in talking about housi ng that the Housing New Zealand Corporation,
which owns about 65,000 houses across New Zealand—almost one in 20 houses—is
making sure that it is better using the land. It is subdividing quarter acre sections now
and building two houses on those sections instead of one. It is keeping an eye on interest
rates and making sure resource consent processes are timelier too. So National is doing
its bit. John Key and the National Government will continue to do its bit in housing, and
we will not compete with the Labour when it comes to spraying cash around.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: E te Kaihaut ū o te Whare nei, tē nā koe. E ōku
rangatira, e ōku tuākana hoki, tēnā koutou katoa. Ng ā mihi nui o te tau hou ki a koutou
katoa. E tū pōuri ana au mō te matenga o tō tātou rangatira a Pīmia Wehi, e takoto ana i
waenganui i t ōna hap ū me t ōna wh ānau. N ō reira, e P īm ia, haere atu r ā, haere atu rā ,
haere atu rā.
[Greetings to you, Mr Assistant Speaker of th is House. Greetings to you, as well, my
leaders, and honourable members. Huge greetings  of the new year to you all. I stand
saddened at the death of one of our illustrious ones, P īmia Wehi, who lies in state

I want to first of all congratulate thos e who got a promotion and commiserate with
those who got a demotion. I have certainly known and experienced both of those

8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16545
why my good friend and colleague had b een demoted unceremoniously from his

items.speaker: Hon Mita Ririnui
items.text: Our kaumātua.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: I will get back to that one . Then I saw the Hon Parekura
Horomia deliver his speech in the Hous e today, and now I understand why he was
demoted.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: To continue on from where I was rudely interrupted by
time—

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: Time has been so unkind to the member.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: It has. I used to have a full h ead of hair. I want to say a few
more things. One of them is about the prev ious Labour Government’s ability to play
around with unemployment figures. I congr atulate Labour on getting unemployment
down—it is no mean feat—apart from it employing thousands and thousands more
public servants. The only job cr eation in the 9 years of the Labour Government was in
the Public Service.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: The member got a job in the public service.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: I was a public servant once.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: In here. It got you off the dole queue.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Oh, that is right. This is the new education spokesman for
Labour. He has not left school! He has not had a proper job! He has been at college, he
has been at university, and that is all he has done.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: Never been a union organiser.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: He has never been a union organiser, never worked for the
Department of Internal Affa irs, and never worked on the streets—sweeping the streets.
He has never had a proper job in his life, and now he thinks he can get up in this House
and pretend that he is going to  be the Minister of Educati on. Well, I have news for that
man: it ain’t going to happen. Come 27 November, what will happen is this: there will
be no change on this side of the House, and there will be a few ch anges on that side of
the House. Some of those members will be gone for ever, and some of them will be
back for another 3 years in Opposition.
I will now talk about something I think deserves a good debate in the House, and that
is vulnerable children, that is child abuse. It is an issue that we in this country should all
hang our heads in shame about. Child abuse is not our fault, and it is not their fault; it is
not the fault of anybody other th an those who perpetrate it on our babies. Quite frankly,
there is a way out of it. Ch ild abuse does not happen in a strong culture. Child abuse
does not happen among Mā ori in kapahaka. Child abuse is not part of the norm of a
culture. My wish is that we take hold of a renaissance of Māori culture and run with it. I
lived through the last recession, the big reces sion—in fact, I was one of the people who
were laid off in the 1980s. In that recession, people in the M āori community thought to
themselves: “OK, what about the rejuvenatio n of our language?”. Members should look
at kōhanga reo and look at kura kaupapa M āori. I will stand in this House and say that,
yes, the odd one or two gr aduates from
kura kaupapa M āori have gone off the rails, but
that it is very rare—very rare indeed.
I am talking about a part of our community, the Māori community, that is continually
under the spotlight. My cousin—my relation, or whanaunga—Hone Harawira got on
TV tonight and spouted on, blaming National for poor statis tics in housing, education,
and the economy. I was the Minister of Maori Affairs way back in 1996 and the
unemployment figures then were no different  from what they are today. We have had
three or four Governments since that time.
16546 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
It is time for our people to rise up, take th e bull by the horns and do it themselves as
they did back in the 198 0s, as they did with kō hanga reo and kura kaupapa M āori, and
not rely on handouts or any sort of goodwill from Government—of either party. We can
do it. Culture is all about the good things. It is not about the nasty stuff. Culture is about
the good things: waka ama, kapahaka , te reo classes, kura kaupapa M āori, k ōhanga
reo—they are all the good things that our t ūpuna, our ancestors, have left us. So my call
to our people is if they ar e not happy with the system, by all means they should go out
on their own. They should look at what happened in the 1980s, they should look at
people like Dame Iritana T āwhiwhirangi, they should look at the k ōhanga reo
movement, and they should look at the kura kaupapa M āori movement for what I
consider to be some of the answers staring us in our faces.
My hat goes off to those people in our community who, on the smell of an oily rag,
were able to run an early childhood centre. Here is something that the Labour
administration did. It required 100 percent of  the staff in an early childhood education
centre to be qualified.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: Good idea.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: It might be a good idea in la-la land, but who will pay for it?

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: The same people who paid for primary education.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Hang on. There have been $5 billion in promises so far.
Under Labour’s regime, it will steal money ha nd over fist from good working people,
just to pay for some promises it made to get back into power. At the end of the day, my
mother-in-law’s early childhood centre does not  need 100 percent qualified staff; what
she needs is qualified staff and the support of  mums and dads and her community. That
is what she needs, and she gets it. She does not need 100 percent of the staff to be
qualified.
I think it will be a great year this year, notwithstanding our massive win on 27
November.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: 26th.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: The day after. I will be suffering from a hangover after
beating Twyford in Te Atatū.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: Of course I hung on every word  of the Prime Minister’s
speech today, and what a disappointment it wa s to hear him utter no word about the
environment or conservation. I have to say that last year it was similar, although we did
have that little coded secti on of the Prime Minister’s statement that was entitled
“Unlocking Resources”, where the Prime Mini ster laid out his plans for mining our
schedule 4 conservation lands and expropriating fresh water in Canterbury for further
industry. I think his words were that any drop of water that reached the sea was
wasted—such a profound understanding of th e New Zealand environment and ecology!
So it was a disappointment to hear the Prime Minister’s speech, a disappointment that
was only deepened, I am afraid to say, when Kate Wilkinson, the Minister of
Conservation, got up to speak. She uttered no word in her speech about conservation,
either. She may well have been under instruc tions not to show up the Prime Minister’s
omissions, of course.
Sandwiched between those two statements from the Prime Minister last year and this
year we have been living through the International Year of Biodiversity. I guess the idea
of that international year was to celeb rate the success of th e Rio Declaration on
Environment and Development. But the way it has turned out in New Zealand and
around the world has been more of a requiem fo r the thousands of species that we have
lost and are still losing rapidl y. Lester Brown has talked abou t the crisis in biodiversity
the world is going through as the “sixth gr eat extinction”. The last was some 65 million
years ago when an asteroid hit the Earth. Th is one, of course, has been caused by the
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16547
actions of human beings. He calls it a “massive evolutionary se tback and a wholesale
impoverishment of life on Earth.”
New Zealand is a biodiversity hot spot and one of the world’s treasure chests of
unusual and fascinating life forms. Our plants  and animals are utterly unique—they are
not found anywhere else—and this is one of th e reasons that we love species like kiwi,
kereru, kahawai, kauri, and all of the othe r species that we work hard to protect.
Unfortunately, New Zealand also has a long record of extinctions. Many of our plants
and animals remain now on the verge of extin ction. We have a special responsibility to
protect the plants and animals that we love. The Department of Conservation has
identified some 2,788 species in New Zealand as being under threat. That includes all of
our frogs and bats, 89 percent of our reptiles, 65 percent of our freshwater fish, and 57
percent of our birds. They could disappear for ever with in our lifetime. There are
thousands more native species that we simply do not know enough about to know what
their level of risk is.
For over 100 years New Zealanders have been achieving some remarkable successes
in conservation against this tide, but righ t now only 6 percent of  those threatened
species identified as being at risk in New Zealand are actively managed to avoid
extinction. The risk to the remaining 94 percent is acute. It is true that the Wildlife Act
makes it an offence to intentionally kill  a native animal, and there are similar
protections for some plants. But the major threats to our plants and animals are
introduced predators, invasive weeds, and the ongoing loss and disruption of habitat. So
far we have failed to respond effectively to even one of those factors.
I have been in Parliament for only a shor t time, but I have already witnessed this
Government taking major backward steps in the protection of these native plants and
animals that we love. The most horrifying of  these was the Government’s step to cut
$54 million from the Department of Conser vation’s budget over 4 years, which has
massive implications. But that is not the only one. National has also cancelled the $4
million Community Conservation Fund that the Green Party established, in conjunction
with Labour, to fund community involvement  in local environmental conservation
work. National has closed an important po ssum control research programme, based at
Invermay, that was close to delivering new forms of possum control. National has failed
to move decisively to protect the M ōkihinui River from Meri dian Energy’s proposed
85-metre high dam. National has allowed commercial eeling of the endangered long-
finned eel, a species that is found nowhere else in the world and is listed by the
Department of Conservation as a threatened species in gradual decline. That is the same
status given to the great spotted kiwi, the little blue penguin, and the rifleman.
The Government has issued a new busines s-focused statement of intent for the
Department of Conservation, which has left  major questions around the Minister’s
statutory responsibility to be the primar y advocate for the conservation estate. The
statement of intent is entirely about commercial objectives for the department. The
House is about to debate—probably next week—the Regulatory Responsibility Bill,
which will tie the department’s hands even further when it comes to issuing businesses
with concessions on the c onservation estate, with the department losing statutory
responsibility to put the interests of our plants and animals first. At a time when New
Zealand is facing arguably the greatest crisis  in biodiversity in the history of human
habitation, one might have expected the Government’s priorities to emphasise a
response to these problems, rather than pr eparing the conservation estate for greater
exploitation and further losses.
Green Party members set themselves up to be the champions for the environment,
working alongside committed individuals and organisations right around the country, to
try to turn this tide on biodiversity loss. One small practical measure has been to launch
16548 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
the $4 million pilot project—in conjunction wi th the Government, which I recognise—
that aims to protect New Zealand forests a nd native species with be tter pest control,
using resetting traps. If that project is successful, it will reduce the costs of pest control
and the reliance on poisons. But the most significant work we are doing is yet to come. I
am working on a new member’s bill to enhance the protection of our most treasured
plants and animals. The United States, Canada, and Australia have all passed
benchmark legislation to protect and secure their native flora and fa una, and the critical
habitat that they rely upon. New Zealand, by comparison, lacks similar legislative
protection.
The Wildlife Act is antiquated and offers no effective legal protection against the
biggest threats. Even our native fish are left  without legal protection, or a plan for their
recovery. In the United States 85 percent of their threatened species are now covered by
a recovery plan. In New Zealand the comparable figure is the 6 percent I mentioned. My
bill will amend the Wildlife Act by revising  the purpose of the original Act to extend
the legal protection to all native flora and fauna, including fish. The bill will give effect
to the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development and the New Zealand
Biodiversity Strategy. The Minister will be required to  develop and implement a
thorough and science-based recovery plan for each of these native species that is
identified as threatened.
Like most New Zealanders, we in the Gr een Party love this country and all its
people. Our environment and our natural heritage are what makes this country unique
and precious. We are committed to doing whatever it takes to protect these features. It is
important for its own sake, of course, but  also because so much of our economy,
everything that we sell on the international stage, is dependent on that clean, green
image. We set out to make that clean, gr een image real. No environment; no economy.
If we trash the environment we sabotage our  economy and, more important, we rob our
grandchildren of their birthright. It is another form of borrowing from our grandchildren
to pay for short-term profit today, incurring a debt that neither this Government nor any
Government ever will be able to repay.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BOSCAWEN
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise on
behalf of the ACT Party to respond to th e Prime Minister’s speech. I take this
opportunity to acknowledge and congratulate the Government on much of what it has
done during its first term. I say “much”, but not all. However, amongst the
achievements have been the reform of th e Resource Management Act, which the ACT
Party has participated in, and the rati onalisation and streamlining of various
Government departments, and I should also mention the passing of ACT’s “three
strikes” law, which has alr eady started to make New Zealand citizens safer in their
homes and on their streets. I say it is AC T’s “three strikes” law because no one can
deny that that law would not be on our statute book but for the promotion of it by the
ACT Party. The Prime Minister freely acknow ledges that the “three strikes” law would
not have been passed without the ACT Party nudging and cajoling the National
Government at every step along the way.
The ACT Party and National have also im plemented, and then expanded, the 90-day
trial period for employment contracts. This has helped to align our employment
practices with those of the rest of the de veloped world. But, more important, it has
given employers the opportunity to take on new employees in the confidence of
knowing that if they make a mistake, they are able to find an altern ative employee. It is
important to give confidence to  employers so that new employees can be taken into the
workforce. The ACT Party, once again, was instrumental in getting that policy extended
to cover not just employers of fewer than 20 employees but all employers in New
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16549
Zealand, to give all empl oyers the opportunity  to improve their productivity and
employment of New Zealanders.
Although unemployment, at 6.5 percent, is hi gher than Australia’s  rate, we can take
some comfort from the fact th at it is not around the levels of the United States and the
United Kingdom, which have rates of around 9 and 10 percent. We are told informally
that if we included those peopl e who are looking to work fu ll-time in the United States,
the level would be closer to 15 percent. But the fact that our unemployment rate is
higher than Australia’s should be a concern to us. Already we have seen in the last week
the New Zealand Herald report that net outwards immigra tion to Australia is back on
the increase. We need to focus continually  on our relationship with Australia, because
unless we do and unless we move to reduce the income gap between New Zealanders
and Australians, we will see ever-greater numbers of New Zealanders move overseas,
and move overseas permanently. It is a fact  that for generations young New Zealanders
have travelled overseas to gain experience: to  gain job experience, and to seek out new
endeavours and new experiences. Traditionally they have always returned to New
Zealand, but increasingly they are not doing so. That should be a concern to all New
Zealanders, as more and more of our children and grandchildren grow up in countries
other than New Zealand.
It was this concern about the declining liv ing standards of New Zealand versus those
of Australia that caused the ACT Party to  campaign on reducing that gap. We made it a
fundamental plank of our 2008 election campaign. In fact, we put out a 20-point plan to
reduce that gap. As part of our confidence and supply agreement w ith National, we got
National to commit to the concrete goal of reducing that gap, eliminating that gap, and
bringing our living standards alongside t hose of Australia by 2025. The ACT Party,
once again, was instrumental in nudging National, and in convincing National to
appoint the 2025 Taskforce, chaired by Don Brash. It is a big challenge. As the task
force pointed out in its most recent report la st November, if we continue on as we are
doing now, we face the risk that a furthe r net 400,000 New Zealanders will leave our
shores for Australia by 2025.
It is interesting, then, that we have in this morning’s New Zealand Herald an
editorial entitled “National needs new policy for closing the gap.” The New Zealand
Herald reminds us that from the convenience of Opposition, National was able to make
promises, and was able to criticise the previous Labour Government’s position on the
economy. But the  New Zealand Herald  points out that the challenge of raising our
living standards is still there. It says the Government knew, and certainly knows now,
that comparative success relative to Aust ralia would require bold and disruptive
interventions. The New Zealand Herald says National is standing up and making that
commitment. Making a commitment to a concre te goal of lifting our  living standards to
the levels of Australia’s requires bold polic ies and courage. The ACT Party has always
led the way in promoting policies to raise New Zealand’s living standards and align
them with those of our closest neighbour. The editorial concludes by stating: “For its
own sake, New Zealand needs bold economic in itiatives that will  position the country
for sustained growth.” Let me repeat that  to the members in the House from the

items.speaker: National Government tonight
items.text: “For its ow n sake, New Zealand needs bold economic
initiatives that will position the country for sustained growth.”
It is the role of the ACT Party to advocat e for those bold initiatives and to promote
those policies. When I first rose this evening, I congratul ated the National Government
on much of what it has done. Tragically, it has done som e things that have not been
helpful for the economy, and that have not moved the country in the direction of
reducing that gap. I think of youth rates. I think of the National MPs voting against Sir
Roger Douglas’ member’s bill to reinstitute  youth rates. I will remind members for a
16550 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
brief minute of that debate. We saw the pr evious Labour Govern ment legislate to
abolish youth rates: legislate to require employers to pay 16 and 17-year-old young
people the minimum wage. What is the natural reaction of an employer when faced with
employing someone who is, say, 30, who has life experience, who has had jobs and has
gained skills experience, or when faced w ith employing a 16 or 17-year-old? It is a lay
down misère; it is obvious. Anyone who ha s spoken to employers knows that an
employer will go for the most experienced person.
Young people are being denied the chance to get on to the bottom rung of the ladder.
This Parliament has denied young people, young 16 and 17-year-olds, the opportunity
to go out and get a job at $11 an hour, $10 an hour, $9 hour, or whatever their economic
value is to an employer. We have said we will throw them on the scrap heap and give
them the unemployment benefit of $4.50 an hour. How does that help to raise New
Zealand’s productive capacity? How does it ra ise our prosperity? We have seen that
there has been a significant increase in yout h unemployment since th e previous Labour
Government first passed the legislation that abolished youth rates.
We have also seen a very significant cost  to the economy from the emissions trading
scheme. This scheme was introduced by the previous Labour Government. It came into
effect on 1 January 2008, and it  operates as a massive subs idy to foresters—a massive
subsidy to foresters. Essentially, what the previous Labour Government put in place was
a massive grant, a grant that essentially gi ves tree planters a one-o ff gain of about 230
tonnes of carbon. Mr Chauvel knows that is about $5,000 a hectare. The previous
Labour Government put into place a grants sy stem that requires New Zealanders to pay
some $500 million a year more for their electricity and petrol in order to subsidise those
massive subsidies. Nothing annoys me mo re, nothing makes me laugh more, than to
hear Mr Goff stand up and talk  about the price of electric ity and the price of petrol
going up. Mr Goff knows full well that the emi ssions trading scheme established under
the previous Labour Government would have resulted in not a 5 percent increase in
electricity but a 10 percent increase—a 10 percent increase in the price of electricity.
We can be thankful that the emissions tr ading scheme was modified by National, but
it should not have been put there in the fi rst place. It should not operate as a $500-
million-a-year subsidy to foresters. Mr Chauve l thinks that is funny; he thinks it is
funny. But I tell him that his Government put into place a system to pay massive
subsidies to foresters, and the Nationa l Government carried it on. Anyone in the
industry who is smart knows that. All New Z ealanders are paying for that subsidy with
their electricity and th eir petrol costs. If anything c ontributes to the gap between New
Zealand and Australia, it is the emissions trading scheme. Thank you.

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: This afternoon John Key to ld the House that he
thought Governments should be judged on how th ey treat the most vulnerable people in
the community. I would like him to know that that is exactly how this Government will
be judged on 26 November. If fairness is to  be the benchmark, th en the record of
National, ACT, the M āori Party, and Peter Dunne is shameful—it is shameful. No
matter how many catwalks John Key struts down, he will not be able to hide the fact
that his Government is just failing hard-working Kiwis. No amount of smiling and
waving will be able to hide the most worrying gap that New Zealanders face, the rapidly
widening gap between what John Key promised  in 2008 and the grim reality that we all
now face. That reality is that now, under National, ordinary people are just worse off.
No amount of spin from the Prime Minister’s  public relations team can hide the fact
that prices are rising faster than wages. He can smile all he likes about raising GST, but
at the end of the day Kiwis know that the real effect is that they ha ve to pay a lot more
for a lot less at the supermarket checkout . Mr Key can sm ile all he likes about
rebalancing the economy, but at the end of the day Kiwis feel in their pockets that prices
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16551
are rising a lot faster than their wages. The Prime Minister can smile all he likes about
leading a Government of aspiration, but at the end of the day Kiwis know that there are
no jobs and that there is no plan. They know th at the brighter future he promised is not
coming.
I had to laugh when I heard Mr Boscawen talk about the promise to stem the net
migration to Australia. A t housand Kiwis a week are leavin g these shores for Australia
at the moment. Two jumbo jetloads of Kiwis are leaving, because they know that there
is no plan for recovery in this country.

items.speaker: Hon John Boscawen
items.text: What’s the price of electricity in Australia?

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: Mr Boscawen asks about th e price of electricity in
Australia. He needs to understand that wh en Australia puts a price on carbon, as it
undoubtedly will, New Zealand’s renewable adva ntage will finally be recognised, and a
lot of people who think that the grass is greener on the other side of the fence on
electricity prices will have a big surprise coming.
On 26 November New Zealanders will have a very clear choice. They can stick with
the Government that has got us to th e point where 158,000 people are out of work,
including 25,000 Mā ori and almost 40,000 young people. The Government claims that
it is aspirational, but to have almost 30,000 young people aged 15 to 24 out of work and
in no form of training or education is sham eful. People could choose to stick with the
Prime Minister who promised not to raise GST, and who then did, and with the Prime
Minister who said that he would make su re that early child hood education remained
free, but who then cut its funding so that f ees have to rise fa r beyond what a lot of
ordinary families can afford. They can choos e to keep a Prime Minister who obviously
has no plan to create jobs or grow our economy, but who is hell-bent on selling off
assets that all New Zealanders already own, cu tting Public Service j obs and benefits to
all New Zealanders, and borrowing hundreds of millions of dollars at the expense of
ordinary Kiwis in order to fund unaffordable tax cuts.
But there is a fairer option—a Labour-l ed Government. Governments should be
judged, as Mr Key said earlier, on how they  treat the most vulnerable members of our
society. The difference is that our actions will match our words. A Labour Government
will not borrow for tax cuts or to raise GST,  or sell off assets that we already own. Our
team has a plan. We will put middle-income New Zealanders at the core of what we do,
and create jobs and growth by investing in research and development, by boosting skills
and trade training, and by changing the way in  which monetary policy works so that we
actually support our productive exporting sector. We will make sure that we own our
own future by preventing the indiscriminate sa le of farmland and other strategic assets
that ought always to stay in Kiwi ownership.
I have the privilege of being Labour’s environment spokesperson, and I was
delighted to be here in the House earlier to  hear the excellent contribution from Kevin
Hague, when he spoke about the shabby record that this Government has on
environmental matters. Anybody listening to th e outcome of the so-called Bluegreens’
conference in Christchurch a couple of week ends ago would absolutely despair at the
direction that this Govern ment is taking New Zealand on the environment. I do not
know how John Key and Nick Smith expect us to have a brighter future if they are bent
on destroying the environment that our future and our economy depend on.
It is amazing to me that National is so undemocratically pushing through so-called
national standards in schools while at the sa me time Nick Smith wants to relax the
standards for the air we breathe and to a llow more air pollution for a longer period of
time. Members on that side of the House need to know that the New Zealand Institute of
Economic Research says that we will s ee 635 avoidable deaths from respiratory
illness—Jacqui Dean thinks that is f unny, but I think th at anybody looking at it
16552 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
objectively would not have that smile on their face—as well as 505 unnecessary
hospital admissions and over 1 million extra si ck days. That is not a laughing matter, I
say to Ms Dean; that is something that any Government putting in place those decisions
ought to hang their head in shame about. The fact that John Key can talk about looking
after the sick and the vulnerable while allowing decisions like that speaks volumes
about the utter lack of compassion from members on that side of the House.
What I think is most telling about National’ s lack of commitment to the environment
is the refusal to set a 2020 target fo r reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Any
Government can wax lyrical about window dr essing and statements, as Nick Smith did
a couple of weekends ago about a 2050 target years and years away in the future, but
that is not showing real co mmitment to putting immediate ac tions in place to match the
Government’s words. Of course there is a reason why we are not going to see a 2020
target for greenhouse gas pollution reduction. Th is Government would not be able to
meet one, because every policy that it has im plemented in this term will make pollution
rise rather than fall, in the long term. Th e Government has watered down the emissions
trading scheme—and Mr Boscawen very conveniently failed to mention that—so that it
effectively operates as a—

items.speaker: Hon John Boscawen
items.text: I did—I did.

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: He says that he did, but it was so hard to understand what
he was saying that I did not realise it. The Government has watered down the scheme so
that it effectively operates as a massive subsidy from taxpayers to big polluters. The
Government has done away with Labour’s biofuels obligations, and it has scrapped
Labour’s plan to have 90 percent of energy generated from renewables by 2025. There
has been an absolute failure to invest in public transport—

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: It’s not possible.

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: Ms Dean, the genius on the benches opposite, says that it
is not possible. It is possible, I say to Ms Dean. I ask her to read  the Energy Strategy
that her Government has watered down, where there was a plan to get to exactly that
target. But what happened? Gerry Brownlee abolished it, because he has no
commitment to the environment, just like all of the Ministers in that Government on that
side of the House.
In Government, Labour would commit str ongly to supporting industries like the
cleantech industry, which has the potential not only to help to save our environment but
to add value in the order of, say, 10 percen t extra to our economy. But things like
cleantech are jeopardised by National’s appr oach to policy. Many fledgling cleantech
companies just cannot succeed without access to research and development assistance,
like the tax credits that National slashed. Ther e is no point trying to sincerely market
New Zealand’s cleantech businesses when the other Government policies that I have
mentioned already are fast destroying the clean image that we rely on to trade
internationally. The cleantech industry is so mething amazing that should be nurtured,
but I fear that it may never get the head start it needs when National is in charge.
Nobody looking at the record could rationa lly have any confidence in this
Government, because it has failed Kiwis and it has no plan. There is no plan and no
regard for the well-being of ordinary working New Zealanders. I am proud to be part of
a team that does have a plan and that w ill offer Kiwis a real alternative on 26
November.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: That contribution from the member Charles
Chauvel just highlights what an ideologically  driven party Labour is when its members
talk about the ordinary New Zealander. Mr  Chauvel says that Labour will put middle
New Zealanders at the core of what it does. We ll, that is a very interesting thing to say
in the context of the report that came out very recently from the New Zealand Institute
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16553
of Economic Research, which looked at the impact of the 90-day trial period over a 6-
