month period following its introduction in March 2009. The results of that trial period
are very interesting, and I will  read from a section of the press release about the report:
“Unemployment peaked at 7.1 percent th at year and considering the economic
conditions small businesses”—that is, ordina ry New Zealanders to the ideologically
driven members—“were operating under, the indication that hiring was almost 6 percent
points higher than expected is extremely good.”  Furthermore the repor t said that total
job numbers for these firms were also higher by about 2 percent.
In her contribution earlier today in this  debate the Minister  of Labour, Kate
Wilkinson, told the House that figure repr esented some 13,000 jobs. That is, 13,000
good, ordinary New Zealanders so beloved by the ideologically driven Labour members
have jobs. That, in my eyes, is success,  but how did Labour and Helen Kelly react?
They hated it. Why did they hate this initia tive, this 90-day free trial that has provided
13,000 jobs and has saved jobs fo r ordinary New Zealanders? Why did they hate that, I
ask Simon Bridges—

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: Because we did it.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: It was because we did it. If that is not ideologically driven to the
detriment of ordinary New Zealanders, I think it is a shame that Labour has the blinkers
down.
Charles Chauvel also talked about some ot her aspects of policy that National can be
very proud of. Minister Nick Smith relaxed the rules around air-qua lity standards. Do
members know why? It was because they were simply undoable. Those air-quality
standards were going to adversely affect places like Ranfurly and Alexandra down in
the South Island that have inverted air shed s over them and that were due to breach
those air standards a number of times per year. They simply could not conform to the
standards. We would have ended up with re gional councils prosecuting district councils
and citizens, and for what? Because the citiz ens in those towns could not afford to buy
clean-burning fuel. What is this Govern ment doing about that? We are providing
subsidies for people to put clean-burning wood fires into their homes. That is a success.

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: That’s Bluegreens.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: That is a Bluegreen initiative. What does Labour think about that?
It cannot stand it. Why can it not stand it?

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: It doesn’t involve more taxing.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: It does not involve more ta x and more borrowing, and because
National did it.
The drinking-water standards are anothe r example where National is in good touch
with the needs of community. Under the Labour Government, th e drinking-water
standards were unaffordable and were not doable. National is the Government that has
put the interests of the good New Zeala nd Kiwi—Charles Chauvel’s middle New
Zealanders—first. It has taken a National-led Government to do that.
This year the National-led Government will continue the work of the previous 2
years under the leadership of Prime Minister  John Key. Our focus will be on building a
stronger economy. This year the people of Ne w Zealand will have a clear choice. Come
26 November, they can choose. They can choose the tax-and-spend policies of the back-
to-the-future Labour Party, where taxing the so-called rich and either driving them out
of business or driving them over to Australia is its recipe for economic success. Or New
Zealanders—even Charles Chauvel’s middle New Zealanders; I thank Mr Chauvel—
will have another choice. They can have the choice of a Government that is focused on
building a strong economy and moving away from  the debt-fuelled consumption so
beloved of Labour towards real and enduring economic growth. This is the year for
good, strong economic policy and for growing the pie, if you like— to put it in the
16554 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
simplest terms—rather than just cutting it  up a different way, which is the sum of
Labour’s lack of aspiration for New Zealanders. Shame on Labour! Shame on Labour
for its lack of aspiration for New Zeala nders. Building a stronger economy is the only
way we will provide New Zealanders and their families and kids with better jobs, higher
incomes, and improved living standards.
I want to talk about education. We need to make sure that New Zealand kids have the
skills that they need to succeed. Our early childhood education investment has increased
by $100 million above the original 2010 Budget allocation.

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: $1.4 billion.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I thank my colleague Simon Bridge s, who is so on  the ball about
these issues—$1.4 billion is now being invest ed into our kids through early childhood
education. We are now at the stage where the taxpayer is subsidising early childhood
education centres at an average of $7,600 per ch ild per year. Is it not interesting that
although early childhood educa tion funding has trebled over the past 5 years, the
number of little kids r eceiving early childhood education has increased by only 1
percent. It makes no sense th at in some parts of New Z ealand up to 40 percent of
preschool kids receive no early childhood ed ucation before they go to school. So
National is bringing spending under control an d targeting funding at children who need
it most.
Members should not tell me that tired ol d story of mothers, grandmothers, and
aunties who cannot make a contribution to th eir child’s learning. They should not tell
me that sad old story that we need to ha ve 100-percent trained early childhood teachers
in early childhood centres. They just should not tell me, because as a mother and a
grandmother I know that I can make a very good contribution to my own children, my
grandchildren, and anybody else’s children who care to have that contribution to their
early childhood education. Labour should try selling that story to the parents of the kids
who go to Papakai ō School, whose kids in a little coun try town mostly went to parent-
led early childhood centres—they  went to playcentre. They should not give me that
story. Of course, Labour has said that it wi ll reverse this Government’s sound financial
decisions, but it has no idea how it would pay for it.
Let us talk about national st andards. Let us ta lk about a story about a mother who
came into my office to tell me about her little  8-year-old kid. This  little 8-year-old boy
brought home his first nationa l standards report. Mum and Dad were surprised and a
little concerned to learn that their 8-year-old boy was falling behind in his mathematics.
What did they do about it? They went straight to school and they talked to the teacher.
The teacher was a little surprised and a li ttle concerned, but said: “Why don’t we try
this?”. So the parents and the teacher worked out a plan for that kid. They went home,
they did the Cuisenaire rods—my colleague  Simon Bridges will not even know what
Cuisenaire rods are.

items.speaker: Simon Bridges
items.text: I thought you said “questionnaire” wrong.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: They are little counting sticks . They did the homework, and in
about 3 weeks’ time that little 8-year-old boy was re-tested—[Interruption] Labour does
not like to hear this. That is the thing about La bour: it does not like to hear the truth.
That little kid, after about 3 weeks, was re -tested, and guess what! He was back up to
doing maths at the normal standard. That is na tional standards, and that is why Minister
Anne Tolley is absolutely on the right track and has the support of  parents and students
up and down the length of New Zealand.
Mem
bers should try telling otherwise to the parents who go into the schools, talk to
the teachers, and fix the problems for thes e kids, who know they are not achieving. The
mother said this little kid knew he was not do ing so well, and he di d not feel very flash
about it. Actually, I was not very good at maths—I still am not, but never mind. This
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16555
kid knew that he was not doing so well. Now he is. His self-confidence has come back
up. That is a success, and under this National-led Government, led by John Key, we will
continue this good work. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: That was an interesting
speech.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: It was a very good speech.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: It was a good speech for the evidence that it
provided, and will provide, to the Oppositio n. I asked my colleague Pete Hodgson
whether this was the first Government si nce the Lange Government of, I think, 1986-

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: —1987-88, which professionalised the whole
industry, that has believed in cutting early childhood education. I think it is. That
member, I think, failed to acknowledge, or did not know, what H2O or water was, so for
that member to stand up in this House, bag early childhood education, and say that the
Government has not cut the funding is absurd. I challenge that member to answer this
question: if the Government has not cut the funding, why has Swannanoa Preschool,
which has publicly stated that it loses $100,000 per year, lost that money?

items.speaker: Michael Woodhouse
items.text: Blind ideology.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Well, here is another bit of blind ideology. That
early childhood education centre happens to be 300 or 400 metres from the residence on
Tram Road of the Minister of Labour. Ms Wilkinson came out and said that the
Ministry of Education has said that the 34 early childhood education centres that would
receive a cut in funding—there were abou t 54, but 34 would receive a cut, which
equates to around $800,000 to $1 million a year —would lose in total $29,500. At least
she acknowledged it was a cut! Yet the centr e closest to where she lives—as Jacqui
Dean has a giggle on a lapt op or a BlackBerry—loses $100,000, which is three times
what the member said the total amount would be. Redwood Early Childhood Centre
loses around $70,000 to $75,000. If it is not a cu t in funding, can the member with her
Cuisenaire rods tell us w hy those two early childhood edu cation centres are losing a
total of $174,000? She should get out the ab acus, borrow the Cuisenaire rods from
Gerry Brownlee—I am sure he is still using them—and answer that simple question.
Will the member answer me?

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: I’ve got you going.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: She will not answer the question. Anybody with
half a brain—I know that member may struggle—knows that if an early childhood
education centre loses in their budget $100,000, $74,000, or $1, that is a cut.
I want to talk about abandonment. That member talked about aspiration. I recall John
Key a year or two ago talking about aspiration. He said we need to aspire to greatness as
a country—we need to pick ourselves up, be lieve in ourselves, do better, and upskill
ourselves.
Returning to the great early childhood edu cation debate, the National policy states
that if an early childhood education centre like Swannanoa  Preschool, which is 300
metres from where Kate Wilkinson lives, though I do not think she has ever visited
there, decides it will upskill and go for the aspiration of having 100 percent qualified
staff, that does not mean—Jacqui Dean is a silly member—that parents will not take
part in the education of their children. Fo r goodness’ sake! Of course they will. But
because the early childhood education centr e says it will have 100 percent qualified
staff, what signal does the Government send ab out aspiration? It says if early childhood
education centres are going to go for gold and for 100 percent qualified staff, it will cut
their funding.
16556 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
I ask the member Jacqui Dean whether sh e would tolerate her children going to a
secondary school, university, polytech, or pr imary school in this country where the
principal fronted up and said that about 20 percent of the teachers who are teaching her
child will not be qualified. Would the memb er tolerate that situation, get out her
Cuisenaire rods, and say that she is qualifie d as a parent to teac h children algebra,
mathematics, English, or geography and prep are them for the National Certificate of
Educational Achievement and all those things? I do not think a parent in the land would
accept that. Maybe the Cuisenaire rod expert at the back of the Chamber would accept
it, but I do not believe that any parent—a nd I have talked to many parents—would
accept it.
So we had the politics of aspiration. What  are the politics of aspiration from John
Key, 2 years down the track? There is $2.5 bi llion worth of tax breaks to the top 10
percent of income earners, and 1,000 Kiwis a week are leaving the country. Remember
the election campaign? Everybody was going to come home. Everybody was going to
aspire to greatness and come home to New Zealand because John Key and National
were in office. Well, we know the immigr ation statistics: 1,000 people a week are
leaving the country, and 158,000 people are unemployed. What  a great statistic of
aspiration that is for the member over there, as she has a wee giggle. Every week $120
million is being borrowed to fund a tax cut primarily for the top 10 percent of income
earners. I ask the member to show me so mething that is aspirational about those
statistics. They come from the member’s own Government departments and agencies.
Then we come to the doozy that is Stat e-owned enterprises.  The person who has
played the most ghost-like role  in the whole State-owned enterprises debate, the person
who has been transparent, absent, AWOL, an d not in the debate at all has been the
Minister for State Owned Enterprises, Sim on Power. He is a smart guy. I will tell
members why. This guy does not want his fing erprints on anything that is negative,
anything that the people do not like—

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: He’s focused on the future.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: He has an eye to the future, as my colleague Mr
Hughes says.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: He’s got a 3-year plan.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: He has a 3-year plan. Do members remember the
“three strikes and you’re out” legislation? It  was a justice bill, but the member Simon
Power was invisible. The le gislation was reasonably p opular with some in our
communities—especially with David Garrett, of course. We know where he ended up,
although he is back on the ACT payroll, Trevor tells me. Now we have the State-owned
enterprises debate. If we go round the commun ities we learn that people have worked it
out. People say “Hang on a minute! Mr Engl ish says generously that the National
Government will be so benevolent that it will offer State-owned enterprises, which the
punters, the community, already own, to Kiwis, ordinary men and women.” The
Crown—that is, the community—purchased these State-owned enterprises over
generations with our taxes, but Mr English is  going to be very ge nerous and benevolent
and say to folks that they can use their ow n money to buy them back for a second time.
People ain’t silly. So the ordinary mum and dad Kiwis have so much disposable income
that when the energy companies go on the block they will be rushing to the New
Zealand Exchange with all their free money, all their disposable income, to shell out and
buy shares. Where are these people? Are they some of the 158,000 people who are
unemployed? Are they some of the people on the minimum wage who got a measly 25c
extra an hour? They must have a heap of disposable income, because there are going to
be hundreds of thousands of mums and dads , ordinary Kiwis, flocking to the New
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16557
Zealand Exchange to use the discretionary  money they are awash with to buy these
shares.
That is a fantasy; that is an utter fant asy. We know that the only people who can
afford to buy a share in State- owned enterprises, which of course they already own as
taxpayers, are the top 10 percent of people earning a thousand bucks a week whom Mr
Key and National cut into the deal of the tax cuts. They will be there, of course, along
with the big institutions and the foreign ow ners. People are not su cked in by the view
that mum and dad Kiwis can get a slice of it. I say to National members that mum and
dad Kiwis already own State-owned enterprises and they do not have the disposable
money to buy them back for a second time.
Then we come to the other interesting issue in respect of State-owned enterprises,
which is whether it is logical to sell them off. People say: “Did the National
Government not try that last time?”. It did, and it told everybody in New Zealand that if
it sold those assets, then everybody would be better off. We know the truth of the 1990s.
People were not better off and we lost more and more of the family silver. We know,
through precedent, who will buy those assets, we know they will fall into foreign hands,
and we know that any dividend  stream—even it is only 49  percent—will not go back
into the Crown coffers to pay for education and to reinstate the early childhood
education cuts, the adult and childhood educati on cuts, the health cu ts, and all the other
cuts that Government members have put in place. That will be lost, and it will be lost
offshore.
I say to members that people are not silly. Simon Power is a smart guy. He has kept
his fingerprints absolutely away from this i ssue. He has not put out one press statement
as Minister for State Owned Enterprises. He has left it to Bill English and John Key. He
has been utterly, 100 percent invisible, and we  have to ask why. It is the same with the
“three strikes and you’re out” legislation. He  did not want a bar of it. He knew it was
wrong. He kept away from it. Why? He does have a 3-year plan. He can say “It was not
me.”, when the people roll up and say they do not want this as it was tried before and it
failed. I ask National members where the aspiration is for the 158,000 people who are
on the dole as we speak—the one in four  young people on the scrap heap, as Phil Goff
said. They are going straight on to the dole queue. Where is the aspiration for them? I
say to Paula Bennett, who loves kicking be neficiaries around, that the headline on the
Waikato Times, which featured on the news tonight, is true. Wh ere are the jobs? Where
is the Job Summit? Where are the 40 jobs th at were created from the cycleway? Where
is the plan? Paula Bennett can boot the beneficiaries around, tell them they are bludgers,
and tell them to get off their backside and get a job, but there is one problem. If there
are no jobs, then that presents a terminal obs tacle to them. There is no aspiration in this,
there is no plan, and John Key has abandoned ordinary New Zealanders.

items.speaker: PAUL QUINN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker Roy.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: There’s a genius!

items.speaker: PAUL QUINN
items.text: I will be a genius at the end of this speech, as the previous one was
made by Clayton Cosgrove.
It gives me great pleasure to stand a nd support the Prime Minister, following his
speech to the House this afternoon, in which he laid out how this Government intends
building a strong economy based on real, e nduring growth. One thing Labour has failed
to understand throughout the previous 9 year s of its administra tion—appalling as it
was—as demonstrated by the th rowaway lines that its members have shared with the
public since the start of this year, and th e shopping lists and lolly scrambles it has
created, is that it has learnt nothing. Labour has learnt nothing from the mismanagement
of its previous period in Government, which left this country with a decade of deficits.
16558 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
Let us briefly, by way of example, look at the wool Labour pulled over our eyes in
just its last year in office. When the th en Labour Government presented the Budget and
economic statement in 2008 it forecast a surplus of $1.3 billion. Even in the Pre-election
Economic and Fiscal Update it published it  basically tried to hoodwink the public and
say that there would be a balanced outcome in 2008. Of course, the people saw through
this and elected John Key as their Prime Minister and National as the Government. We
received notification from Treasury in the December update that there was a deficit.
That deficit had been hidden from the pe ople by the Labour administration, which now
wallows in the benches of the Opposition. As we  have seen, we have been left with a
decade of deficits.
How could that be? It basically came a bout because the focus of members opposite
during their time in Government was to dish  out lollies. Productiv ity decreased every
year during the time they were in Govern ment. There was a current account deficit
throughout that whole period. If this country is to survive and have enduring growth, it
needs productive investment. The previous administration did absolutely nothing to
create that opportunity.
When Labour was finally kicked out by th e people of New Zealand, household debt
had risen from $5 billion, when it came into power, to $19 billion. Th e interest charges
that the average householder was paying on th at debt had risen to 14 percent of their
disposal income. That amount was going to service the debt that those vagabonds on the
other side of the House had created by show ering lollies on their so-called supporters,
thereby creating a mountain of debt.
That is why we find ourselves in the situ ation today where this  Government is not
scared to address the debt issues. That intention was announced by the Prime Minister,
John Key, in his state of the nation speech and again today in the Prime Minister’s
statement. His focus is on restoring equilibrium, just as the householders of New
Zealand have come to realise and understand that they have to reduce debt and create
savings, not create a whole lot of debt. Members opposite have not understood that fact,
and in their lust for power they have decided that they will send the country into even
more debt with programmes that, so far,  cost over $5 billion. Labour has already
announced programmes that will require $5 bi llion additional debt. Does Shane Jones
really think that the people of New Zealand will be as gullible as  that? Of course he
does not. He should jump now.
If we are to have enduring growth in th is country, we will have to base it on
productivity gains, investment, and getting bus inesses to invest. It is the businesses in
New Zealand that create the job opportunities. The Governme nt’s job is to create a
framework to enable the economy to grow. It  is not the Governme nt’s job to be the
economy, to employ all the public servants, an d to dish out handouts to all and sundry
so they can go and spend lots of money. The Government’s job—

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: Whose job is it to hire th e public servants, if not the
Government’s?

items.speaker: PAUL QUINN
items.text: Oh, Labour’s new spokesman on education, who is wearing lovely
professorial glasses, interjects. I look forward to his contribution.
I turn briefly to the contri bution made by the co-leader of the Green Party Metiria
Turei this afternoon. Although I have no doubt th at she was sincere in her contribution,
I was not moved by it. The simple reality of  life is that many people on both sides of
this House no doubt have a similar story to te ll. I do not agree with her solution, which,
like Labour’s solution, is to th row the lollies out there. Her solution was to increase the
m
inimum wage to $15, which would create all so rts of jobs, but that solution just does
not work. The only way to deal with the issue that Metiria Turei describes is to create a
sustained economy. I was not moved by her contribution.
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16559
A classic example is our own Prime Minister . He has a similar story to tell, but he
chose a different path. Those on this side of the House believe that that path is the way
to prosperity and the way to getting this country back on the road to recovery.
The National Government is about i nvesting and prospering—investing and
producing. The Labour Opposition is about sp ending and consuming. With those few
words it gives me great pleasure, once again, to endorse the outstanding leadership of
the Prime Minister of this country. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: I acknowledge Mr Quinn’s hardness of heart
and meanness of spirit. I acknowledge Simon Bridges’ comment that Metiria Turei’s
speech was a good speech. We know who has a political future.
The Prime Minister’s statement is simp ly a reiteration of Government policy
enunciated first in the Speech from the Throne 2 years ago and recycled every February
and May. The Government identifies as its pr incipal goal building the foundations for a
strong economy. That is the platform upon whic h our aspirations are said to rest. There
was no mention of what those aspirations actually are. Th ere was no mention here of a
decent society, a far-sighted nation, or a gl obally responsible citizen—just a strong
economy. I thank the Prime Minister for his far-sighted statesmanship. What is meant
by a strong economy? Building a strong economy is based on “enduring growth”. The
immediate task is to stabilise the economy and put it back on a growth path. Putting the
economy back on a growth path is taking long er than expected, but that is good because
the Prime Minister has no clear insight into the relationship between a growth path to a
strong economy and a level path to a sust ainable economy. Can a sustainable economy
be a strong economy? Of course it can, but not the way this Prime Minister sees it. The
Prime Minister has no conception of the cau sal link between his plans for a growth
economy today and a failed economy a few decades after his departure.
He talks about the emissions trading scheme and wanting to ensure that it is working
as well as possible. He believes that the emissions trading scheme prepares New
Zealand for a carbon-constrained future by providing business and consumers with the
incentives and encouragement they need to  reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. Of
course the emissions trading scheme does nothing of the sort. It is accurately described
by Geoff Bertram and Simon Terry as a mech anism not for reducing emissions but of
transferring wealth as emissions increase.  They say that the scheme has not been
designed to promote economically efficient ab atement; it has been designed, first, to
protect and promote the position of vested interests that are unwilling to shoulder the
asset write-downs required to  recognise a price on carbon, a nd, second, to transfer the
costs of this to future generations. Although the original design of the emissions trading
scheme, they conclude, aimed to confront polluters with the full cost of a nation’s
obligations under the Kyoto Protocol, the scheme legislated for in 2008 went only
halfway towards this and the 2009 amendments all but abandoned the concept.
The original concept, of course, was th e carbon tax, but that foundered on vested
interests. So we all converted to a cap-and- trade system, except that  here in God’s own
we forgot the cap. But we kept the trade, so that we can all succumb to the siren call of
auctioning off free credits for next to nothing. The Kiwi bran d of the emissions trading
scheme is now a licence to pollute without  restraint. It allo ws industry to pass on
today’s modest costs within this generati on to households and small business, and to
allow all of us to pass on the much larger co st to our children. Are we too blind to see
what is going on? The classic example of th e insanity of what we are doing is Solid
Energy and its Government-backed plans to utilise lignite in Southland, the lowest
grade of coal that is possible to mine. Solid Energy’s plans include four projects for the
extraction of lignite over the next decade. The projects are diesel plants, a urea plant, a
16560 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
briquette plant, and an electricity plant. Each  of these is certain to increase our national
greenhouse gas emissions.
In 2009 the Government committed New Zealand to a 10 to 20 percent cut in
emissions off the 1990 level. This is inadequa te in light of the UN prescription of 25 to
40 percent cuts by 2020. But let us at least a ddress the weak target the Government has
adopted for itself. At present, with the emissions trading scheme in place, our emissions
are projected to be 30 percent above the 1990 level by 2020. That is a national shame,
yet that excess is calculated without the massive injection in to the atmosphere that will
come from Solid Energy’s cheerful contri bution to the betterment of humankind. The
two lignite-to-diesel plants alone will incr ease that 30 percent emission overshoot by
half as much again—that is to say, they will in crease the 30 percent overshoot to a 45
percent overshoot. The other projects will make the total worse. How clever is that?
What pride are we to take as a nation in  that magnificent plan for low-carbon energy
at the pure cost of the planet? A country that has been requested by the UN to cut
emissions by some 30 percent by 2020, but consci ously plans to engage in fossil-fuel
extraction, and whose emissions will result  in an overshoot of the 1990 level by 45
percent, is a country without shame, a country with no moral in tegrity, and a country
with no sense of global responsibility. But never mind. Who is looking? We can make
some money by extracting this atrocious materi al that will choke the life forms on this
planet, and we can export some of it so th at it will not appear on our national carbon
account. What is more, we hear the claim from Solid Energy—clearly an objective
authority on the subject—that the plans for these projects will result in a reduction in
greenhouse gas emissions. How do we understand this breathtaking claim? How are we
to credit Solid Energy with any credibility  on that? And how are we to reconcile the
increasing inconsistency in the various stat ements being put out by the Hydra-headed
creature that this Government has become? The Government has become victim to its
own timidity in the face of global climate change, national respons ibility targets, and
local interest group pressure.
Mr Brownlee is Minister of Energy and Res ources; Dr Smith is Minister for Climate
Change Issues. We would think that as Mini sters in the same Cabinet, serving under the
erstwhile Mr Key, they would speak with one voice, or at least with harmonious voices,
singing melodically from the same song sheet, but what do we hear? What faint melodic
harmony do we discern in New Zealand’s official thinking in early 2011? Dr Smith said
the following: “It is ironic that while we tr y and design pricing instruments to recognise
the environmental cost of emissions, the worl d spends hundreds of bi llions of dollars a
year subsidising fossil fuels and pollution. If  we are serious about addressing climate
change in the most efficient way, we need to be discussing a phase out of such support.”
Mr Brownlee, who prefers ener gy security to climate responsibility, said the following:
“The PCE report on the emissions increase to  be caused by the lignite projects is a
separate report. It has nothi ng to do with the Energy Stra tegy.” Well, I suggest to the
Minister that he revise the dr aft energy strategy and make sure  that it does . I suggest to
the Prime Minister that he devotes his consid erable analytical skills to reconciling what
his Ministers are saying, becau se his Government is appr oaching dysfunctionality in
policy. Senior Ministers are sa ying irreconcilable things. Th ey are saying things that
cannot be matched in logic, and, after all, this is a logical and rational—if visionless—
Government.
So when the Prime Minister said in hi s speech this afternoon that “This year’s
election will be about w
hich party has a realistic plan to achieve faster economic growth
for New Zealanders.”, we agr ee. Where we disagree is over his blithe assumption that
raping the planet for 19 th century - style profit is a realistic plan. It is unrealistic to the
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16561
point of criminal negligence, and this Prim e Minister, whether or  not he enjoys it,
presides over a group of Ministers who are meant to be saying the same thing.
Let me say to the Ministers and to Solid  Energy that the amount of fossil fuel
remaining on the planet is finite. If all the remaining fossil fuel is extracted and burnt,
we shall massively exceed the planet’s  climate-change boundary. Neither energy
efficiency nor renewable energy will save us , unless most of the fossil fuel that would
otherwise be mined stays in the ground, and stays there forever. It is implausible that
any conventional oil will be le ft in the ground, but it is pos sible and necessary to phase
out coal, on a straight-line basis, up to 2030. That is an unpalatable truth, I say to
anyone who thinks that coal is sexy and dirty coal is the sexies t of all. It remains a truth
none the less, and this Government had bette r get over it. We simply cannot afford to
be, in the 21st century, “filthy” rich.
I say to the Government and to Solid Energy that every tonne of coal that stays in the
ground in New Zealand forever is two tonne s of carbon that will never reach the
atmosphere. Both the Government and Solid Energy have an obligation to ensure that
the lignite never sees the lig ht of today, lest tomorrow’s daylight becomes clouded by a
hot and stifling atmosphere. It is time we came to our senses.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: That intervention from Kennedy
Graham was cool. It was calm; it was cereb ral. Some would use another “C” word—
crazy, say—but I would not say that, I te ll Kennedy Graham. But I would lay down a
challenge to Kennedy Graham. His party, it seems, has in the past been bound to
Labour, and there is every chance that Labour  would like that to happen again. My
challenge to Kennedy Graham is that if he thinks Labour, with its big tax, big spend, big
borrowing programme, is the answer to any ki nd of environmental question that this
country, and indeed this world, faces, then I te ll him that he is sadly mistaken. Maybe it
is for different reasons, but I think the least we can say about National is that we on this
side of the House accept things cannot go on the way they are, with borrowing,
spending, and taxing in the unsustainable way—and maybe we mean different things by
“unsustainable”—that Labour wants them to go on.
There will be a very, very clear contrast at this election between the two major
parties. We could dress up all of this. On  the one side, we ha ve prudent financial
management, fiscal prudence, etc—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: On the other side, people who talk sense.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: —and on that side, from Phil Tw yford and the rest of them,
there is more debt. On this side there will be  less debt. We have a guy there, Phil Goff,
who, in the first month of this year, I think—I ask what promises he was getting up to.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Mr Goff to you, Simon.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Mr Phil Goff promised $5 billion worth of borrowing. OK, we
will come to how he says he will pay for that, but there was a stage when every day we
had new spending pledges. I wonder, and I ask Phil Twyford, whether he had talked
about those spending promises or whether they were off the hoof, because they certainly
seemed to be just rolling out of his mouth. There was a new one every single day when
he was under pressure from interviewers.
We all know what that spending means.  Ultimately, it means a downgrade by the
credit rating agencies, it means higher interest rates because money costs more, and then
for ordinary Kiwis—those middle Kiwis whom Charles Chauvel was talking about
earlier—it means higher interest rates and higher mortgage rates, which are not good for
anyone. It probably means even more people will go to Australia and overseas. Phil

items.speaker: Goff says
items.text: “Yes, but we could pay for this by taxing the rich more.”

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: I thought you were going to fix th at thing about people going to
Australia.
16562 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Those so-called rich probably le ft when Labour was last in
Government. I have news for Phil Twyford. The real rich do not pay tax anyway, so we
are not talking about the real rich. When we are talking about those so-called rich, who
are they? They are doctors,  lawyers, accountants, engineers, information technology
professionals.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Police officers.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: As my friend here says, they are police officers. They are all
sorts of ordinary New Zealanders, who will be  forced to rearrange their affairs as a
result of what Phil Goff wants to do when he taxes these so-called rich. They already
got used to doing that under Labour. That is not good for anyone except lawyers and
accountants. They will rearrange their affa irs or they will leav e this country. I
acknowledge that we still have that problem  of people leaving this country, but the
policies of Phil Goff will make that problem worse.
Phil Goff’s other policy, the other thing we have heard from him—and the next
speaker from Labour can correct me if I am wrong—is that he is effectively saying that
we just will not spend money on our military force. He is saying that we do not need a
military force. We do not need a navy, an air force, and an army, so that is where we
will find the money. Well, we on this side th ink that having a military force is kind of
important. It is not actually about being ji ngoistic, nationalistic, or anything like that.
Those are some big words that Phil Twyford may know from his time in Oxfam. I tell
Phil Twyford that it is about pl aying our part in the world. That is why we are in other
countries around the world. We want to play our part as a little  country down at the
bottom of the world.
We have Phil Goff on the other side with unsustainable spending pledges. He says
that we should tax the rich, which will not bring us anywhere near the money, and that
we should slash the military forces. That is no recipe. The recipe for this country—and
ordinary New Zealanders are learning this and know this; they are getting this—is to
spend less, to slow down the growth of sp ending that went up by over 50 percent under
the previous Labour Government—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Sell off the family silver.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: —and, yes, to explore the mixe d-ownership model. Here is
something that Phil Twyford does not unde rstand. Actually, Phil Goff understands it,
because he is the guy who has more expertise in selling off the family silver than
anyone else in this House. Someone said he  has been around for 26 years; I read that
somewhere. But there are different ways to do these things. We are not talking about
trade sales, such as those that Phil Goff and the Government he was a part of specialised
in.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Contact Energy was a great success.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Tens of thousands of New Zealanders in this country, I tell Phil
Twyford, have shares in Contact Energy. I am not saying that that is  the perfect model,
but I would remind members opposite that th ey were the ones who sold down Air New
Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: They did.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Yes, because they had to, a nd we can look at the success of
that. There are plenty of other successful models like that, such as the Port of Tauranga.
There is also TrustPower, from which social dividends are paid.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Air New Zealand a successful  model as a private-public
company—you’re joking.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Oh, here we go. I ask whether Trevor Mallard is saying that Air
New Zealand is not working. Right now, ordi nary Kiwis—yes, that is the phrase Jim

items.speaker: Anderton does not like
items.text: ordinary m
um and dad Kiwis—own shares in Air New Zealand,
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16563
and the Government has the majority stake. It is working. In fact, not only is it working;
it is thriving. It has had all sorts of innovativ e ideas for its seats, such as its “cuddle
class”. I do not know whether Ph il Twyford may have experi enced that already on one
of his trips to the Third World, to do good in other parts of the world. Air New Zealand
is thriving, and we can do this . Yes, we have some explai ning to do, but we will do it,
and people will know.
It is not just about economics ; that is not the on ly matter we differ on. It is not just
that we understand the economy and know we cannot spend, spend, spend, and that
members on the other side of the House want to do just that—spend, spend, spend—and
go on a lolly scramble, as my friend Paul Quinn said. It is also a question of style, and I
am not talking about the way that someone walks down the runway, or anything like
that. We have a Prime Minister at th e moment who, unlike Phil Goff, is a non-
traditional Prime Minister. He is actually prepar ed to give away tactical advantage. We
have seen that in the way he has given away the election date  for the good of this
country, for the certainty of this country. He has been straightforward with the public in
the lead up to the Rugby World Cup and then, after that, we will have the election.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: He just doesn’t want to be in terrupted while he’s waving for the
cameras.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: We would never have seen that  from Chris Hipkins’ “mother”,
Helen Clark. We never would have seen that.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: You keep my mother out of this.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Ha, ha! If I had more time we would go into that, but we do not
have the time. But we would never have se en Helen Clark give away that tactical
advantage, yet we saw it from this Prime Minister.
Then there was the ruling out of Winston Peters. Labour said that that was arrogant. I
say that the public of New Zealand have th e right to know what the parties will do and
where we stand on these issues, and we ha ve ruled him out. It would be good to see
some of that clarity coming from Labour.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Will you come to Te Atatū and explain your asset sales policy?

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Unlike Phil Twyford, I have lived in Te Atat ū. Unlike Phil
Twyford, I know Te Atat ū. Phil Twyford does not know that he is lucky because his
middle-class TomTom tells him where Te Atat ū is, but I grew up in a place called
Gloria Avenue in Te Atatū North. When I grew up there, it was called Te Atat ū North,
not Te Atatū Peninsula. It became Te Atat ū Peninsula when Laila Harré and all her
middle-class lefty mates moved in, but when I was there, it was called Te Atat ū North. I
then moved up in the world, to a place called Te Atat ū South—Strid Road—and that
may be part of the electorate Phil Twyford is standing in. I would be happy to come and
talk to the people of Te Atat ū about our mixed-ownership model, because we have the
Prime Minister and the policie s that will see this country through the bad times into the
good times, and I am proud to be part of this Government.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: I was very disappointed
in the Prim
e Minister’s statement, because it confirmed to me that the pre-2005 election
promise about being ambitious for New Zeala nd had really turned out to be the empty
slogan I thought it was. I al ways thought they were empty words, that he never was
ambitious for New Zealand—he was certainly  ambitious for John Key, but he was not
ambitious for New Zealand.
I should be grateful because, of course, this makes our task easier as an Opposition
determined to win back the confidence of New Zealand, and to restore the principles of
fairness that underpin our way of life. The New Zealand way of lif e is actually about
those principles of fairness. That is what we  believe in as a nation, and that is what we
need to have restored. I am not grateful, however, because I see the consequences for so
16564 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
many people that I am privileged to represent in this House of the betrayal that this
National Government has represented to those who put trust in it. I see the people in the
supermarket struggling with the reality of th e tax switch that was not a switch for them
at all. They are paying more, and they are getting no more than they were getting before
in their hands. John Key told them that not one person would be worse off as a result of
the tax switch. That is why we can say it was a tax swindle, because  it was not capable
of delivering what he said.
I have to say that a lot of people in Christchurch East, when they hear that nobody
will be worse off after this tax switch, have the riposte yeah, right! They are not only the
people we would expect me to be talki ng about—the lower socioeconomic group. I am
talking right to middle New Zealand when I say that they are feeling the pain at the till,
the pain at the pump, and the pain when th ey pay for their power. I am talking about
those people who do not feel  better off since 15 percent became the new GST rate, and
when National decided to squander over 40 percent of the tax cuts on only 10 percent of
New Zealand’s highest-income earners.
I ask members to talk to homeowners in one of the five particularly damaged suburbs
in my electorate, and to ask them what th ey think of the Prime Minister’s reassuring
words now, 5 months after the earthquake has occurred. He  and all the Ministers who
were so happy to parade through the street s of my electorate when there were photo
opportunities to be had are now nowhere to be seen.
Gerry Brownlee will make a statement tomorrow or the next day about what the
Government will do for those whose alte rnative accommodation funding has run out.
Guess what has brought on this sudden burst of energy from the Minister of Energy?
Guess what has done that? The first group of people to run out of money will run out of
money in 3 weeks’ time. Three weeks’ time! It is absolutely disgraceful that he has kept
all of those people on tenter hooks for month after month af ter month, knowing that the
first ones would run out when their 6 months ’ period after the earthquake was up. It is
absolutely outrageous.
I have been asked by many constituents to lobby the Government for choices to be
made available. What does one say to the 80-year-old who stands up at a public meeting
and asks whether they will still be alive when their house is rebuilt in 3 to 4 years’ time?
What does one say to somebody in that situ ation? What about the couples who have
split up and their mutual ownership of a wr ecked property is holding them back from
getting on with their lives? These are cases I have written to the Minister about. One
knows that something needs to be done when people need to move to another job and to
another town. What do they do with the equity  in their land when they have to walk
away from their land in the meantime? It is clear that those circumstances require some
form of intervention.
I have said to the Government that it does not have to be funded by the taxpayer, or
the ratepayer, or by either of them alone. Maybe there is a private sector solution that
could be facilitated, or maybe even a public-private partnership. We hear the
Government talking about it, so here is a classic exam ple of where we could get
everyone working together and singing off the same song sheet. But I am very fearful
that nothing will happen and we will see someth ing that is evidenced internationally in
situations like that, which is called desertification. Th e house is bowled, the cash
settlement is taken from the insurer, and then the empty section is sold later on. What
does that look like for the people remaining in their houses in the meantime while the
suburb is being rebuilt?
I arranged for a local group called Pr oject Employment and Environmental
Enhancement to come and tidy up some of th e frontages of the abandoned properties in
Seabreeze Close and Pacific Park, but it is a m ajor task and it needs ongoing attention. I
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16565
wonder whether the Prime Minister has been back to look at th e mess in Seabreeze
Close. He was certainly happy to front up with the television cameras, but I wonder
whether he is willing to front up now. In f act, I challenge the Prime Minister of New
Zealand to come back without the camera s and see how the people are feeling now, 5
months on after the earthquake. But if he ha s to bring the cameras, then maybe that
would be a good thing. There are a few things those constituents would like to say to the
Prime Minister, who is happy to be there at th e time of the event, but not happy to front
up when times are getting tougher.
The trouble with the Prime Minister is simp ly this: during his first few weeks as
Prime Minister he earned himself the nickname “Mr Smile and Wave”. No matter what
the circumstances, he just smiles and waves. He seems to think that everything can be
managed with comforting words, a reassuring hug, a warm handshake, and a smile that
never quite makes it to the eyes. But that is not leadership. That is not how one delivers
an ambitious agenda for the country, and it certainly does not do anything for my
constituents in Christchurch East.
I wrote a book review on Red Alert about a book I had read over the break called The

items.speaker: Gods that Failed
items.text: How the Financial Elite Have Gambled Away Our Futures . The
original version of the book was called The Gods that Failed:  How Blind Faith in
Markets Has Cost Us Our Future . The metaphor within the na rrative of that book is
inspired by the 12 gods of ancient Greece wh o lived on Mount Olympus. Elliot and
Atkinson have styled the super-financiers and the internationa l organisations—the
central banks, the International M onetary Fund, the World Bank—the “New
Olympians”, and the 12 gods of the m odern Mount Olympus are globalisation,
communication, liberalisation, privatisa tion, competition, “financialisation”,
speculation, recklessness, greed, arrogance, oligarchy, and excess.
One of the last chapters in that book is called “Last Tango on Wall Street”, which has
a very simple explanation of how the “New Olympians”—and that is the Prime
Minister’s background—found ways to make money out of nothing, creating securitised
financial products like collateralised debt ob ligations out of the subprime market and
then hiding the risk behind triple A rated institutions. The “New Olympians” made
personal fortunes, as we know, with bonuses th ey never had to repay when it all turned
to custard, and they were happy to see the taxpayers of the world pick up the tab for
their multitrillion-dollar insanity. The financ ial elite referred to in this book do not
create wealth; they amass wealth for themselves personally and their mates.
The book reminded me of a comment I made about John Key when he was Leader of
the Opposition. The only difference between a gambler and a money market trader is
that a gambler is a money market trader who has lost his or her edge. I guess that is why
he has retired from that chapte r in his life, but the instinct is still there. It is no wonder
he wants New Zealand to be the Wall Street of the Asia-Pacific. He wants to sell our
country’s assets to the financial elite he left behind—and make no mistake that that is
exactly whose hands it will end up in. I do not  know about members, but I do not know
any mums and dads who sit around the kitc hen table wondering when the Government
will allow them to invest in assets they  already own. The mum and dads I know are
sitting around the kitchen table trying to wo rk out how to make th eir budget stretch to
the end of the week. There is an old saying that to make r eal money one needs to make
real things, and that is what New Zealand need to be doing as a nation.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Today the Prime Minister, John Key,
talked in his speech about opportunity, and ou tlined this Government’s priorities for
2011. Just last week the Prime Minister a nnounced the date of th e general election, 10
months ahead of the da
te, which is 26 Novemb er. It is pretty clear to those who have
been watching or listening to the debate today that there is a clear divide between those
16566 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
over there and those of us on this side of the House. I think it is also fair to say that
listeners have probably heard that the gloves are off.
If we look at the National side in the bl ue corner, we see a clear focus on spending
less and borrowing less, and a focus on building the foundations for a stronger economy
and for building better results from public serv ices. If we look at th e Labour side in the
red corner, we see that the focus is on spending more and more, and borrowing and
creating debt, not just for our generation bu t for the next generation and the one after
that. Labour has already idly promised to sp end another $5 billion, and I am sure that
that amount will go up as the months creep to wards the election. But it has not told us
how it will pay for that extra spending. We  have heard—even from the previous
speaker, Lianne Dalziel—criticism of the G overnment’s tax switch.  But Labour is not
promising to reverse the tax cuts or to reduce GST. I am looking forward to hearing that
from that side of the House:  if those members hate the tax switch, they should make a
promise to reverse it.
Tonight I will look at the priorities that th is Government has laid out today through
the eyes of my constituents, whether they  be a chef in Cambridge, a plumber in
Pūtāruru, a labourer at Kinleith, or perhaps someone who owns a shop in Taupō. Those
are the people I am listening to every day. Those are the hard-working New Zealanders
who, although they may be doing it tough toda y because we have been in a global
economic recession, hope for, and aspire to, a better tomorrow.
Let us look at that small-business owner; there is a large number of them in my
electorate. I am sure many of us deal with  these constituents every day. Do members
know what they are telling me? Do members know what they are actually saying? They
know that if they are in busin ess they have to do better bu siness. They have to work
smarter, they have to be more efficient, a nd they have to look at ways that they can
streamline and improve the performance of their business.
Earlier today we heard Prime Minister J ohn Key talk about the fact that the
Government needs to look at reforms that will streamline and improve the performance
of the Government bureaucracy. It is not rocket science. Small businesses are doing it,
so why would we expect that the Government  would not do it? John Key says that by
international standards, New Zealand’s Public Service is bloated and inefficient. We
need to be lean, quick, and nimble. We believe  that it is possible to have a public sector
like that. Small businesses, medium-sized businesses, and large businesses up and down
this country have been forced to do that in the economic recession that th is country has
faced. The Government sector is no different. We will not let it grow at the rate that it
grew under the Labour Government of 9 years. We need to make sure we have a high
performing public sector.
It is interesting that when I talk to people in Taup ō they are quite clear about what
they expect the Government to provide. They expect a world-class health service, not a
Third World one. They expect an education service that provides for every single New
Zealand child, not four out of five. They e xpect a strong and eff ective justice system
and social services that protect the most vulnerable.
Just last night I was in Hamilton at the launch of the Regional Business Partners
initiative, which is TechNZ’s regional technology partner work ing with Waikato
Innovation Park. The whole conversation wa s about supporting businesses to grow
through using research and de velopment. The presentation covered things like our
technology transfer vouchers for sm all companies and th e technology development
grants, which give more research and deve lopment investment to research-intensive
industries. We all know that Ki wis are great at inventing thi ngs, but we are actually not
as great at turning those id eas into opportunities that ra ise money for companies and,
more important, turning them into export dollars for our country. Growing businesses is
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16567
how we create jobs, and that is how we are able to increase our wages. We know that
this is what improves the lifestyles of hard-working New Zealanders.
I will now focus on education. We on this side of the House know that improving
education and skills is critical to lifting the standard of living for every single New
Zealander. As a mother of three young children I want my children to be well prepared
and to be able to take the most from every opportunity that is before them. I believe that
every New Zealand child should have the opportunities in life  that come from a great
education.
I will start very deliberately with th e early childhood sector and set the record
straight. National is spending $1.4 billion this year on this sector. That is the largest
amount of money ever spent in early childhoo d education. So when that side of the
House tells us that we are cu tting the funding, I say that that is absolute rot. We are
spending $1.4 billion. That is right—members  opposite can look up. Th at is three times
as much as the Labour Government was spending 5 years ago.
Let us look at this sector in a bit more detail. We have tripled spending, so one might
think that we would be gett ing a bit more for what we are spending. Actually, the
number participating has not increased by even 1 percent. On this side of the House we
believe that young children should be ab le to access early childhood education
regardless of race or income. That is why our priority is to lift participation. In some
areas 40 percent of 5-yea r-olds start school having had no early childhood education
whatsoever. I have talked to  teachers who have faced thos e 5-year-olds in schools, and
it is incredibly difficult for those children because they are already behind. We need to
target Māori, Pasifika, and children from low-in come backgrounds, and that is exactly
what we are doing with our investment of  $91.8 million into these targeted spaces,
providing 3,500 extra spaces.
I will also touch on national standards, because it would not be a good day in the
House if I did not stand here and mention nati onal standards. I think they are absolutely
stunning. After 9 years under Labour, four out of five children left school without
sufficient skills in reading, writing, and maths. If we think about the number of children
who started school last week—60,000 five-year-o ld kids started school last week—we
see that 12,000 of them would spend 10 years at  school and not be able read, write, or
do maths. I say that that is just an absolute  disgrace. With national standards, if parents
have a report come home, they will find it a damn sight easier to understand, and their
children can understand it as well. I think that is a really important part of the learning
journey: the parent, the chil d, and the teacher all working together to improve the
child’s outcomes at school.
With National it is pretty clear. We get a Government committed to building a better
future, and we get responsible economic ma nagers creating the conditions for growth,
which leads to better lifestyles for every single one of us.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Deputy
Speaker, ngā mihi o te tau hou ki a koe; otirā, ngā m ihi o te tau hou ki a tātou katoa. Hei
whaiwahi haere i te āhuatanga o te kōrero i te ahiahi nei, ka tuku i āku poroporoaki ki te
hunga kua ngaro ki te tirohanga kanohi. Ko t ērā o ngā kuia o te Waihīrere kua ngaro atu
i te tirohanga kanohi i ēnei rā. Waiho ia kia moe i te taha o ōna mātua tūpuna. Ka huri
mai ki a tātou o te Whare, huri noa, tēnā koutou, kia ora tātou katoa.
[Greetings to you, Mr Deputy Speaker. Acknowledgments of the new year to you, and
indeed to all of us. To follow up the address on this afternoon’s statement, I express my
condolences to those who have passed away and will no longer be seen, particularly
that one of the elderly womenfolk of Waihīrere of recent times, who will not be seen any
more. Allow her to remain there with her ancestors. I turn now to us throughout the
House; greetings to you, and to all of us, greetings.]
16568 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
There has been a lot of talk today in th e House about a very special group of New
Zealanders. They are the 60,000 children whom we call the Year 1 cohort. They are
children, one might say, who are on the brin k of opportunity and children with the
promise of a big huge future in the world ah ead. One in four of those children is M āori;
that is 15,000 people who have every potential to be the en trepreneurs, the innovators,
and the breadwinners—the talent pool of our labour market.
Now let us look at another group—t he 800,000 children throughout the school
sector. Of these, 160,000 are classified as  living in poverty. I w onder how it could be
that in the Prime Minister’s  address to the nation toda y he failed to acknowledge a
report that has been widely aired across th e nation. That is the United Nations report
that has described as staggering the rates of  child abuse and poverty in Aotearoa. Let us
break that down a bit. Presumably, that is  what was implied by the recognition in the
Prime Minister’s statement that “Despite decades of good intentions from government,
we’re still failing too many of our kids.” I have to ask how good those intentions have
been for all of our children.

items.speaker: There are two groups
items.text: tangata whenua and children living in poverty. Unfortunately,
those groups are both closely linked together . As a teacher and a former principal
myself, I can say with some authority th at much of the poorer performance and
disengagement experienced in the case of M āori children is correlated with their socio-
economic status. How can any Government, re d or blue, live with itself knowing that
the rate of poverty for children in households with no full-time worker is six times—six
times—higher than it is for children living in homes where there is at least one full-time
worker? What that translates into is levels of hardship that have immediate
consequences.
This is how a group of young Ne w Zealanders described living in poverty in a report
entitled A Fair Go for all Children : Actions to address child poverty in New Zealand
“Can’t afford school uniform … Lack of books … Can’t go on school trips … No lunch
… Not accepted by their peers … Left out … Get picked on at school … Stress …
Shame … Low self-esteem … Unhappy … Lonely  … Feelings of worthlessness.” We
are not talking Charles Dickens here; this  is from a 2008 report of the Children’s
Commissioner, which is a report that Labour will for ever be judged against, a report
that should have, but has not, become the blueprint to make the National Government
take bolder action in the interests of our ta mariki—children who are born in homes that
have endured long-term poverty, have poorer health, and do less well at school. Those
same children will achieve lower earnings if indeed they are equipped to leave school
without any substantial qualifications. Tragically, childhood poverty is associated with a
higher risk of antisocial and criminal behaviour, which Mr Goff alluded to this
afternoon.
Taking the cycle of despair even further, it was pretty depressing to hear the views of
my brother-in-law, Ruakere Hond, in Ta ranaki, who has been involved in M āori
education since the 1980s. In an  article in the Taranaki ne wspaper he talked about the
fact that a lot of unemployed M āori lacked motivation from being trapped in “a cyclic
paradigm” that filtered down through older members of the wh ānau. In fact, he
described this cycle as becoming “culturally ingrained in certain family groups”. Where
does this come from? What can we do to address the seemingly intractable problems
that lead to underachievement and under-parti cipation? It is not about just a poverty of
income. It is also about a poverty of spirit, demonstrated in schools in which the culture
of the school and the attitude and expect ations of teachers have been shown to
contribute to their students’ disengagem
ent.
There is a longstanding rec ognition that there is a cl ear disconnect between the
majority of teachers and M āori students. We recall two separate surveys. One was
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16569
conducted by the New Zealand History Teach ers’ Association, a nd the other by the
academic Richard Manning. They indicated that M āori content was often sidestepped,
and this has had major educational and political implications for Māori.
I come back to Mr Key’s view about good in tentions. I presume he  is talking about
the Taha Māori programme of the 1970s, the various interventions, such as the bilingual
units in general-stream schools, perhaps th e marae on school-grounds, Treaty clauses in
the charter, and the like. They were a ll great, but they actually benefited P ākehā
students more than th e target group of M āori. But what Russell Bishop of Waikato
University has demonstrated so effectively is that recogni tion of our lan guage, culture,
and identity is an essential part of the pathway to success for M āori. But the Māori edge
is not just about having a M āori name or the school pupils being able to sing “T ūtira
mai ngā iwi”.
The M āori edge is to understand that whā nau are the critical factor to ensure
achievement in education. Whānau, hapū, and iwi have a special role in making success
happen. We call it whanaungatanga, where ev eryone who is involved with the people
who care most about our students, their wh ānau, are welcomed at the door. It is about
allowing Māori to have a space and providing  support, but still allowing M āori to have
our own say and to take up models that work for us, like T ū Toa in Palmerston North. It
is about celebrating Māori innovation and initiative.
Politicians on both sides of the House have spoken about the im portance of literacy
and numeracy programmes, and of our kids be ing able to speak well, count well, read
well, and write well. What is new? That is  the same catchcry that New Zealanders from
all ethnic backgrounds have been calling for since the missionaries arrived with their
pencils and slates.
But literacy and numeracy on their own are but one part of the solution. If we really
want to make a difference for M āori education, we must understand that M āori
solutions are required. The M āori Party has talked about cultural competency. We have
called for responses that reflect M āori aspirations for edu cation—aspirations that
inevitably include the social, political, economic, and cultural sustainability of Māori as
a people. It is about including M āori culture in meaningful ways. It is about
incorporating M āori knowledge, culture, and perspec tives inside and outside of the
curriculum. Ultimately, it is about Wh ānau Ora. This is fundamentally what Tariana
intended would happen with Whā nau Ora—that the education sector would take on the
challenge of working with whānau.
Although we could easily identify the succes s factors inherent in kura kaupapa
Māori, we must as a nation a pply those same conditions for success in the mainstream
school system. In my electorate of Waiariki, for example, M āori children comprise
approximately three-quarters of the school  role in the areas of Kawerau and Ōpōtiki.
What about them? A revolution is not impossi ble. The results of Te Kotahitanga show
us that the academic engagement of Mā ori students dramatically improved. Their
completion levels of work increase d, there were higher levels of M āori student
attendance, and short-term achievement rose.
The State, principals, teachers, and, for their part, whānau need to be held to account.
Whānau must play their part, bu t it is also about time the education sector was put on
notice, too. They are paid to do the job. Fift y percent - plus of M āori boys leaving
school without qualifications is just not good enough; in fact, it is a disgrace. We have
to invest in the success that is the M āori edge that the M āori Party is pursuing. We are
determined to make a difference to achieve the change that our nation needs. We will do
it, but not just for the 15,000 M āori children who started school last week but for the
future of all descendants who will carve out a future for Aotearoa. Tēnā tātou.
16570 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: Before I begin I would like  to wish everybody a happy
New Year. We have had a long break over Christmas,  and I hope everybody has
returned safely and well rested. To those celebrating the lunar new year, I would like to
greet them in their mother tongue. Gong xi fa chai. Xin nian kua i le. Sun nin fai lok.
Akemashite omedetou gozaimasu. Se hae bok mani baduseyo. Those greetings were in
Chinese, Japanese, and Korean, wishing those people a happy New Year. May they
receive lots of luck and blessings in this Year of the Golden Rabbit.
Lianne Dalziel is right, and that is probably a very strange thing for members to hear.
She said that New Zealanders got empt y promises in 2005, and she is right. She
probably meant to say 2008, but maybe it was her subconscious that was talking. She
said that New Zealanders got empty promises in 2005. That is right. New Zealand voted
for the wrong party to become Government in 2005. Labour returned to Government
and continued to mismanage New Zealand’ s economy. Had New Zealanders voted for
National back in 2005, perhaps growth would not be as small as it is now. If a John Key
- led National Government had been in pow er in 2005, we would have implemented the
recovery process sooner and th e growth would have taken be tter, faster steps. Perhaps
Ms Dalziel is seeing 20/20 and in hindsight realises in her heart of hearts—and she does
have a heart; I know, I serve on a select co mmittee with her—that John Key is doing so
well that she wishes Na tional had been in Government in  2005. Maybe she realises that
in 2005 the Labour Government gave New Z ealand the empty promises and raw deal
that she was talking about.
Building a brighter future is the key for New Zealand, and that is the message our
Prime Minister, the Rt Hon J ohn Key, gave in today’s stat ement to Parliament. I am
right behind him in his visi on to make New Zealand a mu ch better place for all New
Zealanders. To make New Zealand a better place for all of us to live in we need a
stronger economy. To achieve a stronger econo my we need to build  the foundations. It
is like growing vegetables. We cannot just throw seeds on to rock and hope they will
grow. We need to prepare the soil, sow the s eeds, water them so that they do not drown,
have a good amount of sunshine, and for me, since I am not much of a gardener, I
suppose a little bit of prayer as well, so that  the seeds will turn into something yummy
that one can harvest and put on the dinner table.
Labour leader Mr Goff, in his state of th e nation speech, promised to make the first
$5,000 of annual income tax free for everyone, in cluding the wealthiest of Kiwis. That
is a $1.3 billion promise. That is like thro wing seeds on to rock and hoping they will
turn into a fruitful harvest. Well, he is dreaming. This is Labour’s borrow and hope
recipe—borrow more, owe more overseas, and hope for the best for this economy. It
would add hundreds of millions of dollars more to the Government’s borrowing. How
else will he pay for his spending promises ? They are currently sitting at around $5
billion and climbing as the days go by. Labour will borrow, borrow, and borrow more
and hope that everything will be OK. That is what Labour did in its 9 long years in
Government. Where did New Zealand end up? In the best economic times, we did not
have the growth we should have achieve d. New Zealanders are not going to be
hoodwinked again. The only way New Zealanders and their families can get better jobs,
higher incomes, and achieve the living standards they aspire to—and actually deserve—
is to make sure we build the foundations for a stronger economy.
One of the ways we can achieve a stronge r economy is to rebalance the way New
Zealand has operated for a long time. Earlier, other speakers mentioned that we cannot
spend until we have earned. That is  one of the basics that we teach our children. No one
in this whole House would even dream of managing their own finances in that way. It is
so irresponsible to earn nothing but to go on a spending spree. But that is what Mr Phil
Goff is hoping we will do. We cannot afford debt-fuelled consumption and Government
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16571
spending. We need to save. We also need to  invest in sectors wh ere we can earn export
dollars. Anyone who runs a household budget knows that if one has overspent in one
month, one must tighten the belt and reduce spending for hopefully the next month.
That is what New Zealand must do as well, so we can return to surplus sooner rather
than later. We must get out of the habit of spending more than what we can earn.
Let me speak about the Korean community in New Zealand for a little while. They
came here with great hopes. My  parents were among the very first to settle here in the
late 1980s. They came with great hopes, but settled into a new country where there were
language issues, cultural issu es, and no friends or family to turn to for support in
difficult times. They had nobody to turn to. When our migrant communities, like my
parents, settled here they did not turn to  the Government and say “Give me money.”
They worked hard. Most of them learnt. They  had this attitude: they would work their
normal job, and they would get a second job, even a third, even a fourth to make sure
they could secure a brighter future not just for themselves but for their children and their
grandchildren. They do not want the taxes they paid through sweat and tears to be
pilfered away to pay for the interest we  will owe if we keep borrowing more from
overseas, as the Labour Party is suggesting we do in its spending promise.
Labour is promising to borrow another $400 million to increase spending on early
childhood education. Earlier my colleague Louise Upston mentioned that the National
Government is spending $1.4 billion on early  childhood education this year. That is
more than anything that Labour has ever done for early childhood education. They keep
talking about the apparent cuts that th e National Government is making to early
childhood education. That is an outright lie. It is a lie.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: The member cannot say “That is a lie.” Speaker’s ruling
42/5 says that you cannot use that word. I ask the member to withdraw that comment.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: I withdraw that comment. It is wrong to claim that we are cutting,
because we are not. We are spending more on early childhood education than Labour
has ever done.
What about Labour’s promises to cut GST on fresh fruit and vegetables? That is
another $250 million a year. What will honest, hard-working New Zealanders who work
hard for their money to pay taxes say about their money being pilf ered away like that?
They will not accept it.
Under the previous Government one in fi ve New Zealand children left school
without reading, writing, or maths skills. That  is a disgusting leg acy of the previous
Labour Government. There were 30,000 people culled from surgical waiting lists across
New Zealand; that is the legacy Labour left behind. Doubling the health budget,
doubling the bureaucracy, reducing services—that is what Labour is known for. In the 2
years that National has been in Governme nt it has provided elective surgery for 20,000
more people a year—20,000 more people a year  are getting elective surgery, like joint
replacement and cataract surgeries. That is  400 extra New Zealanders getting surgery
every week. That is how this Government is turning round the terrible legacy that the
previous Labour Government left behind.
We need to grow this economy. We need  to grow this country. A National-led
Government is the way to go. I stand by our Prime Minister, the Rt Hon John Key, in
his vision for delivering and building a brighter future for all New Zealanders. Thank
you.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour) : The best I could say about John Key’s
speech would be that it was dishearteni ng. I think anyone in this country who has
played a part in their community, who ha s worked in any part of government, or,
indeed, just goes out to do a decent, honest day’s work would have been absolutely
disheartened by that pathetic speech.
16572 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
John Key puts himself up as an aspirational leader for this country. Well, the first
thing he should do is get his facts straight wh en trying to explain a few things to this
country. Firstly, this country has an issu e with debt because this National-ACT
Government is borrowing $300 million every week. The reason it is having to do that in
part is because it has given $14 billion in tax cuts over 5 years, with the vast majority of
that going to 10 percent of the population—the wealthiest 10 percent of the population.
That money should still be in  the Government coffers and it should be spent on the
things that have been cut in the last 2 years.
National Governments have always harmed this country. I go back to Mr Muldoon;
he had Think Big projects, but he at least left us a legacy of some infrastructure. We had
Jim Bolger, who did not think at all. His G overnment just cut bene fits and privatised
anything it could. Now we have  John Key, who wants to thi nk small. He thinks that
Government should be doing less, spending less,  and that the private sector should be
doing more. The basic flaw in that is that th e debt problem of this country is in the
hands of the private sector. John Key will not acknowledge that. I do not think any
Government will intervene in basic private pr operty rights unless it feels there is a good
reason to, so our ability to limit private sector  debt is limited in itself. But John Key’s
solution to the debt problem it is to ta ke assets from the State—State-owned
enterprises—which have a low level of debt.
