I can just see Michael Cullen fuming as he  listens—he is probably not watching TV
tonight—to this debate. He spent the surpluses—the additional money that we had over
and above Government spending—on lowering debt right down t o, I think, 22 percent
of GDP or thereabouts. It was one of the lo west levels of Gove rnment debt in the
OECD, and that put this country in a very good position to take on the international
financial crisis. That was wh ere we had left it when the Tories came into Government.
But their flawed philosophy, which is one of doing less in Government and allowing the
private sector to take over, means that we will  have less ability to lo wer the debt of this
country overall. I have to say that that private sector debt was fuelled by the banks, most
of them foreign-owned. They were quite ha ppy to take the profits when things were
going well, but they are now showing a little b it of caution, indeed a bit of fear, in their
inability and reluctance to fund capital, particularly in the primary sector.
I think we are in a shocking situation, and this Government has shown absolutely no
plan as to what it is going to do to get us out of that. It has cu t $14 billion from the
Government spend and handed that back to ab out the top 10 percent of the country. It
has increased GST. It has increased the co st to each and every New Zealander across
this economy, and we are starting to really feel that.
Mr Key, the so-called aspirational leader of this country, aspired to take us along the
path of Ireland. In fact, in 2008 he was s till championing the wonderful benefits of
Ireland as an economy. The “trappings of a considerable economic success story” is
what he said. Well, it is a measure of his poor judgment that just over 2 years ago he
was claiming Ireland as an amazing success story.
The thing I agree with Mr Key on, which I cannot quite reconcile with his policies, is
his saying that “we need to own more of our own future”. He then set about to justify
selling off our State-owned enterprises. What a bizarre situation and contradiction to put
before this country. I do not think New Zealanders are conned in any way at all. I do not
think they are fooled for one moment about the so-called 49 per cent threshold and the
so-called preferential allocation to Kiwi mums  and dads. I have been challenged not to
use that term, because, as we know, that w ill not happen ; preferential rights will be
given to the wealthy people who can afford to  buy shares, and they will onsell them to
foreign investors. The New Zealanders I have spoken to up and down the country are
not fooled for one moment. They know that it means effective privatisation, the selling
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16573
off into private hands of our  State-owned enterprises, starting with the electricity
sector—notably, Solid Energy.
I say to members—National members have been too scared to say it—that Landcorp
will be next, of course. David Carter has said a number of times that he does not think
the Government should be in the business of farming. That means that Landcorp will be
on the blocks, as well. The question is where that will leave us as a country. If the
private sector is too keen too often to sell shares to foreigners—because there is a nice
handsome profit in it; because it might see a windfall gain somewhere—what path does
that lead us down? It certainly does not take us to John Key’s stated aim of our owning
our own future; indeed, we are heading in the wrong direction.
John Key, David Carter—though Da vid Carter less so, of c ourse—and a few others
made statements against the sale of the Craf ar farms to the Chinese. We should be very
concerned. John Key has made other statem ents about not wanting us to become
workers in our own land. He also said he w ould not want to see th e “wholesale sale of
New Zealand’s land productive sector”. Well, I agree with him, but what has he done
about it? Zippo, nothing! What happened afte r his statement of 7 March 2010 raising
concerns about the sale of the Crafar farms? Indeed, on 1 February this year we saw that
Germans had paid $109 million for 10 farms down in Southland, and what did he say
about that? Nothing, absolutely  nothing! If he is passionate about our owning our land,
then perhaps he should stand up, be true to  his principles, and be consistent for a
change.
It is not only the sale of land that Labour  has indicated we will move to restrict. We
want New Zealanders to have  some control over our future , but National has refused to
move in that area. In fact, it is refusi ng to move in the area of PGG Wrightson’s
potential sale, as well. I have not heard a squeak from the National Government about
whether it thinks the purchase by Agria of PGG Wrightson, the No. 1 agricultural
service company in this country, is a good or a bad thing. Maybe it should be taken over
by Agrium, another foreign-owned company.
It goes on and on, and the problem is that National members sitting over there think
the private sector will deliver a wonderful  future for this country. We have to
acknowledge their wonderful efforts, but G overnment has to ensure the provision of
core infrastructure, so that we can pay for early childhood education, adult and
community education, or the Tr eaty settlements of the Minister for Treaty of Waitangi
Negotiations—if he ever has one that was not negotiate d by the previous Labour
Government—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: More in 2 years than Labour had in 9.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR: We will wait and see how he performs tomorrow with
his legislation, I say to the Minister. We will see how well he does negotiating with his
coalition partners. I say good luck to hi m. We will be pointing out a few double
standards, I guess, in the posit ion that National has taken ov er the issue of the seabed
and foreshore. That Minister should be very, very quiet. In fact there is an “h” word that
is a wonderful description of his position on many, many issues.
The National Government has to stand up and provide some plan, some real
aspiration, and some true c ontrol over our economy; otherw ise, the Prime Minister’s
claim that we need to own our future will be a fallacy, along with most of the other
policies and claims that the National Government has made while it has been in power.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: I remember in 2005
being at a meeting in Blackball with the member who has just spoken, Damien
O’Connor, prior to the election. I said I had written to the then National spokesperson
on finance, Mr John Key, and proposed that So lid Energy shares be made available for
West Coasters to buy. The member opposite will p robably remember the meeting. It
16574 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
was the one in which the Blackball people told him they were going to vote him out—
indeed, they did.

items.speaker: Hon Darren Hughes
items.text: Not that time.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Well, it did not take long. The member is quite right: he
lost only 5,500 votes at that time; he lost 3,800 the next time.
West Coasters have an affinity with mining. I know that members on the Opposition
side of the House do not like mining. I know they do not like success. The problem, of
course, for Solid Energy, as far as a Labour  Government goes, is that not only does
Solid Energy do mining but it does it succes sfully: $600 million, I think, comes from
the Stockton Plateau—$600 million. Indeed, So lid Energy is a community sponsor to a
great extent.
I was delighted when I heard the Prime Minister say he was looking at a proposal for
a partial sell-down in Solid Energy, Meri dian Energy, Genesis, and Mighty River
Power. Mixed ownership, a partial sell-down, and a guaranteed 51 percent Government
investment—it is a win-win-win. It wins fo r the families who can invest in proven
companies. What a wonderful opportunity that is. Why should New Zealanders be
denied that opportunity? Why should West Co asters be denied th at opportunity? The
companies get fresh capital. Jobs, security, and everything else gets better. The

items.speaker: Government reinvests in new assets
items.text: schools and hospitals—and health will determine
the outcome of the election on the West Coast. What is wrong with that? What is wrong
with those things?
What does Labour have a problem with? Wh y are there the pani cked headlines? It
was even in the paper today, I think. The list member opposite said the Government was
going to sell Landcorp. When will he lear n that people do not like to be panicked?
Indeed, the very people whom he is trying to impress will bite him where it hurts for
constantly crying wolf. Labour does not like mining, and it does not like success. Mr
Goff says he wants the Government to k eep the profits. Mr Goff would probably like
the Government to keep everything. Those members have not changed. What was it that
they used to say—the old socialist cry?  It was about controlling the systems of
production, distribution, and communication. The Labour members have not changed at
all. They certainly would love to keep controlling all of that.
We on this side of the House ask why we should not let hard-working Kiwis reap the
benefit from Kiwi companies: more capital and more assets. I am glad to report that
from the work we have done we find that that message has gone down well on the West
Coast, in spite of a Labour list member saying we would sell Landcorp and other things.
Again, that member needs to learn that constantly striving to cause panic—and there
have been a number of instances of that in the last few months—will only bring
criticism from those whom he tries to alar m. There is no risk of overseas ownership,
which is the other bogey that Labour puts up. A 51 percent Government shareholding is
guaranteed. Kiwi investors will  have a preference, be they  individuals or investors
through KiwiSaver. Air New Zealand has done well with mixed ownership—it has done
well—and will continue to do so.
Another factor has to be taken into acc ount, and it will be the clear difference
between the Government side of the House a nd the Opposition side of the House. It has
been mentioned by a number of speakers tonight, and I make no apology for repeating
it: debt. Debt, debt, debt—there are clear differences between National and Labour on
it. Goff is rushing to cause panic, yet he  promises to spend $5 billion—$5 billion—on
Labour’s promises. That would be a disastr ous policy. Those practices are not reflected
by business in New Zealand, and they are no t reflected by families in New Zealand.
Labour wants us to become like Portugal, Ireland, Spain, and Greece. We need to get
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16575
the books in order, and it is policies from the Government side of the House that will do
that.
Labour’s policy of promising that there would be more spending is irresponsible. It is
not designed for economic good; it is not desi gned for the country’s good. What, then,
is it designed for? It is the same stuff th at I have heard from successive Labour leaders
from Rowling onwards. It is what they trot out when they face electoral disaster. That is
what they will be facing this time, if they persist with this programme. If members do
not believe me, they should look at Sir Wa llace Rowling’s pre-election speech in 1975.
Goodness me! It was full of promises that c ould not be paid up. Some of them are
highly amusing. And here we go again, with Labour pursuing a polit ical strategy that
takes away our economic future and prospe rity for our children, for the sake of a
desperate grab for power by a leader with an  old team whose members know that this is
their last chance as individuals. It is a strategy that takes a risk with our future, simply to
secure an electorate respite for Labour.
What is the risk? A major risk  of not bringing our debt unde r control is the risk of a
credit downgrade from the international cred it rating agencies. Standard and Poor’s has
New Zealand on a negative outlook as we speak. The only countries with worse foreign
debt than New Zealand are Spain, Portuga l, Ireland, and Greece. Those are not the
economies that we should be comparing ourselves with. Foreign debt, a negative
outlook, and lower international credit ratings  may not be a concept that most people
will be familiar with. That is what Labour, frankly, is depending on. Labour knows the
very real risk that poses in relation to personal financial situations. With a credit
downgrade interest rates rise, increasing the cost of mortgages. That will hit everybody.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Everyone.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Everyone. Starting a business becomes harder. We should
not forget that business creates jobs.
I think of a young couple in Westport who have  scrimped and saved for a deposit for
their first house. A Labour-inspired credit downgrade might be what puts it out of reach.
I think of a solo mum in Motueka with a great business idea. A Labour-inspired credit
downgrade could be what makes it too hard for her to get a business loan. I think of an
employer in a small business in Greymouth who would face rising interest costs. A
Labour-inspired credit downgrade could mean downgrading his business and
redundancy for some of his staff.
These are not complex economic issues; they are basic, real situations for real people
around the country. There are people who need  economic leadership, which they will
get from this side of the House, not from  the prospect of a Labour Government taking
risks with everybody else’s future  in order to try to secure  its own. Those are the risks
that would be taken by a Government that embarks on a programme of increasing debt
at this crucial stage. It is no wonder that the members over there are ashamed. Those are
the risks that Phil Goff wants to take. Those are the risks that the National Government
will not take. New Zealand needs to have s ound financial leadership and management.
That is what it is getting from John Key and Bill English. They are charting the path.
For the last 2 years they have provided the economic leadership th at this country has
benefited from, and they will continue to do so.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: Ehara taku toa i te toa takitahi engari, he toa takitini
taku mana e. One’s strength is not purely a result of one’s own efforts but of the many
people who have helped along the way. This Government is committed to helping and
protecting the most vulnerable people in our  society and to creating an environment
where all New Zealanders can dare to dream our dreams, unlock the potential that lies
within us all, and achieve our goals and aspirations. Despite the Government having to
deal with the ongoing ripple effects of the wo rst global recession in seven decades, we
16576 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011
remain committed to building a brighter future for all New Zealanders and their
families.
We have insulated over 85,000 homes in New Zealand. Tens of thousands of New
Zealanders are living in healthier, warmer, and drier homes. Residents of Manurewa tell
me they feel safer in our community. In the course of this year we will be extending and
supporting our police in commun ities the length of New Zealand, with the provision of
more uniformed officers to protect th e vulnerable in our society. Neighbourhood
policing teams based in communities are helping young people to find jobs and go on
training courses, to divert them from involvement with gangs and a life of crime.
The Youth Guarantee scheme is providing pathways for young people in relation to a
host of skills. The innovative tertiary high school programme at the Manukau Institute
of Technology is providing a template for allowing year 11 pupils, who otherwise might
have chosen to leave education altogether, to  undergo flexible education with a mix of
secondary and tertiary subjects that interest and inspire them. They may be able to study
National Certificate of Educational Achievement level 1 English and level 1 maths, and
also do a study course in boatbuilding or automotive engineering. Those skills will
stand them in good stead in their future life and help them to become productive
members of our society.
Our health services are providing over 400  more elective procedures each week—
more hip operations, more cataract operations , more gall bladder operations. More New
Zealanders are receiving the health care that they need when they need it.
There are no simple, easy answers in this  economic climate, and we do not have a
magic wand. We cannot change things overn ight, but John Key’s principled, pragmatic
Government is putting in place the many buildi ng blocks necessary in order to lift New
Zealand’s economic performance and provide a better future for all New Zealanders. It
is only by lifting our economic performan ce and growing a bigger economic cake that
we can deliver the jobs, the higher incomes,  and the better living standards that New
Zealanders aspire to and deserve.
Our 2009 Budget concentrated on cushioning New Zealanders from the worst effects
of the recession. In last year’s Budget we concentrated on reforming the taxation
system. This year a likely dominant theme will be savings and investment. We realise
that just as a household that r uns up a bill at the corner sh op cannot continue to do so
forever, no country can run up bills forever. We have a proven track record of
responsible management of our economy, and we will continue to take a considered and
responsible approach to building a platform for sustainable future growth.
We have made considerable progress. Over  the last 12 months  we have introduced
the biggest tax reform in 25 years, tilting th e economy in order to encourage investment
and savings. We have improved public servic es by freeing up about $4 billion for front-
line services, by reducing back-office services  and ineffective programmes. We have
invested billions of dollars in  roads and have beg un the roll-out of ul tra-fast broadband,
which is a crucial development for the future prosperity of this country. We have started
New Zealand’s first public-private partne rships. We are focusing on improving
education in schools, with the development of national standards. We brought about the
amalgamation of eight councils into one in  Auckland, very successfully. We have a
considered, logical plan to grow our economy. We are delivering world-class
infrastructure to unblock the arteries of  the economy, and we are demanding better,
more efficient public services. We have in troduced a number of regulatory changes to
make it easier to do business, and we are fostering better skills in the workforce.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.

First Session, Forty-ninth Parliament, 2008-11 
 
 
 
 
Parliamentary Debates 
(HANSARD) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Tuesday, 8 February 2011 
(Week 64, Volume 670) 
 
 
 
 
WELLINGTON, NEW ZEALAND 
Published under the authority of the House of Representatives—2011 
 
 
 
TUESDAY, 8 FEBRUARY 2011 
TABLE OF CONTENTS 
 
DEBATE ON PRIME MINISTER’S STATEMENT ..........................................16495 
 
 
 
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16495 
TUESDAY, 8 FEBRUARY 2011 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
DEBATE ON PRIME MINISTER’S STATEMENT 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : I move, That this House express its 
confidence in the National-led Governme nt and commend its programme for 2011 as 
set out in the Prime Minister’s statement to Parliament . The year 2011 will be a very 
important year for New Zealand. For one thing, it will be the year that New Zealand 
hosts the Rugby World Cup 2011. Eighty-five thousand tourists from overseas will 
enjoy the finest of New Zealand. There will be a thousand events up and down the 
country, and, of course, the mighty All Bl acks will be on display on their home turf, 
trying to win the Rugby World Cup in 2011.  
The year 2011 is also likely to be a year in which the world grows at a faster clip 
than it has done in the last 3 years. It will be a year to cement in the structural changes 
that are so necessary for our economy. It will be a year in which we must continue to 
move from having a debt-fue lled, consumption-based economy to having one in which 
there are savings, investments, and exports. The year 2011 will be a year in which we 
must continue the rebuilding of the New Zealand economy—an economy that must be 
competitive. But maybe, most of all, 2011 has to be a year in which we do not write 
cheques that the New Zealand taxpayer cannot a fford to cash. It is a not a year for wild 
promises; it is a year for good, strong economics. There is no room for “pixienomics” in 
2011.  
The year 2011 will also be an important year for the families of the 29 men who lost 
their lives at the Pike River mine. It is a year in which they deserve to be given answers, 
and the royal commission will have good work to  do. It is a year in which we will start 
in earnest on the rebuilding of Canterbury after the devastating earthquake, and we will 
start the work on the 175,000 claims that have resulted from that earthquake. It is a year 
in which we will tackle some very long-term problems and some long-term issues, and 
in which will we turn round from the very expensive years of the previous Labour 
Government. The year 2011 will be a year in which we continue to work hard for the 
hard-fought gains between M āori and P ākehā. It is a year in which there needs to be 
hope and promise and aspiration. The year 2011 needs to be New Zealand’s year.  
There are some very positive signs. The global economy is starting to look much 
stronger, and we are seeing higher commodity prices: the Fonterra auction was up by 7 
percent just last week, lamb prices are star ting to rise, and wool prices are starting to 
rise. Of course, the Rugby World Cup is likely to have a big impact on the economy, 
and we will have the stimulus impact from  the earthquake rebuild ing work. That may 
well be the case, but we also n eed to lock in the trends that  we have seen in the last 2 
years of the National Government. Despite the fact that we inheri ted books that were a 
complete mess and despite the fact that we  had to contend with  the worst recession 
since the Great Depression, in th e 2 years that our Government  has been in office after-
tax wages have risen by 16 percent, while co sts rose by 6 percent. That is a 10 percent 
net gain in 2 years. I am ashamed to even  talk about Labour’s record, which was a 
miserable 4 percent gain over 9 long years.  
There are risks, of course, to the global economy. We have seen that in recent weeks, 
with the risk that there will be a great period of unsettledness in the Middle East. There 
are also risks, of course, in China if ther e is an asset bubble. There are risks around the 
global capital markets. We saw that last year with regard to Portugal, Greece, Spain, and 
Ireland. There is the risk that our exchange rate will continue to rise against a very weak 
16496 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011 
US economy. There is the risk—although on e would not know it was there, from 
listening to the Opposition—tha t comes from a rating agency like Standard and Poor’s, 
which has put New Zealand on negative outlook.  So the situation could be patchy, and 
there could be periods when it is a case of one step forward and half a step back, but 
overall this economy has to change from being one based on consumption and property 
to being one based on savings and exports.  
One of the first things the Government wi ll continue to work  on is getting its books 
back in order. Over the last 5 years of the previous Labour Government, spending 
increased by an average of $2.8 billion a year in every si ngle year. My Government has 
managed to pull that back to $1.1 billion a ye ar in the last 2 years. In Budget 2011 that 
increase is likely to be $800 million. The me ssage is pretty simple: we are going to 
spend less, we are going to borrow less, and we are going to take the pressure off the 
Reserve Bank and off New Zealand interest rate s. Any political part y that has not even 
got out of January before promising $5 bil lion worth of more expenditure, and that 
thinks this might help the New Zealand taxp ayer, is completely wrong. We have to get 
our books back in order. We cannot afford the decade of deficits that we inherited from 
the previous Labour Government.  
One of the places where we will be starting is  in relation to the Public Service. New 
Zealanders deserve to have be tter value and better service. We have started to work on 
that. In the 2 years that we have been in office we have reduced fulltime-equivalent staff 
in the State sector by 5 per cent. We have started the pr ocess of merging Government 
departments: Archives New Z ealand and the National Librar y have been merged into 
the Department of Internal Affairs, a nd the Ministry of Research, Science and 
Technology and the Foundation for Resear ch, Science and Technology have been 
merged into one new Ministry of Science and Innovation. But we have a long way to 
go. There are 80 Crown entities, all with their own boards; 38 Government departments; 
70 portfolios; and 60 separate Budget votes. We are, by international comparison, 
bloated and inefficient. So there has to be  change. We have put together a group of 
officials, asking for advice on how we can stre amline the Public Service. There will be 
core principles, and they are simple: we n eed to ensure that, in costing less, we 
ultimately deliver more to the taxpayers of  New Zealand. So a big focus of attention 
will be around the State sector.  
The second thing we need to do is to move towards having greater savings and 
investment. We cannot, as a country, continue to  have external liabi lities that are at 85 
percent of GDP. We cannot be in the same company as Portugal, Greece, Spain, and 
Ireland, and, if we are, we will know what that picture looks like. We are prepared to be 
responsible economic managers; the Labour Opposition, quite simply, is not. For that 
reason we will be looking at not only the operating budget but also the capital budget. 
Late last year we recognised that New Zeal and taxpayers have about $220 billion worth 
of assets. As a Government we want to ac quire $33 billion worth of new assets over the 
next 5 years. We have a number of options . One is to borrow more. That will not be 
acceptable to the rating agencies. The second op tion is to not build that infrastructure. 
That will not deliver us the jobs and the economy we want. The third option is to release 
some capital from assets that we already ow n. Through the course of this year we will 
be finalising our policy on mi xed-ownership models whereby we will be looking to 
control 51 percent of Meridi an Energy, Mighty River Po wer, Genesis, and Solid 
Energy.  
Let us understand the tests in those models. The first test is that the Crown will 
always, as a minimum, retain 51 percent contro l. The second thing is that we will be 
asking Treasury to provide advice to us on how  we can ensure Kiwi mums and dads are 
at the top of the list for buying any of the equity that we release, and that includes the  
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16497 
$1.6 million KiwiSaver accounts. It is interestin g that we as a Government want those 
$1.6 million KiwiSaver accounts and New Zealande rs to invest in our economy and in 
our future, and Labour wants them to invest in Australia. That is what Labour wants; 
Labour does not want to let them invest in New Zealand. We will ensure that the Crown 
financial institutes, the Accident Comp ensation Corporation, and the New Zealand 
Superannuation Fund invest in those kinds of assets, along with iwi.  
So Budget 2011 will have a focus on savings and investment, and it will take on 
board the information that we have received from the Savings Working Group. Again, 
the message is very simple: we need to ow n more of our own future, we need to fund 
more of our own upsides, and we need to have a stronger economy. Although the 
members on the Labour benches cannot add, th e issue is quite simple. When we own 
$220 billion of assets, we maybe release $8 bi llion to $10 billion of capital, and we buy 
another $33 billion of assets, we will end up owning more assets over 5 years, not 
fewer.  
The economy has to change and become a more export-led economy. We have to get 
away from the position we inherited from Labour, which was quite simple. It was a 
world where we bought more from the rest of the world than we sold to it. It was a 
world where, in 9 years, Labour created no new jobs in the export sector. 
Hon Phil Goff: Oh, rubbish! 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: It is not rubbish, actually. It was the period when Labour spent 
so wildly that interest rate s rose and the exchange rate rose. Maybe overall the way to 
test Labour’s commitment to exports is qui te simple: turn back the clock to 2007, and 
look at exports under Labour in that year. Labour did about 10 th ings, and do members 
know what happened? Exports fe ll in 2007. Why did exports fa ll? It was because in the 
end, if we want to have a competitive econom y we have to allow it the freedom to be 
competitive. We have to reform the Resource Management Act, we have to have a 
flexible labour market, and we have to be pr epared to build the infrastructure and invest 
in science and innovation.  
This year the Government will be focusing its attention on extending the free-trade

country the unique place it is, putting those on display a nd sharing them, and learning

lauded individual New Zealanders for demonstrating? Why in talking about our 
nationhood can we not show the spirit and i ndomitability that Hillary showed in 
conquering Everest? Why can we not show th e sense of innovation of Peter Jackson or

identity? Why can we not bring these strands together to say to all New Zealanders that 
these rem
arkable individuals, for instance, w hom we laud as being our great achievers,

Alongside the opportunities th at events like the Rugby World Cup 2011 and other

increase in core Government spending was $2.8 billion and we have tried to hold it to a

absolutely central part of moving away from debt-fuelled consumption. 
Secondly, we are trying to streamline the public services and although we will hear

Prime Minister and Mr English have so very clearly laid out. We will retain 51 percent

talks about electricity prices , we are reminded that the average annual increase in

Nothing has changed. The more houses there are on the market, the lower the price of

prices of the houses. That is because when there are plenty of houses to choose from 
and there are just a few buyers, house vendor s and people building houses have to drop

Government, particularly during those middl e years, were around 8, 9, and 10 percent,

went up because fewer houses were being built and more and more people wanted them.

difficult, no land was made available to bu ild the houses on, and in terest rates were 
high.

quite simple. I will go back to those initial principles. More people want to rent houses 
than there are houses available to rent. So what happens is that 10 houses are available 
to rent but 100 people want them, so the rents go up. Why are there fewer houses to

whether one is buying or renting, the fact is that in New Zealand we need to build more 
houses. The first way we will be able to do that  is simply to maintain interest rates at a 
level where people want to borrow to either build or buy. Maintaining interest rates at 6 
or 7 percent, which we have now, would be a good thing for New Zealand. John Key 
and Bill English have laid out their economic pl ans to make sure that we keep interest

16544 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011 
people to be prepared to build and to  buy. The second thing we can do—as we are

KEVIN HAGUE (Green): Of course I hung on every word  of the Prime Minister’s 
speech today, and what a disappointment it wa s to hear him utter no word about the 
environment or conservation. I have to say that last year it was similar, although we did

schedule 4 conservation lands and expropriating fresh water in Canterbury for further 
industry. I think his words were that any drop of water that reached the sea was 
wasted—such a profound understanding of th e New Zealand environment and ecology! 
So it was a disappointment to hear the Prime Minister’s speech, a disappointment that 
was only deepened, I am afraid to say, when Kate Wilkinson, the Minister of 
Conservation, got up to speak. She uttered no word in her speech about conservation, 
either. She may well have been under instruc tions not to show up the Prime Minister’s 
omissions, of course. 
Sandwiched between those two statements from the Prime Minister last year and this 
year we have been living through the International Year of Biodiversity. I guess the idea 
of that international year was to celeb rate the success of th e Rio Declaration on 
Environment and Development. But the way it has turned out in New Zealand and 
around the world has been more of a requiem fo r the thousands of species that we have 
lost and are still losing rapidl y. Lester Brown has talked abou t the crisis in biodiversity 
the world is going through as the “sixth gr eat extinction”. The last was some 65 million 
years ago when an asteroid hit the Earth. Th is one, of course, has been caused by the 
8 Feb 2011 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 16547 
actions of human beings. He calls it a “massive evolutionary se tback and a wholesale 
impoverishment of life on Earth.”  
New Zealand is a biodiversity hot spot and one of the world’s treasure chests of 
unusual and fascinating life forms. Our plants  and animals are utterly unique—they are 
not found anywhere else—and this is one of th e reasons that we love species like kiwi, 
kereru, kahawai, kauri, and all of the othe r species that we work hard to protect. 
Unfortunately, New Zealand also has a long record of extinctions. Many of our plants 
and animals remain now on the verge of extin ction. We have a special responsibility to 
protect the plants and animals that we love. The Department of Conservation has 
identified some 2,788 species in New Zealand as being under threat. That includes all of 
our frogs and bats, 89 percent of our reptiles, 65 percent of our freshwater fish, and 57 
percent of our birds. They could disappear for ever with in our lifetime. There are 
thousands more native species that we simply do not know enough about to know what 
their level of risk is.  
For over 100 years New Zealanders have been achieving some remarkable successes 
in conservation against this tide, but righ t now only 6 percent of  those threatened 
species identified as being at risk in New Zealand are actively managed to avoid 
extinction. The risk to the remaining 94 percent is acute. It is true that the Wildlife Act 
makes it an offence to intentionally kill  a native animal, and there are similar 
protections for some plants. But the major threats to our plants and animals are 
introduced predators, invasive weeds, and the ongoing loss and disruption of habitat. So 
far we have failed to respond effectively to even one of those factors.  
I have been in Parliament for only a shor t time, but I have already witnessed this 
Government taking major backward steps in the protection of these native plants and 
animals that we love. The most horrifying of  these was the Government’s step to cut 
$54 million from the Department of Conser vation’s budget over 4 years, which has 
massive implications. But that is not the only one. National has also cancelled the $4 
million Community Conservation Fund that the Green Party established, in conjunction 
with Labour, to fund community involvement  in local environmental conservation 
work. National has closed an important po ssum control research programme, based at 
Invermay, that was close to delivering new forms of possum control. National has failed 
to move decisively to protect the M ōkihinui River from Meri dian Energy’s proposed 
85-metre high dam. National has allowed commercial eeling of the endangered long-
finned eel, a species that is found nowhere else in the world and is listed by the 
Department of Conservation as a threatened species in gradual decline. That is the same 
status given to the great spotted kiwi, the little blue penguin, and the rifleman.  
The Government has issued a new busines s-focused statement of intent for the 
Department of Conservation, which has left  major questions around the Minister’s 
statutory responsibility to be the primar y advocate for the conservation estate. The 
statement of intent is entirely about commercial objectives for the department. The 
House is about to debate—probably next week—the Regulatory Responsibility Bill, 
which will tie the department’s hands even further when it comes to issuing businesses 
with concessions on the c onservation estate, with the department losing statutory 
responsibility to put the interests of our plants and animals first. At a time when New 
Zealand is facing arguably the greatest crisis  in biodiversity in the history of human 
habitation, one might have expected the Government’s priorities to emphasise a 
response to these problems, rather than pr eparing the conservation estate for greater 
exploitation and further losses.  
Green Party members set themselves up to be the champions for the environment, 
working alongside committed individuals and organisations right around the country, to 
try to turn this tide on biodiversity loss. One small practical measure has been to launch 
16548 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 8 Feb 2011 
the $4 million pilot project—in conjunction wi th the Government, which I recognise—
that aims to protect New Zealand forests a nd native species with be tter pest control, 
using resetting traps. If that project is successful, it will reduce the costs of pest control 
and the reliance on poisons. But the most significant work we are doing is yet to come. I 
am working on a new member’s bill to enhance the protection of our most treasured 
plants and animals. The United States, Canada, and Australia have all passed 
benchmark legislation to protect and secure their native flora and fa una, and the critical 
habitat that they rely upon. New Zealand, by comparison, lacks similar legislative 
protection.  
The Wildlife Act is antiquated and offers no effective legal protection against the 
biggest threats. Even our native fish are left  without legal protection, or a plan for their 
recovery. In the United States 85 percent of their threatened species are now covered by 
a recovery plan. In New Zealand the comparable figure is the 6 percent I mentioned. My 
bill will amend the Wildlife Act by revising  the purpose of the original Act to extend 
the legal protection to all native flora and fauna, including fish. The bill will give effect 
to the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development and the New Zealand 
Biodiversity Strategy. The Minister will be required to  develop and implement a 
thorough and science-based recovery plan for each of these native species that is 
identified as threatened.  
Like most New Zealanders, we in the Gr een Party love this country and all its 
people. Our environment and our natural heritage are what makes this country unique 
and precious. We are committed to doing whatever it takes to protect these features. It is 
important for its own sake, of course, but  also because so much of our economy, 
everything that we sell on the international stage, is dependent on that clean, green 
image. We set out to make that clean, gr een image real. No environment; no economy. 
If we trash the environment we sabotage our  economy and, more important, we rob our 
grandchildren of their birthright. It is another form of borrowing from our grandchildren 
to pay for short-term profit today, incurring a debt that neither this Government nor any 
Government ever will be able to repay.

same children will achieve lower earnings if indeed they are equipped to leave school 
without any substantial qualifications. Tragically, childhood poverty is associated with a 
higher risk of antisocial and criminal behaviour, which Mr Goff alluded to this 
afternoon.  
Taking the cycle of despair even further, it was pretty depressing to hear the views of 
my brother-in-law, Ruakere Hond, in Ta ranaki, who has been involved in M āori 
education since the 1980s. In an  article in the Taranaki ne wspaper he talked about the 
fact that a lot of unemployed M āori lacked motivation from being trapped in “a cyclic 
paradigm” that filtered down through older members of the wh ānau. In fact, he 
described this cycle as becoming “culturally ingrained in certain family groups”. Where 
does this come from? What can we do to address the seemingly intractable problems 
that lead to underachievement and under-parti cipation? It is not about just a poverty of 
income. It is also about a poverty of spirit, demonstrated in schools in which the culture 
of the school and the attitude and expect ations of teachers have been shown to 
contribute to their students’ disengagem
ent.  
There is a longstanding rec ognition that there is a cl ear disconnect between the 
majority of teachers and M āori students. We recall two separate surveys. One was

conducted by the New Zealand History Teach ers’ Association, a nd the other by the 
academic Richard Manning. They indicated that M āori content was often sidestepped, 
and this has had major educational and political implications for Māori.  
I come back to Mr Key’s view about good in tentions. I presume he  is talking about 
the Taha Māori programme of the 1970s, the various interventions, such as the bilingual 
units in general-stream schools, perhaps th e marae on school-grounds, Treaty clauses in 
the charter, and the like. They were a ll great, but they actually benefited P ākehā 
students more than th e target group of M āori. But what Russell Bishop of Waikato 
University has demonstrated so effectively is that recogni tion of our lan guage, culture, 
and identity is an essential part of the pathway to success for M āori. But the Māori edge 
is not just about having a M āori name or the school pupils being able to sing “T ūtira 
mai ngā iwi”. 
The M āori edge is to understand that whā nau are the critical factor to ensure 
achievement in education. Whānau, hapū, and iwi have a special role in making success 
happen. We call it whanaungatanga, where ev eryone who is involved with the people 
who care most about our students, their wh ānau, are welcomed at the door. It is about 
allowing Māori to have a space and providing  support, but still allowing M āori to have 
our own say and to take up models that work for us, like T ū Toa in Palmerston North. It 
is about celebrating Māori innovation and initiative.  
Politicians on both sides of the House have spoken about the im portance of literacy 
and numeracy programmes, and of our kids be ing able to speak well, count well, read 
well, and write well. What is new? That is  the same catchcry that New Zealanders from 
all ethnic backgrounds have been calling for since the missionaries arrived with their 
pencils and slates.  
But literacy and numeracy on their own are but one part of the solution. If we really 
want to make a difference for M āori education, we must understand that M āori 
solutions are required. The M āori Party has talked about cultural competency. We have 
called for responses that reflect M āori aspirations for edu cation—aspirations that 
inevitably include the social, political, economic, and cultural sustainability of Māori as

incorporating M āori knowledge, culture, and perspec tives inside and outside of the 
curriculum. Ultimately, it is about Wh ānau Ora. This is fundamentally what Tariana 
intended would happen with Whā nau Ora—that the education sector would take on the 
challenge of working with whānau.  
Although we could easily identify the succes s factors inherent in kura kaupapa 
Māori, we must as a nation a pply those same conditions for success in the mainstream 
school system. In my electorate of Waiariki, for example, M āori children comprise 
approximately three-quarters of the school  role in the areas of Kawerau and Ōpōtiki. 
What about them? A revolution is not impossi ble. The results of Te Kotahitanga show 
us that the academic engagement of Mā ori students dramatically improved. Their 
completion levels of work increase d, there were higher levels of M āori student 
attendance, and short-term achievement rose.  
The State, principals, teachers, and, for their part, whānau need to be held to account. 
Whānau must play their part, bu t it is also about time the education sector was put on 
notice, too. They are paid to do the job. Fift y percent - plus of M āori boys leaving 
school without qualifications is just not good enough; in fact, it is a disgrace. We have 
to invest in the success that is the M āori edge that the M āori Party is pursuing. We are 
determined to make a difference to achieve the change that our nation needs. We will do 
it, but not just for the 15,000 M āori children who started school last week but for the 
future of all descendants who will carve out a future for Aotearoa. Tēnā tātou.

Zealanders aspire to and deserve.  
Our 2009 Budget concentrated on cushioning New Zealanders from the worst effects 
of the recession. In last year’s Budget we concentrated on reforming the taxation 
system. This year a likely dominant theme will be savings and investment. We realise 
that just as a household that r uns up a bill at the corner sh op cannot continue to do so 
forever, no country can run up bills forever. We have a proven track record of 
responsible management of our economy, and we will continue to take a considered and 
responsible approach to building a platform for sustainable future growth.  
We have made considerable progress. Over  the last 12 months  we have introduced 
the biggest tax reform in 25 years, tilting th e economy in order to encourage investment 
and savings. We have improved public servic es by freeing up about $4 billion for front-
line services, by reducing back-office services  and ineffective programmes. We have 
invested billions of dollars in  roads and have beg un the roll-out of ul tra-fast broadband, 
which is a crucial development for the future prosperity of this country. We have started 
New Zealand’s first public-private partne rships. We are focusing on improving 
education in schools, with the development of national standards. We brought about the 
amalgamation of eight councils into one in  Auckland, very successfully. We have a 
considered, logical plan to grow our economy. We are delivering world-class 
infrastructure to unblock the arteries of  the economy, and we are demanding better, 
more efficient public services. We have in troduced a number of regulatory changes to 
make it easier to do business, and we are fostering better skills in the workforce.
